findings: Only 8% of firms, even in advanced economies, report having deliberately adopted AI, despite widespread informal/incidental use. High-income countries host 86% of the world's top-500 supercomputers and 77% of data-center capacity, while fewer than 5% of people in low-income countries have basic digital skills versus 66% in high-income countries. Middle-income countries are nonetheless emerging as major GenAI users, generating over 40% of ChatGPT's global traffic by mid-2025.
magnitude: High-income countries hold 86% of top-500 supercomputers; under 5% of low-income-country populations have basic digital skills

design: nationally representative demand-side household survey with new digital-connectivity module
title: The Global Findex Database 2025: Connectivity and Financial Inclusion in the Digital Economy
data: Global Findex household survey plus the new Digital Connectivity Tracker measuring mobile-phone ownership and internet use alongside financial inclusion
findings: Introduces the first globally comparable demand-side Digital Connectivity Tracker, jointly measuring mobile-phone ownership, internet use, and financial-account access. Finds mobile money continues to expand access to formal financial services, with over 80% of adults worldwide now holding a formal financial account, though gender gaps in both account ownership and mobile connectivity persist, and roughly 1.6 billion adults remain unbanked or poorly served.
magnitude: Over 80% of adults worldwide now hold a formal financial account, per the new Findex Digital Connectivity Tracker

design: Harmonized household/labor-force survey analysis combined with task-exposure scoring
authors: World Bank Group, International Labour Organization
title: Buffer or Bottleneck? Employment Exposure to Generative AI and the Digital Divide in Latin America (Quantifying the Jobs Potential of AI in Latin America and the Caribbean)
venue: World Bank / ILO joint policy report
data: Harmonized household and labor-force surveys across LAC countries combined with task-exposure scoring, adjusted for slower technology-adoption speeds in developing economies
findings: 30-40% of jobs in Latin America and the Caribbean are exposed in some way to generative AI, but only 2-5% are at risk of automation, while 8-12% could see productivity gains. Women workers are twice as likely as men to be in jobs at risk of automation, and up to half of exposed workers (about 17 million jobs) lack the digital infrastructure needed to benefit; exposed jobs are disproportionately held by younger, educated, urban workers.
magnitude: 30-40% of LAC jobs exposed to generative AI; only 2-5% at automation risk; women 2x more likely to face automation risk

design: Bottom-up engineering-economic model of the US AI server fleet, 2024-2030, with net-zero pathway scenarios
authors: Xiao, T., Nerini, F.F., Matthews, H.D., Tavoni, M., You, F.
title: Environmental Impact and Net-Zero Pathways for Sustainable Artificial Intelligence Servers in the USA
data: Bottom-up life-cycle model of US AI server deployment combined with regional grid-emissions and water-stress data
findings: Under projected growth, US AI servers could generate an annual water footprint of 731-1,125 million cubic meters and 24-44 megatons of additional CO2-equivalent emissions per year by 2030. The AI server industry is judged unlikely to hit net-zero-by-2030 targets without heavy reliance on uncertain carbon-offset and water-restoration mechanisms, though best-practice efficiency measures could cut emissions by up to 73% and water use by up to 86%, especially if sited using clean Midwestern US power.
magnitude: US AI servers could emit 24-44 megatons CO2e and use 731-1,125 million m3 of water annually by 2030; best practices could cut these 73%/86%

design: Three encouragement-design field experiments with randomized Copilot adoption incentives
authors: Zheyuan (Kevin) Cui, Mert Demirer, Sonia Jaffe, Leon Musolff, Sida Peng, Tobias Salz
title: The Effects of Generative AI on High-Skilled Work: Evidence from Three Field Experiments with Software Developers
countries: United States and multinational (Microsoft, Accenture, Fortune 100 firm)
data: Randomized encouragement to adopt GitHub Copilot among 4,867 developers across three firms (Microsoft: 1,663; Accenture: 311; Fortune 100 company: 3,054)
findings: Pooling data across all three firms and 4,867 developers, Copilot access increased completed tasks by 26.08% (SE 10.3%). Less-experienced developers adopted the tool at higher rates and realized larger productivity gains than more senior developers, consistent with AI substituting for missing experience.
magnitude: 26.1% increase in completed tasks pooling three field experiments (4,867 developers)

design: Staggered rollout
findings: Show that the improvement in information dissemination due to the introduction of 4G leads to an increase in productivity, fertilizer consumption, and credit uptake. The identification strategy exploiting the staggered state-level introduction of Rights of Way (RoW) policies meant to promote the growth of telecom infrastructure echoes similar results. The paper finds that six years after the introduction of 4G internet, the annual income of agricultural households grew by 14.5%. Using detailed farmer-level internet-browsing data, the paper shows that the introduction of 4G is related to internet adoption and acquiring agri-related information.

design: Legal/policy analysis (non-empirical review of space law, telecom law, and internet governance)
title: Equitable access to satellite broadband services: Challenges and opportunities for developing countries
data: Legal/regulatory review of outer-space law, telecommunications law, and internet-governance frameworks as applied to LEO satellite broadband (e.g., Starlink, OneWeb)
findings: Argues that existing international frameworks (space law, ITU spectrum/orbital-slot coordination, internet governance) do not adequately guarantee developing countries a voice in shaping norms for satellite broadband, even as LEO satellite constellations become increasingly central to closing rural/remote connectivity gaps. Calls for governance reform to ensure equitable, affordable access as satellite broadband scales globally.
magnitude: Non-quantitative legal/policy review; argues governance gaps could undermine equitable developing-country access to satellite broadband (Starlink-type constellations)

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Employed a theoretical macroeconomic multi-sector model to analyze the effects of artificial intelligence (AI) on sectoral and aggregate employment, output, and inflation. Using an industry exposure index, they found that AI adoption significantly increases output, consumption, and investment in both the short and long run. If AI's productivity boost is unanticipated, it initially leads to disinflation, which later turns into moderate inflation through increased demand. Conversely, if AI's productivity boost is anticipated, inflation rises immediately. The theoretical model underscores that AI's impact on output is twice as large when it affects sectors producing consumption goods rather than investment goods.

design: Large-scale worker survey linked to matched employer-employee administrative registers
title: The Adoption of ChatGPT (published as 'The Unequal Adoption of ChatGPT Exacerbates Existing Inequalities Among Workers')
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS); SSRN/NBER Summer Institute working paper
data: Survey of ~100,000 workers across 11 exposed occupations linked to Danish matched employer-employee administrative registers
findings: Half of workers in exposed occupations had used ChatGPT, but women were 16 percentage points less likely than men to have used it for work, and adoption skewed toward younger, less experienced, higher-achieving, male workers. Employer restrictions and lack of training were cited as key barriers despite workers perceiving large productivity potential. Adoption had minimal short-run effects on wages or hours, with precisely estimated null effects of less than 2% two years after ChatGPT's release.
magnitude: Women 16pp less likely than men to use ChatGPT at work; wage/hours effects <2% after two years

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: [India] Assam’s government embarked on a transformational journey using GovTech tools to overhaul its public finance management systems. By adopting digital platforms for budgeting, accounting, and procurement, Assam increased transparency and financial accountability across departments. The reforms are associated with improved service delivery and financial discipline.

design: Firm panel with novel AI-investment measure from resumes/job postings
authors: Babina, T., Fedyk, A., He, A.X., Hodson, J.
title: Artificial Intelligence, Firm Growth, and Product Innovation
data: Cognism resume data (~64% of US workforce) and Burning Glass job postings (180 million vacancies) merged to firm financials
findings: Firms with larger AI-oriented hiring show significantly higher subsequent growth in sales, employment, and market valuations than otherwise-similar peers, with the growth channel running mainly through increased product innovation (new patents and product announcements) rather than cost-cutting. AI-driven growth is concentrated among already-large firms and is associated with rising industry sales concentration. Firms with higher initial shares of STEM and highly-educated workers invest more in AI, reinforcing skill-biased effects.
magnitude: AI investment predicts higher firm growth via product innovation, concentrated among large firms and linked to rising industry concentration

design: Difference-in-differences (3-wave household panel x mobile-operator 3G/4G rollout)
authors: Bahia, Castells, Cruz, Masaki, Pedros, Pfutze, Rodriguez-Castelan, and Winkler
title: The Welfare Effects of Mobile Broadband Internet: Evidence from Nigeria
data: Three waves of the nationally representative Nigeria General Household Survey panel plus mobile-operator data on 3G/4G coverage rollout
findings: Mobile broadband coverage increases total household consumption by more than 10%, with the gain growing over time at a decreasing rate; effects are driven mainly by rising labor force participation and employment, especially among women, large enough to explain the consumption increase and associated poverty decline. Rural households benefit through both higher food and non-food consumption.
magnitude: +10%+ household consumption from mobile broadband coverage, sufficient to explain the observed poverty reduction

design: Quasi-experimental evaluation (population-threshold targeting) of a state smartphone-distribution program, with an embedded RCT digital-literacy-training arm
authors: Barboni, Bhattacharya, Field, Moore, Pande, Rigol, Schaner, and Shukla
title: Hold the Phone: The Short- and Long-Run Impacts of Connecting Indian Women to Digital Technology
venue: Yale Economic Growth Center Discussion Paper No. 1109
data: 20,000+ household surveys across 13 districts evaluating the Sanchaar Kranti Yojana (SKY) program, which gave 2+ million free smartphones to women household heads plus built LTE towers and 1GB free data; a sub-sample was randomized into group-based digital-literacy training
findings: SKY initially reverses the gender gap in smartphone ownership, but within about five years many women lose ownership/use as men appropriate the household phone, so gains in ownership, information access, and local economic activity are not durable. A low-cost digital-literacy training add-on, however, has lasting effects, increasing women's smartphone use and improving their mental health.
magnitude: Free-smartphone-plus-towers program reverses the gender gap short-run but fades within ~5 years; low-cost digital-literacy training has durable effects on women's phone use and mental health

design: Firm-level panel analysis of cloud service adoption and long-run size growth rates
title: Scaling up to the cloud: Cloud technology use and growth rates in small and large firms
data: French firm-level panel data on cloud service adoption and firm size/growth
findings: Cloud service adoption positively affects the long-run size growth rate of French firms, with smaller firms benefiting substantially more than larger firms. The authors interpret this as evidence that cloud technologies reduce barriers to digitalization that disproportionately constrain smaller enterprises, in contrast to much of the broader ICT literature where technology adoption tends to favor larger incumbents.
magnitude: Cloud adoption raises long-run firm growth rates in France, with smaller firms gaining disproportionately more than larger firms

design: Nationally representative repeated cross-sectional survey of individuals and workers
authors: Bick, A., Blandin, A., Deming, D.J.
title: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI
data: Nationally representative surveys of US adults aged 18-64 on generative AI use at work and at home, through late 2024
findings: Found that 32 percent of men use generative AI at work, compared with just 23 percent of women. GenAI usage declines with age, from about 34 percent for workers under age 40 to 17 percent for workers age 50 or above. About 40 percent of workers with a bachelor’s degree or more use generative AI at work, compared with about 20 percent for those without a college degree. 46 percent of workers who majored in science, technology, engineering, or mathematics (STEM) use generative AI at work, compared with 40 percent for workers who majored in business, economics, or communication and 22 percent for all other majors, including liberal arts and humanities.
magnitude: 40% of US working-age adults use generative AI within about two years of ChatGPT's release, faster adoption than PCs or the internet

design: Randomized experiment
findings: Randomized the placement of mobile towers enabling use of mobile phones across rural locations in the Philippines. The share of households in treated villages increased the probability of placing a call by 0.416 standard deviations. Annual household income for treated households increased by 17 percent relative to control group, household expenditure over the last week increased by 10 percent, income earned per household member while away over the last year increased by 43 percent. The benefits are especially large for self-employed and those who migrate for work.

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Analyze the adoption of AI by U.S. firms using data from the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS) covering September 2023 to February 2024. They find that an increase in AI usage from 3.7% to 5.4% among firms. AI adoption is higher in large firms and sectors like information, which reports an 18.1% usage rate. Common AI applications include marketing automation, virtual agents, and data analytics. Notably, firms using AI reported better overall performance and higher employment growth.

design: Theoretical Melitz-style heterogeneous-firm trade model with endogenous AI adoption
title: Heterogeneous Firms and AI Adoption
data: No empirical data; calibrated theoretical extension of the Melitz (2003) trade model with log-normal productivity distribution and stochastic AI-adoption gains
findings: The model shows that when AI adoption costs are high and productivity spillovers are limited, AI adoption produces pronounced endogenous market concentration, especially when adoption follows an exponential (self-reinforcing) rather than sigmoid trajectory. Uncertain implementation success amplifies competitive inequality among firms and can push markets from monopolistic competition toward oligopoly, with implications for trade patterns as AI-adopting firms gain disproportionate export capacity.
magnitude: Theoretical result: high AI adoption costs plus low spillovers endogenously push competitive markets toward oligopoly

design: Cross-sectional association
findings: Examine the impact of IT capabilities on productivity and innovation, noting traditional IT measures are outdated. They create new IT metrics based on demands for IT skills from 2010 to 2022. These metrics correlate strongly with official productivity measures, showing that a 1% increase in IT skills results in a 0.009% sales increase ($540,000). These metrics are positively associated with firm innovation, measured by the number of patents, citations, and the real value of patents.

design: Quasi-experimental
findings: Carlana and La Ferrara (2024) study the Tutoring Online Program (TOP), where: (i) tutoring is entirely online; (ii) tutors are volunteer university students, matched with underprivileged middle school students. The paper leverages random assignment to estimate effects during and after the pandemic (2020 and 2022), investigating channels of impact. Three hours of individual tutoring per week increased math performance by 0.23 SD in 2020 and 0.20 SD in 2022. Higher-dosage yielded stronger effects, while group tutoring smaller effects. TOP enhanced students’ aspirations, socio-emotional skills and psychological well-being, but only during school closures. We also estimate the impact of TOP on tutors, finding increases in empathy.

design: machine-learning estimation from social-media advertising audience data, validated against household surveys
authors: Casey Breen, Masoomali Fatehkia, Jiani Yan, Xinyi Zhao, Douglas R. Leasure, Ingmar Weber, Ridhi Kashyap
title: Mapping subnational gender gaps in internet and mobile adoption using social media data
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
data: Meta/Facebook advertising audience estimates calibrated against Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) and MICS benchmarks
findings: Develops and validates a method for estimating gender gaps in internet and mobile adoption at the subnational (region/district) level using social-media advertising data, revealing substantial within-country heterogeneity in the digital gender divide that is masked by the national-level averages used in most official statistics and by agencies like the ITU and GSMA.
magnitude: Reveals wide subnational variation in mobile/internet gender gaps that is invisible in national-level statistics

design: Composite cross-country index construction plus task-based AI exposure analysis
authors: Cazzaniga, M., Jaumotte, F., Li, L., Melina, G., Panton, A.J., Pizzinelli, C., Rockall, E., Tavares, M.M.
title: Gen-AI: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work
countries: 125-174 countries (AI Preparedness Index coverage varies by vintage)
data: Task-level occupational exposure measures combined with the new IMF AI Preparedness Index (digital infrastructure, human capital/labor policy, innovation/economic integration, regulation/ethics) across advanced, emerging, and low-income economies
findings: Roughly 60% of jobs in advanced economies are highly exposed to AI, compared with 42% in emerging markets and just 26% in low-income countries, reflecting low-income countries' more agrarian, less digitized job structures. Within exposed jobs, women and college-educated workers are more exposed but also better positioned to benefit; older workers are seen as less able to adapt. The Index shows Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries scoring less than half of North America's preparedness score, implying AI could widen, not narrow, the global income gap absent policy action.
magnitude: AI exposure hits 60% of jobs in advanced economies vs. 26% in low-income countries -- a readiness gap that could widen global inequality

design: Descriptive analysis
authors: Compute energy and water demand estimates
findings: The insatiable energy and cooling demand from compute can strain existing energy and water infrastructure and exacerbate environmental impacts if not managed properly. Training GPT-4 consumed 52,000 Megawatt hour of electricity, an amount that can power an average US home for 5,200 years. It is estimated that a single ChatGPT query consumes 15 times more energy than a Google search query. An International Energy Agency (IEA) report found that data centers consumed 460TWh electricity in 2022, a figure that could exceed 1,000 TWh by 2026. At present, data centers worldwide consume 1-2% of overall power, but this percentage will likely rise to 3-4% by the end of the decade. Along the way, the carbon dioxide emissions of data centers may more than double between 2022 and 2030. The training and application of these massive AI models also generates prodigious heat output that pose cooling challenges. A lot of water is used in cooling for the servers that run AI applications. Half a liter of water evaporates for each ChatGPT conversation of about 29-50 queries. As these generative AI tools are used billions of times every month, the water usage quickly adds up to enormous sums.
cite: Compute energy and water demand estimates (2024)

design: Difference-in-differences (staggered arrival of fibre-optic submarine cables)
title: High-Speed Internet, Financial Technology, and Banking
countries: Multi-country panel of African economies with submarine cable landings
data: Panel of 551 banks and 28,171 firms matched to submarine fiber-optic cable arrival dates across Africa
findings: D’Andrea and Limodio (2023) exploites the staggered arrival of fiber-optic submarine cables and show that high-speed internet promotes the role of banks and credit in Africa. Variation within country and across multicountry bank networks indicates that high-speed internet induced a 22% expansion in credit supply. The paper investigates the role of plummeting telecommunication costs in promoting the bank adoption of new financial technologies and study a specific technology used in the interbank market, the real-time gross settlement system (RTGS). It finds that upon connecting to high-speed internet, banks adopt the RTGS more extensively, reduce inside liquidity, and increase interbank transactions and lending. High-speed internet particularly strengthens firms in countries with weak preexisting interbank markets.
magnitude: +22% credit supply expansion after high-speed internet arrival; weak-interbank-user banks see -10% liquidity hoarding, +40% interbank transactions, +37% lending

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Some reports have found that large data centers use five million gallons of water per day, equivalent to the water use of a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people. And U.S. data centers consumed 183 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024, roughly 4% of the country’s total electricity consumption and approximately equal to the annual electricity demand of Pakistan. By 2030, that consumption is expected to more than double.

design: 2x2 randomized controlled trial: digital-skills training x job-referral guarantee
authors: David Atkin, Antoinette Schoar, Kiara Wahnschafft
title: Evaluating Sama's Digital Skills Training and Job Referral Programs for Youth in Nairobi, Kenya
data: 1,115 low-income youth aged 18-35 from underserved Nairobi communities who applied to Sama's digital-skills program
findings: Digital skills training combined with a job-referral guarantee raised monthly earnings by 37% relative to control (women gained 60%, men 26%) and cut unemployment by 10 percentage points; weekly hours worked rose 22% (5.7 hours). Training alone, without the referral, produced no significant gains in earnings or employment. The combined treatment also raised bank-account ownership by 10pp and savings by 58.8%, and helped sustain incomes through COVID-19.
magnitude: Digital-skills training plus job referral raised earnings 37%; training alone had a null effect on earnings

design: Conceptual/perspective essay synthesizing evidence on expertise and AI capability
title: Applying AI to Rebuild Middle Class Jobs
data: No new empirical dataset; synthesizes evidence on expert decision-making tasks and AI capabilities
findings: Argues that unlike earlier computerization, which favored elite experts and hollowed out middle-skill jobs, AI could extend the reach of non-elite workers into high-stakes expert decision-making tasks (medical care, document production, coding, teaching), potentially rebuilding middle-class job opportunities. Emphasizes this outcome depends on deliberate policy and firm choices to direct AI toward complementing rather than merely replacing workers.
magnitude: Conceptual framework: no single quantitative estimate; central claim is AI's potential to extend expert-level decision-making to non-elite workers

design: Historical job-title and patent-text analysis linked to Census occupational records, 1940-2018
authors: David Autor, Caroline Chin, Anna Salomons, Bryan Seegmiller
title: New Frontiers: The Origins and Content of New Work, 1940-2018
venue: Quarterly Journal of Economics (NBER Working Paper 30389)
data: Eight decades of new job-title data linked to US Census occupational records and patent texts distinguishing labor-augmenting from labor-automating innovation
findings: The majority of current US employment is in job specialties created after 1940. The locus of 'new work' shifted from middle-paid production/clerical jobs (1940-1980) to high-paid professional work and, secondarily, low-paid services (since 1980). New work emerges from augmenting innovations and rising occupational demand, while automating innovations suppress it; the demand-eroding effect of automation has intensified over the last four decades while the offsetting effect of augmentation has not kept pace.
magnitude: Majority of current US employment sits in post-1940 'new work'; automation's demand-eroding effect has outpaced augmentation's offsetting effect since 1980

design: Difference-in-differences
findings: Demirer et al. 2024 study how firms respond to privacy laws in the context of the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) by using seven years of confidential data from one of the world’s largest cloud-computing providers. The difference-in-difference estimates indicate that, in response to the GDPR, EU firms decreased data storage by 26% and processing by 15% relative to comparable US firms, becoming less “data-intensive.” To estimate the costs of the GDPR for production, the authors propose and estimate an “information” production function framework where data and computation serve as inputs to production. The paper finds that data and computation are strong complements in production and that firm responses are consistent with the GDPR representing a 20% increase in the cost of data on average, with smaller firms bearing higher cost increases than larger ones. The production cost of information increased by 4% on average, with higher costs in more data-intensive industries.

design: Quasi-experimental
findings: Studies the causal impact of GenAI on writers’ creativity. It finds that access to GenAI causes stories to be more creative, better written, and more enjoyable, especially among less creative writers. However, GenAI-enabled stories are more similar to each other than stories by humans alone. These results point to an increase in individual creativity at the risk of losing collective novelty. This dynamic resembles a social dilemma: with GenAI, individual writers are better off, but collectively a narrower scope of novel content may be produced.

design: Randomized experiment
findings: Studies the role of technology to improve tax capacity in the developing world. They focus on local property taxation in Ghana, a potentially significant but under-collected source of revenue. The paper randomizes the use of a new technology designed to help revenue collectors locate property owners to deliver tax bills, which is a major challenge in many developing countries with incomplete property addressing. The paper finds that the technology increases bill deliveries by 27 percent and, surprisingly, increases tax collections by 103 percent.

design: nationally representative household ICT-use survey, disability-status comparison
title: The divide between us: internet access among people with and without disabilities in the post-pandemic era
region: New Zealand (based on the authors' World Internet Project survey program)
data: Nationally representative household internet-use survey comparing respondents with and without disabilities
findings: People with disabilities report consistently lower rates of internet access and are less likely to have fast/reliable broadband connections than people without disabilities, even in the post-pandemic period when overall connectivity rose. The authors document a persistent 'disability broadband divide' in both access and connection quality, not just a gap in basic internet use.
magnitude: People with disabilities report lower home internet access and slower connections than non-disabled people, even post-pandemic

design: Difference-in-differences, Instrumental variables
findings: Examined the relationship between mobile broadband intensity and CO2 emissions using data from 181 countries between 2002 and 2020. Utilizing a difference-in-difference specification and an instrumental variable approach, the study found that while the initial introduction of mobile broadband is associated with an increase in CO2 emissions due to infrastructure investments and increased electricity consumption, a 10-percentage point increase in mobile broadband penetration leads to a 7% reduction in CO2 emissions per capita over time. This effect is significant only in high-income countries where mobile broadband penetration and speeds are higher.

design: randomized controlled trial of mobile-money loan repayment with varied spousal visibility
title: Resisting Social Pressure in the Household Using Mobile Money: Experimental Evidence on Microenterprise Investment in Uganda
data: Randomized microenterprise loan experiment varying whether loan disbursement/repayment ran through mobile money (private) versus cash (visible to household)
findings: Women who received business loans via mobile money rather than cash accumulated about 11% more business capital and earned about 15% higher business profits after 8 months, because mobile money let them shield resources from other household members' claims on their income. Effects were largest for women who reported facing the most pressure to share money with relatives at baseline.
magnitude: Mobile-money loan disbursement raised women's business capital by ~11% and profits by ~15% versus cash

design: Policy report synthesising industry capacity data with country case studies
title: Advancing cloud and data infrastructure markets: strategic directions for low- and middle-income countries
countries: Low- and middle-income countries, global comparison
data: Colocation and hyperscaler capacity inventories, cloud on-ramp mapping, data-centre energy and water statistics
findings: Quantifies a compute divide that rarely appears in the growth literature. Only 52 percent of low-income economies have access to a colocation data center, against 83 percent of high-income countries, and no low-income country has a direct cloud on-ramp to a hyperscaler, versus more than half of high-income countries. California alone has more data-center capacity than all of Sub-Saharan Africa. On the environmental side, data centers plus transmission networks account for roughly 1 percent of energy-related global greenhouse gas emissions, and global data-center workloads rose 340 percent between 2015 and 2022 while energy use rose only 20 to 70 percent thanks to efficiency gains. Fewer than a third of operators measure their water consumption.
magnitude: No low-income country has a direct cloud on-ramp, vs >50% of high-income countries; California exceeds all of Sub-Saharan Africa in capacity

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Goldbeck & Lindlacher (2024, unpublished) use variation in submarine cable arrival timing to show evidence of large effects of internet penetration on economic growth and productivity in Sub-Saharan Africa.

design: Quantitative trade model with firm-product learning-by-doing, plus systematic documentation of subsidy policy
authors: Goldberg, Juhász, Lane, Lo Forte and Thurk
title: Industrial policy in the global semiconductor sector
data: Global semiconductor firm-product output and trade data, catalogue of announced government subsidies since 2020
findings: The compute layer beneath AI is now the object of the largest industrial-policy push in decades, and this paper measures it. Governments have committed over $400 billion in semiconductor subsidies globally since 2020. The structural model finds real learning-by-doing at the firm-product level, economies of scope within firms, and substantial cross-border learning spillovers operating through foreign direct investment, joint ventures and licensing rather than incidental diffusion — which implies subsidy races transfer capability across borders more than their sponsors intend.
magnitude: Over $400 billion in government semiconductor subsidies committed globally since 2020

design: Industry descriptive statistics and forecasting report
title: The Mobile Economy: Sub-Saharan Africa 2024
data: Operator and household survey data on network coverage, device ownership, and mobile-internet usage across Sub-Saharan Africa
findings: Despite mobile broadband network coverage reaching the large majority of Sub-Saharan Africa's population, 65% of the population remains offline even though covered by mobile-internet signal -- a 'usage gap' driven by handset cost, data affordability, digital literacy, and relevant local-language content rather than by lack of network coverage. Global mobile coverage expanded to reach 40 million more people in 2024, and 75% of that growth occurred in Sub-Saharan Africa.
magnitude: 65% of Sub-Saharan Africa's population is offline despite being within mobile-internet coverage -- the usage gap now exceeds the coverage gap

design: Industry analysis/modeling of handset costs and financing options
title: Analysis to Improve Handset Affordability
venue: GSMA report (supporting the GSMA Handset Affordability Coalition)
countries: Cross-country, LMICs with a Sub-Saharan Africa emphasis
data: Analysis of handset retail prices, import taxes/VAT, and financing-scheme availability across LMICs
findings: Identifies device cost, not network coverage, as the binding constraint on mobile-internet adoption for a large share of the 'covered but unconnected' population, and models how tax removal, local assembly, and handset-financing/installment schemes could lower effective smartphone prices; underpins the GSMA Handset Affordability Coalition's call for governments to eliminate taxes on entry-level devices (e.g., those priced under $100).
magnitude: Frames device cost, rather than coverage, as the primary remaining barrier to closing the mobile-internet 'usage gap'; advocates removing taxes on sub-$100 handsets

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: In China, the mountainous province of Guizhou in Southwest has become a pioneer in China’s big data industry. Guizhou has 37 big data centers in operation or under construction as of early 2023, one of the cities with the biggest number of super large data centers globally. Data center investments have powered Guizhou’s digital economy development, achieving top growth rate in China for seven consecutive years since it became the big data pilot area in 2016. Data center investments also transformed the province’s industry structure. The software and ICT service sector’s contribution to local economic growth reached 45% in 2022 in Gui’an New Area and Guiyang, where the data centers are concentrated in.

design: School-level randomized controlled trial, WhatsApp-based AI math chatbot vs. standard instruction
authors: Henkel, O., Horne-Robinson, H., Kozhakhmetova, N., Lee, A.
title: Effective and Scalable Math Support: Evidence on the Impact of an AI-Powered Chatbot on Math Achievement
data: ~1,000 students in grades 3-9 across 11 schools, randomized to two 30-minute weekly sessions with Rori (an AI-powered WhatsApp math tutor) plus regular instruction, or regular instruction alone
findings: The AI-tutored group showed a statistically significant math growth-score effect size of 0.37 (p<0.001) relative to control after one academic year. The tool was designed to run on low-bandwidth mobile networks, making it feasible in low-connectivity settings, though the authors caution these are first-year results requiring confirmation.
magnitude: 0.37 SD math achievement gain from a WhatsApp-based AI tutor over one school year in Ghana

design: Quasi-experimental
findings: Gave a random subset of medium-sized Liberian firms vouchers for a week-long program targeting equal-opportunity access to the input purchases of government, companies, and other organizations—a market that makes up upwards of 80 percent of global GDP. The program exclusively teaches “sellership”: how to navigate large buyers’ complex, formal sourcing procedures. Firms that participate win three times as many formal contracts a year later. The impact is heterogeneous: informational sales barriers bind for about a quarter of Liberian firms. Three years post-training, these firms continue to win desirable contracts, are more likely to operate, and employ more workers.

design: Institutional/macro-financial-stability analysis of systemic cyber risk
authors: International Monetary Fund (Monetary and Capital Markets Department)
title: Cyber Risk: A Growing Concern for Macrofinancial Stability (Chapter 3)
countries: Global, with emphasis on emerging market and developing economies
data: Global database of reported cyber incidents affecting financial institutions, cross-referenced with financial stability indicators
findings: The IMF concludes that cyber incidents affecting the financial sector have not yet been systemic, but the tail risk of extreme losses from a major cyber incident has increased materially. Financial institutions face exposure through loss of confidence, disruption of critical services, and spillovers to other institutions, and the report finds that cyber-risk policy frameworks remain generally inadequate, especially in emerging market and developing economies, warranting stronger supervisory and disclosure frameworks.
magnitude: Tail risk of extreme, potentially systemic losses from a major cyberattack on the financial sector has risen, with policy frameworks judged inadequate especially in developing economies

design: agency statistical compilation from national ICT household surveys
title: Facts and Figures 2024: Measuring Digital Development
data: National household ICT-use surveys aggregated by the ITU across member states
findings: An estimated 5.5 billion people (68% of the world's population) were using the internet in 2024, up 227 million from 2023, yet about 2.6 billion people -- roughly a third of the global population -- remained offline. Internet-use rates ranged from 87%-92% in Europe, the Americas, and the CIS to about 66%-70% in the Arab States and Asia-Pacific, underscoring persistent regional digital divides.
magnitude: 68% of the world's population was online in 2024, but 2.6 billion people remained offline

design: agency global statistical monitoring report
title: The Global E-waste Monitor 2024
data: National e-waste generation, collection, and recycling statistics compiled across UN member states
findings: A record 62 million tonnes (62 billion kg) of e-waste was generated globally in 2022, equivalent to 7.8 kg per capita, of which only 22.3% was documented as formally collected and recycled in an environmentally sound manner. E-waste generation is projected to rise to 82 million tonnes by 2030 while the documented formal recycling rate is projected to fall to 20%, meaning e-waste generation is growing about five times faster than documented recycling capacity.
magnitude: 62 million tonnes of e-waste generated in 2022; only 22.3% was formally recycled

design: critical methodological review of telecom-industry GHG-enablement claims
authors: Jan C. T. Bieser, Vlad C. Coroamă, Pernilla Bergmark, Matthias Stürmer
title: The greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction potential of ICT: A critical review of telecommunication companies' GHG enablement assessments
data: Review of telecom-operator and industry-association (e.g., GeSI SMARTer2030-style) 'enablement effect' GHG assessments, comparing methods against LCA best practice
findings: Finds widespread methodological flaws in industry claims that ICT services 'enable' emissions reductions elsewhere (e.g., videoconferencing substituting for travel), including ignoring rebound effects, using non-representative baselines, double counting, and asymmetric treatment of ICT's own footprint. Concludes that oft-cited claims the ICT sector abates several times its own emissions footprint (e.g., GeSI SMARTer2030's claim of enabling a 20% cut in global emissions by 2030) are not well supported by rigorous evidence.
magnitude: Finds industry 'GHG enablement' claims for ICT are systematically overstated and not methodologically robust

design: Event study / difference-in-differences on Amazon marketplace rankings around DMA compliance
title: Amazon Self-Preferencing in the Shadow of the Digital Markets Act
data: Amazon marketplace search-result rankings and Buy Box allocation data for Amazon's own private-label products versus third-party sellers, EU versus non-EU
findings: Examines whether Amazon altered its degree of self-preferencing of its own products in search rankings and the Buy Box in the EU in response to the DMA's gatekeeper obligations, providing evidence on how large digital platforms adjust ranking algorithms and default allocations when a competition regulation specifically targets self-preferencing conduct.
magnitude: Documents changes in Amazon's self-preferencing of its own-brand products in EU search rankings following DMA gatekeeper obligations

design: Randomized experiment
findings: Conducted a randomized control trial at the US Military Academy during the COVID-19 pandemic to compare online and in-person learning outcomes. The study finds that students in online sections experienced a 0.236 standard deviation decrease in final grades, which is approximately 1.65 percentage points lower than their in-person counterparts. The negative effects were most pronounced among students with below-median academic ability. Male students, those who attended preparatory school, and prior enlisted personnel showed larger learning deficits in the online format. The study attributes the decline in performance to reduced student engagement, concentration difficulties, and weaker student-instructor relationships.

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Unveils the real-time usage patterns of generative AI tools by individuals across countries. As of March 2024, the top 40 generative artificial intelligence tools attract nearly 3 billion visits per month from hundreds of millions of users. Generative artificial intelligence users skew young, highly educated, and male, particularly for video generation tools, with usage patterns strongly indicating productivity-related activities. Middle-income economies have disproportionately high adoption of generative AI relative to their economic scale, accounting for over 50% of GenAI global traffic. Income level, share of youth population, digital infrastructure, specialization in high-skill tradable services, English proficiency, and human capital contribute to higher generative AI uptake. The paper also documents disruptions in online traffic patterns and emphasizes the need for targeted investments in digital infrastructure and skills development to harness the full potential of artificial intelligence.

design: Cross-sectional association
findings: Employ a Structural Equation Modelling to analyze the relationship between ICT development (digital skills being a part of ICT development) and GDP growth using data from the Digital Economy and Society Index, EUROSTAT, and OECD between 2017 to 2022. They find a positive correlation between ICT advancements and GDP growth, highlighting the significant role of human capital (digital skills as a part of human capital, includes basic and advanced digital competencies necessary for effective ICT utilization), e-government, and the integration of digital technology as key factors. The study reports a path coefficient of 0.361, indicating a statistically significant positive relationship.

design: Cross-country panel econometrics linking a data-regulation restrictiveness index to downstream digital-services trade
authors: Martina Francesca Ferracane, Erik van der Marel
title: Governing Personal Data and Trade in Digital Services
countries: Cross-country panel (includes World Bank Digital Services Trade Restrictiveness Index countries)
period: Recent cross-country regulatory and trade data
data: A cross-country index of personal-data regulation stringency (drawing on the World Bank's Digital Trade/Data regulation database) matched to bilateral digital-services trade flows
findings: Building on the authors' related World Bank policy research (Ferracane & van der Marel 2021, "Regulating Personal Data: Data Models and Digital Services Trade"), the paper establishes an econometric link between the stringency of a country's personal-data regulatory regime and the performance of its data-reliant downstream service industries, showing that more restrictive data-governance models (e.g., stricter localization or cross-border transfer conditions) are associated with reduced digital-services trade competitiveness for data-dependent sectors.
magnitude: Countries with more restrictive personal-data regulatory regimes show systematically weaker digital-services trade performance in data-reliant sectors

design: Occupational transition-matrix analysis by AI exposure/complementarity category
authors: Mauro Cazzaniga, Carlo Pizzinelli, Emma Rockall, Marina Mendes Tavares
title: Exposure to Artificial Intelligence and Occupational Mobility: A Cross-Country Analysis
data: Worker-level occupational transition histories in Brazil and the UK, classified by AI exposure and human-AI complementarity
findings: In both Brazil and the UK, college-educated workers frequently transition from high-exposure/low-complementarity occupations into high-exposure/high-complementarity occupations, a pattern especially common among young college-educated workers and associated with wage gains. The authors warn AI-driven structural change could simultaneously expand career-progression opportunities for some young workers while disrupting others by removing traditional stepping-stone jobs.
magnitude: Young college-educated workers disproportionately move from low- to high-complementarity AI-exposed jobs, with associated wage gains

design: Nationally representative firm census/survey (Annual Business Survey)
title: AI Adoption in America: Who, What, and Where
venue: NBER Working Paper 31788 / Journal of Economics & Management Strategy
data: 2018 Annual Business Survey (Census Bureau/NCSES), 447,000 responses linked to the Longitudinal Business Database, weighted to represent over 4 million firms
findings: Fewer than 6% of firms (unweighted) reported using any of five AI-related technologies (machine learning, machine vision, NLP, voice recognition, automated-guided vehicles) in production, but employment-weighted adoption was just over 18%, since large firms adopt disproportionately. AI use appears in every sector but clusters geographically and clusters with adoption of cloud computing and robotics.
magnitude: Under 6% of US firms use AI in production, but 18% of employment is at an AI-using firm

design: Staggered rollout
findings: Investigates how the arrival of high-speed internet in Africa triggered FDI into the region. It also explores the role of complementary infrastructure, such as access to electricity and road connectivity, in amplifying the impact of internet connectivity on investment. To causally estimate impacts, the paper exploits plausibly exogenous variations in access to high-speed internet induced by the staggered arrival of submarine fiber-optic internet cables and spatial variations in terrestrial fiber cable networks across locations on the continent. Findings from the paper indicate that access to high-speed internet induces FDI, the probability of receiving FDI increases by about 6.3 percentage points. Also, the arrival of high-speed internet is associated with an increase in the number and size of FDI receipts by 10.5 percent and 33.4 percent, particularly in the service sector, with the finance, technology, retail, and health services subsectors as the main beneficiaries. Access to (hard) infrastructure, such as electricity and roads, amplifies the impact of internet connectivity on FDI, thus highlighting the role of complementarities in the impact of infrastructure. Further, the results suggest that improvement in quality of governance and increased performance of incumbent firms are plausible mechanisms.

design: Descriptive analysis
authors: MIT Press Reader / data-center energy estimate
findings: Cloud data centers, essential for modern digital infrastructure, are energy-intensive, A single data center can consume the equivalent electricity of 50,000 homes and producing a greater carbon footprint than the airline industry. (Source: MIT Press)
cite: MIT Press Reader / data-center energy estimate (2024)

design: Quasi-experimental
findings: Moritz Moller et al. (2024) present first evidence that generative AI can increase the speed of learning substantially in university students. The paper tested whether using the AI-powered teaching assistant Syntea affected the speed of learning of hundreds of distance learning students across more than 40 courses at the IU International University of Applied Sciences. The analysis suggests that using Syntea reduced their study time substantially—by about 27% on average—in the third month after the release of Syntea. Taken together, the magnitude of the effect and the scalability of the approach implicate generative AI as a key lever to significantly improve and accelerate learning by personalization.

design: Randomized field experiment (GPT-4 WhatsApp business mentor vs. standard guide control)
authors: Nicholas G. Otis, Rowan Clarke, Solène Delecourt, David Holtz and Rembrand Koning
title: The Uneven Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Entrepreneurial Performance: Evidence from a Field Experiment in Kenya
venue: Management Science (published online July 2026); earlier Harvard Business School Working Paper 24-042
data: 640 Kenyan micro/small business owners randomized to a standard business guide (control) or a GPT-4-powered AI business mentor delivered via WhatsApp
findings: Field experiment randomizing Kenyan entrepreneurs to a GPT-4-powered AI business assistant on WhatsApp or a standard business guide. The average effect on revenues and profits is not statistically distinguishable from zero, but the effect for entrepreneurs who were low performing at baseline is over 0.20 standard deviations lower than for high performers: in subsample analyses, low performers did nearly 10% worse because of the AI assistant, while high performers may have gained over 15%. The gap does not appear to come from the questions entrepreneurs asked or the advice the AI gave, but from which advice they chose to implement.
magnitude: No detectable average effect; low performers nearly 10% worse and high performers over 15% better (a gap of over 0.20 standard deviations)

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: [Nigeria] pioneered the use of digital platforms to foster participatory budgeting and project monitoring, enhancing trust between citizens and the government. Through initiatives like the Eyes and Ears App and the Citizens Feedback Platform, residents could report issues and suggest improvements.

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Data centers can drive local economic development, create jobs, catalyze structural transformation, and boost tax revenues. Northen Virginia, the densely populated suburbs located just outside the US capital, is home to 70% of the world’s data centers. A government report in 2020 estimated that the data center industry in Virginia created nearly 15,000 direct jobs with an average annual pay of US$126,000, US$1.9 billion in associated pay and benefits, and $4.5 billion in economic output in 2018 alone. Taking into account the economic ripple effects generated by direct investment generated, the job creation amounts to more than 45,000, with US$3.5 billion in associated pay and benefits, and US$10.1 billion in economic output. Moreover, data centers generated US$600.1 million in state and local tax revenue. Each direct job in the data center industry helps to create 7.4 indirect jobs on average throughout the US economy.

design: Cross-country direct skills assessment of adults (household survey with cognitive testing)
title: Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC), Cycle 2 Results
data: Direct assessment of literacy, numeracy, and adaptive problem-solving in technology-rich environments among representative samples of adults aged 16-65
findings: The second PIAAC cycle assesses adults' proficiency in technology-rich problem solving alongside literacy and numeracy; OECD's companion 'Going Digital' indicators track the share of adults reaching the highest adaptive problem-solving proficiency levels. Results reveal wide cross-country variation in digital-era skills, with direct implications for how much of the workforce can benefit from technology adoption without further training.
magnitude: Cross-country PIAAC Cycle 2 (2022-23 fieldwork) reveals large, persistent gaps in adults' technology-rich problem-solving proficiency

design: Cross-country occupation-level panel using an AIOE-style exposure measure
title: Artificial Intelligence and Wage Inequality
data: Occupation-level wage and AI-exposure panel for 19 OECD countries, 2014-2018, using a Felten-Raj-Seamans-style exposure measure
findings: No evidence that AI affected wage inequality between occupations over 2014-2018. However, within-occupation wage inequality declined more in occupations most exposed to AI (e.g., business, legal, and science/engineering professionals, managers), consistent with AI narrowing productivity differences between higher- and lower-performing workers doing the same job.
magnitude: No between-occupation wage-inequality effect 2014-18; within-occupation inequality fell more in high-AI-exposure occupations

design: Literature review and synthesis of tax-technology evaluations
title: How Can Lower-Income Countries Collect More Taxes? The Role of Technology, Tax Agents, and Politics
countries: Multi-country synthesis (incl. Ethiopia, Tajikistan, Rwanda, DRC, Senegal)
data: Synthesis of experimental/quasi-experimental studies on tax administration technology and tax-agent incentives
findings: Reviewing recent rigorous evidence, the authors show digitization (e-filing, electronic sales registers, third-party data matching) raises revenue and compliance most when paired with reforms to tax-agent incentives and political will; for example, Ethiopian firms adopting electronic sales-register machines saw a robust increase in VAT collections and reported sales. Technology alone, absent complementary institutional reforms, delivers smaller and less durable gains.
magnitude: Synthesizes evidence that digital tax tools raise revenue mainly when paired with tax-agent and political reforms

design: RCT: 152 women's microfinance groups randomly switched to repaying loans by mobile money instead of cash
title: Digital Financial Services and Women's Empowerment in Tanzania
data: 152 female microfinance groups in Tanzania; surveys and an incentivised money-control game
findings: Randomly switching women's microfinance groups from cash to mobile-money loan repayment (66% take-up in the treatment group) raised women's use of mobile money for other transactions by 0.33 standard deviations. Women's control over their finances rose by 0.37 standard deviations and their involvement in household decision-making by 0.22 standard deviations, and spending shifted towards goods plausibly aligned with their preferences — evidence that increasing use of digital financial services, not just account ownership, strengthens women's position in the household.
magnitude: +0.37 SD control over finances and +0.22 SD household decision-making from mobile-money loan repayment

design: Cross-country panel regression of cloud adoption and broadband penetration on sectoral economic outcomes across OECD countries (AWS-funded study)
title: Economic spillovers from cloud computing: evidence from OECD countries
venue: Information Technology for Development, Vol. 30(1), pp. 173-194
data: Cross-country panel of cloud adoption rates, broadband penetration, and sectoral GDP contribution across OECD countries
findings: Estimate the impact of cloud computing on economic performance. The paper uses a multi-equation model in which cloud computing is complementary with broadband to maximize the economic contribution of digital technologies. The paper found that for an average OECD country, an increase of 1% in firm cloud penetration will result in 0.31% increase in labor productivity, while the effect on TFP will range between 0.22% (TFP-FE) and 0.18% (TFP-OP). However, the impact of cloud computing depends on broadband penetration and cloud adoption, which, as expected, vary by country and industry. The sector benefitting from the largest economic impact is information and communications, followed by manufacturing, while in contrast, no impact was detected for the transportation sector.
magnitude: Cloud spillovers are largest in the information/communications sector, with OECD-wide cloud adoption surpassing 50% by 2024 (AWS-funded study)

design: NLP/computational linguistics on earnings calls to construct firm-level cyber-risk exposure measure; predictive panel regressions
authors: Rustam Jamilov, Hélène Rey, Ahmed Tahoun
title: The Anatomy of Cyber Risk
data: Computational linguistics analysis of quarterly earnings-call transcripts for over 14,000 firms in more than 90 countries, validated with human auditors and large language models against actual cyberattack incidents
findings: The novel cyber-risk exposure measure affects stock returns and profits, is priced in the options market, and predicts actual future cyberattacks at the firm level. Cyber risk propagates from individual firms to their sector and across firms in a network pattern. The authors estimate the global cost of cyber risk exposure at hundreds of billions of dollars annually.
magnitude: Global cyber-risk exposure estimated to cost hundreds of billions of dollars annually across 14,000+ firms in 90+ countries

design: Difference-in-differences using firm-level web analytics (page views, e-commerce revenue) around GDPR enforcement
authors: Samuel G. Goldberg, Garrett A. Johnson, Scott K. Shriver
title: Regulating Privacy Online: An Economic Evaluation of the GDPR
countries: European Union (EU users of sampled websites)
data: Adobe Analytics data for 1,084 websites, comparing EU user page views and e-commerce revenue before and after GDPR enforcement
findings: Following GDPR enforcement, EU website page views and website (e-commerce) revenue both fell by about 12% on average, with the effect concentrated among smaller firms, which lack the scale to implement compliance as efficiently as large incumbents. The paper decomposes the drop into changes in actual user behavior versus changes in how user activity is recorded (consent-related measurement effects).
magnitude: GDPR enforcement is associated with a roughly 12% decline in both EU website page views and e-commerce revenue, concentrated among smaller firms

design: Natural experiment: staggered rollout of subsidized debit cards to poor households, two-sided market analysis
title: Financial Technology Adoption: Network Externalities of Cashless Payments in Mexico
data: Administrative data on a government rollout of 1 million debit cards to poor households and merchant point-of-sale terminal adoption
findings: Government-distributed debit cards induced retailers to adopt point-of-sale terminals, which in turn generated a 21% increase in other (non-recipient) consumers' card adoption through network externalities. Small retailers that adopted terminals gained sales and profits, and wealthier consumers shifted about 13% of their supermarket spending toward these small retailers.
magnitude: Merchant terminal adoption triggered a 21% rise in card adoption among other consumers via network effects

design: Difference-in-differences exploiting pincode-level variation in exposure to early UPI-adopting banks
authors: Shashwat Alok, Pulak Ghosh, Nirupama Kulkarni, Manju Puri
title: Breaking Barriers to Financial Access: Cross-Platform Digital Payments and Credit Markets
data: Universe of consumer loans from TransUnion CIBIL merged with RBI bank-deposit data, SBI UPI transaction data, Jio 4G tower rollout data, and Jan Dhan Yojana account data
findings: A 1% increase in UPI transactions is associated with a 0.73% increase in credit; in high-UPI-exposure areas, aggregate credit rose 22% and new-to-credit lending -- driven entirely by fintechs, not banks -- grew 45-fold, with fintechs reaching 72-84% of the loan volume banks extended to marginal borrowers by 2019. Despite this expansion, default rates among new-to-credit borrowers were 5.3% lower, and effects were strongest where low-cost internet (Reliance Jio) and prior bank-account access (Jan Dhan Yojana) were both present.
magnitude: UPI-driven digital footprints grew fintech lending to new-to-credit borrowers 45-fold with no rise in defaults

design: System description and usage analytics from a deployed multi-country AI advisory service
authors: Singh, N., Wang'ombe, J., Nambi, A. et al. (Digital Green / Microsoft Research)
title: Farmer.Chat: Scaling AI-Powered Agricultural Services for Smallholder Farmers
data: Deployment analytics from a generative-AI agricultural chatbot covering over 15,000 farmers and 300,000+ queries across four countries
findings: Within 45 days of use, 57% of surveyed users reported an improved quality of life and 31% said the tool saved them time; the paper documents design solutions for multilingual dialogue, trust, and response quality in low-resource agricultural extension settings. This is an implementation/evaluation paper (usage analytics), not a randomized impact evaluation.
magnitude: 57% of Farmer.Chat users (of 15,000+ across 4 countries) reported improved quality of life within 45 days of use

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Data centers account for 1-1.5% of global electricity use. This high consumption contributes to increased greenhouse gas emissions from electricity generation, particularly if the energy sources are fossil fuels. The heat generated by servers requires substantial cooling, further increasing energy usage and emissions. Data centers, through their substantial energy use, are responsible for nearly 1% of energy related GHG emissions. (Source)

design: Quasi-natural experiment exploiting a UK capital-allowance tax incentive for IT investment, using matched employer-employee administrative data
authors: Timothy DeStefano, Nick Johnstone, Richard Kneller, Jonathan Timmis
title: Do Capital Incentives Distort Technology Diffusion? Evidence on Cloud, Big Data and AI
venue: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper No. 10911
data: UK matched employer-employee administrative data around a capital-allowance tax incentive for IT investment
findings: The UK tax incentive succeeded in raising firms' IT capital investment as intended, but this came at the cost of slowing firms' adoption of cloud computing, big data, and AI, because owned IT capital and cloud/as-a-service technologies act as substitutes for firms; the policy also reduced firm demand specifically for data-analytics workers (not other worker types). The result is a cautionary, policy-relevant finding for governments (including in developing countries) designing digital-technology-diffusion incentives.
magnitude: A capital-allowance tax incentive for IT investment unintentionally slowed firms' adoption of cloud, big data, and AI by favoring owned capital over cloud substitutes

design: Human- and GPT-4-rated occupational task exposure rubric applied to the full US task inventory
authors: Tyna Eloundou, Sam Manning, Pamela Mishkin, Daniel Rock
title: GPTs are GPTs: Labor Market Impact Potential of Large Language Models
data: Human annotators and GPT-4 rate O*NET task statements for exposure to LLMs and LLM-powered software across the full US occupational task inventory
findings: About 80% of the US workforce could have at least 10% of their work tasks affected by LLMs, and about 19% could see at least 50% of tasks affected. Roughly 15% of all US worker tasks could be completed as fast with equivalent quality using an LLM alone; incorporating LLM-powered software raises this to 47-56% of tasks. Exposure rises with wage and education level, unlike prior waves of automation.
magnitude: 19% of US workers have ≥50% of tasks exposed to LLMs; 47-56% of tasks completable with LLM-powered software

design: multi-stakeholder connectivity initiative with survey-based situation analysis
authors: UNHCR, ITU, and GSMA (Connectivity for Refugees initiative)
title: Connectivity for Refugees initiative and "The Digital Lives of Refugees" research
countries: Multi-country, including Jordan, Rwanda, and Chad
period: 2023-2030 (initiative launched at the 2023 Global Refugee Fo…
data: GSMA displaced-population mobile-use surveys and partner-agency connectivity monitoring across refugee-hosting countries
findings: Over two-thirds of refugees surveyed across research locations actively use mobile phones, with usage highest in contexts like Jordan, but access is undermined by identity-documentation requirements for SIM registration, handset affordability, and reliance on shared or borrowed devices. The UNHCR-ITU-GSMA Connectivity for Refugees initiative aims to connect over 20 million forcibly displaced people by 2030, building on examples such as Rwanda's roughly 98% 4G population coverage.
magnitude: Initiative targets connecting over 20 million forcibly displaced people by 2030; refugee mobile-phone use already exceeds two-thirds in several host contexts

design: Policy history and descriptive review
title: Policies, Progress, and Prospects for Internet Telemedicine in China
data: Policy review tracing China's internet health-platform market from early information networks to today's dual public-private telemedicine system
findings: China's internet telemedicine market grew rapidly through a distinctive public-private hybrid model in which physicians employed by public hospitals also deliver care through private internet-hospital platforms, expanding the reach of specialist consultation well beyond major cities, though the review flags unresolved regulatory and quality-assurance gaps.
magnitude: Documents China's public-private hybrid internet-hospital model as a distinct pathway for scaling telemedicine access

design: Differential industry-level exposure to cloud computing and AI infrastructure cost reductions in China
authors: Yao Lu, Gordon M. Phillips, Jia Yang
title: The Impact of Cloud Computing and AI on Industry Dynamics and Concentration
data: Chinese industry/firm-level data on differential cloud and AI adoption exposure
findings: Cloud computing adoption is associated with increased firm entry, exit, and likelihood of M&A, and decreases industry concentration; AI adoption, by contrast, has no effect on entry but reduces the likelihood of exit and M&A and increases industry concentration, with benefits concentrated among larger firms. Firms with greater cloud exposure increase equity and venture capital financing, while only large firms increase equity financing in response to AI exposure.
magnitude: Cloud computing decreases industry concentration while AI adoption increases it, a divergent effect on Chinese market structure

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Study the extent to which machine learning methods can accurately differentiate ultra-poor households eligible for program benefits from ineligible households. The paper shows that machine learning methods leveraging mobile phone data can identify ultra-poor households nearly as accurately as survey-based measures of consumption and wealth; and that combining survey-based measures with mobile phone data produces classifications more accurate than those based on a single data source.

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Focuses on the impact of information technology on the lives and livelihoods of rural households in sub-Saharan Africa, where simple mobile phones have leapfrogged traditional communication and financial technologies, and thus, arguably, offer some of the greatest potential for development. Drawing on primary and secondary research from a variety of disciplines, the authors examine the evolution of mobile phone coverage and adoption in sub-Saharan Africa over the past two decades, before exploring the main channels through which mobile phones can affect development. They then review initiatives on “digitizing development” and evaluate empirical evidence on their impact. The book argues that digital has yet to live up to the hype, ending with a set of questions that stakeholders should ask (and answer) when using digital technology for promoting development.

design: hardware-shipment-based projection and commentary
title: The growing energy footprint of artificial intelligence
data: AI server/GPU shipment and production-capacity data (e.g., NVIDIA), compared against company-reported data centre electricity figures
findings: Documents the rapid 2022-2023 expansion of generative AI and argues the AI server supply chain is on track to become a fast-growing contributor to global data centre electricity consumption. Highlights that major AI operators disclose total company electricity use inconsistently and rarely break out AI-specific compute energy, making independent verification of AI's energy footprint difficult.
magnitude: Identifies the AI server supply chain as a fast-growing, poorly-disclosed driver of data-centre electricity demand

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Analyzed digital technology use among microenterprises in seven Sub-Saharan African countries during 2017-18. Firms using accounting software or inventory control systems are associated with a 1.6-person larger firm size. Female-owned firms use digital technologies significantly less. Men are 3.3 times more likely to use computers compared to females. Over 70% of non-users cite lack of need as the main constraint.

design: Firm panel; workforce composition analysis linked to AI hiring measure
authors: Babina, T., Fedyk, A., He, A.X., Hodson, J.
title: Firm Investments in Artificial Intelligence Technologies and Changes in Workforce Composition
data: Resume and job-posting-based firm-level AI investment measure merged with workforce composition data
findings: As firms invest more in AI, their workforces shift toward higher shares of employees with undergraduate and graduate degrees and more STEM/IT specialists. Organizational hierarchies flatten, with significant increases in junior-level staff shares and decreases in middle-management and senior-role shares. The reorganization pattern suggests AI adoption is associated with de-layering rather than simple headcount reduction.
magnitude: AI-investing firms shift toward more educated workforces and flatter management hierarchies

design: Randomized experiment
findings: Compares how in-kind food assistance, and an electronic voucher-based program affect the delivery of aid in practice. The Government of Indonesia randomized across 105 districts the transition from in-kind rice to approximately equivalent electronic vouchers redeemable for rice and eggs at a network of private agents. Targeted households received 46 percent more assistance in voucher areas. For the bottom 15 percent of households at baseline, poverty fell 20 percent. Voucher recipients received higher-quality rice, and increased consumption of eggs. The results suggest moving from a manual in-kind to electronic voucher-based program reduced poverty through increased adherence to program design.

design: Randomized experiment, Staggered rollout
findings: Evaluated the impact of eBay's Seller Hub on small businesses through a field experiment conducted from May 12 to August 8, 2016. Seller Hub helps sellers track performance metrics, such as sales, traffic, and feedback, enabling quick responses to market changes and improved service quality. The randomized rollout to eBay sellers showed that Seller Hub access increased weekly sales by 3.6% on average, with adopters seeing a 12.5% increase. Benefits included higher quantities sold, better feedback scores, more new listings, and improved inventory management, all without significant changes in average prices. Sellers who actively used performance metrics saw greater benefits.

design: Randomized experiment
title: Is Mobile Money Changing Rural Africa? Evidence from a Field Experiment
findings: Follow the introduction of mobile money for the first time in rural villages of Mozambique using a randomized field experiment. The paper finds that mobile money increased migration out of these villages, where lower agricultural activity and investment is observed. At the same time, remittances received and welfare of rural households increased, particularly when facing geo-referenced village-level floods and household-level idiosyncratic shocks. The paper suggests that mobile money can accelerate urbanization and structural change in Sub-Saharan Africa.

design: Instrumental variables — Bitcoin price movements instrument for local cryptomining electricity demand
title: When cryptomining comes to town: high electricity-use spillovers to the local economy
countries: United States (Upstate New York), with a comparative analysis for China
data: County electricity billing and load data, cryptomining facility locations, Bitcoin price series, local business and employment records
findings: Cryptomining's very large local electricity demand raises bills for everyone else on the same grid. Using Bitcoin price movements to instrument for mining activity, the paper finds that ratepayers in affected Upstate New York counties bore roughly $204 million in additional annual electricity costs for households and $92 million for small businesses. Increased local business tax revenue offset only part of this. In China, mining-related electricity rationing was associated with lower wages and reduced investment, indicating crowding out of other electricity users.
magnitude: $204 million extra annual household electricity costs and $92 million for small businesses in affected counties; tax gains offset only part of the burden

design: Quasi-experimental
findings: Found that an initiative by the Afghan government to modernize its payroll system – requiring teachers to biometrically register and receive salary payments via mobile money – significantly reduced delays and improved educational outcomes and financial inclusion, but did not decrease payments to non-existent ghost workers.

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Find that from 2018 to 2020, establishments with robots tend to be larger, with more employees and a higher share of production workers, while also exhibiting lower earnings per worker. The presence of robot integrators in a locality significantly increases the likelihood of that area being classified as a Robot Hub by 20-25 percentage points. The geographic concentration of robot adoption leads to localized spillover effects, impacting employment and productivity in those regions.

design: Instrumental variables
findings: Make use of the high-lightening area IV approach and focus specifically on Rwanda between 2002 (with no mobile internet coverage) and 2019. They find that “improvements in the coverage of 3G mobile internet technologies increase the share of employed individuals, among whom are both skilled and unskilled workers, with the former increasing at a faster rate, given their relatively small initial size; sectoral shift employment towards services and, within the service sector, to some high value-added and skill-intensive industries. A 10 percentage point increase in 3G coverage increases the share of working age population that is employed by 3.4 percentage points. Education, migration, and shifts in demand are instrumental in explaining these findings. A 10 percentage point increase in 3G coverage increases the average years of schooling by 0.15 years.

design: Instrumental variables
findings: Using an instrumental variable strategy that leverages the distance between municipalities and the nearest optical packet backbone node, Cambini et al. (2023) , covering data from 2013 to 2019, find that ultra-fast broadband access leads to a 2.9% increase in total factor productivity of the firm and a 3.9% increase in labor productivity. The benefits are most pronounced in the services sector. Additionally, firms with full-fiber connections experience higher productivity gains compared to those with mixed copper-fiber connections. The productivity gains from ultra-fast broadband access are largely driven by structural changes within firms, particularly a decrease in the share of low-skilled workers and an increase in the share of younger employees. This workforce reconfiguration facilitates a more efficient allocation of labor and better integration of digital technologies, thereby enhancing overall firm productivity.

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Cambodia’s Financial Management Information System (FMIS) reform aimed to modernize core government financial operations, particularly improving timeliness and accuracy in reporting. The implementation helped streamline disbursements and supported the Ministry of Economy and Finance in making better fiscal decisions.

design: Textual analysis of 10-K/10-Q risk disclosures to build firm-level cyber-risk factor; asset-pricing tests
authors: Chris Florackis, Christodoulos Louca, Roni Michaely, Michael Weber
title: Cybersecurity Risk
venue: Review of Financial Studies, 36(1): 351-407 (NBER Working Paper 28196)
period: Not precisely specified in verified abstract; disclosure-era…
data: Computational textual analysis of cybersecurity risk disclosures in SEC 10-K/10-Q filings, validated against realized hacking incidents and human/LLM auditor coding
findings: The firm-level cybersecurity-risk exposure measure is higher in IT-intensive industries, correlates with the characteristics of firms that later suffer attacks, and predicts future cyberattacks. Portfolios of firms with high cyber-risk exposure outperform low-exposure portfolios by up to 8.3% per year on average, consistent with a priced risk premium, but these same high-exposure firms underperform during periods of elevated realized cybersecurity risk.
magnitude: High cyber-risk-exposure stock portfolios earn up to 8.3%/year excess return as compensation for priced cyber risk

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: The Dalberg study is based on qualitative analysis and case studies across six African countries. It examines the potential of digital jobs to create inclusive economic opportunities and assesses the digital economy's growth potential.
