findings: Investigate the costs and benefits of government support for data centers through the lens of economic theory. Their research focuses on the effects of reduced energy taxes as incentives and highlights the intricate relationship between tax elasticity, electricity prices, and broader economic impacts. The authors find that supporting data centers through tax exemptions could attract investment but might also affect electricity prices and tax revenues, potentially crowding out economic activity in labor-intensive sectors.

design: difference-in-differences exploiting municipality-level variation in an anti-refugee social-media page's local popularity
title: Fanning the Flames of Hate: Social Media and Hate Crime
venue: Journal of the European Economic Association
data: Municipality-level anti-refugee sentiment on Facebook (from a major right-wing party's page) matched to reported hate crimes against refugees, with internet/Facebook outage events as an instrument
findings: Municipalities with higher local social-media usage saw a disproportionate increase in anti-refugee hate crimes in periods of higher anti-refugee sentiment on social media; the relationship attenuates during local internet or Facebook outages, indicating a causal role for social media in translating online hostility into offline violence rather than merely reflecting pre-existing local attitudes.
magnitude: Local internet/Facebook outages measurably reduced the link between online anti-refugee sentiment and hate crimes

design: RCT: randomized introduction of phone-based beneficiary call-back monitoring of frontline program officials
authors: Karthik Muralidharan, Paul Niehaus, Sandip Sukhtankar, Jeffrey Weaver
title: Improving Last-Mile Service Delivery Using Phone-Based Monitoring
venue: American Economic Journal: Applied Economics, 13(2), 52-82 (NBER WP 25298)
data: Administrative delivery data from a ~$1 billion farm-input transfer program covering 5.7 million farmers
findings: Randomly informing frontline officials that beneficiaries would be called by phone to verify receipt reduced the share of farmers who did not receive their input transfers by 7.6%. The intervention was extremely cost-effective, costing only 3.6 cents per additional dollar of transfer successfully delivered to beneficiaries.
magnitude: Phone-based monitoring cut non-delivery of transfers by 7.6% at a cost of 3.6 cents per extra dollar delivered

design: Conceptual development-economics framework on AI, automation, and North-South divergence
title: Artificial Intelligence, Globalization, and Strategies for Economic Development
data: Conceptual/policy analysis, no primary dataset
findings: The paper argues that AI and related automation threaten to reverse decades of developing-country gains from integrating into the world economy, since these technologies reduce demand for the labor-intensive tasks and cheap-labor comparative advantage that drove earlier export-led growth. The authors highlight three mechanisms working against developing countries: labor-saving bias, resource-conserving bias, and winner-take-all market dynamics favoring incumbent (often rich-country) firms. They propose national policy responses and global governance reforms to redistribute AI's gains more equitably.
magnitude: Warns AI-driven automation could reverse the labor-cost advantage that powered developing-country export-led growth since the 1990s

design: Nationally representative firm survey (Census ABS), broader advanced-technology module
authors: Lucia Foster, Emin Dinlersoz, Kristina McElheran, Nikolas Zolas, Erik Brynjolfsson, Catherine Buffington, Nathan Goldsch…
title: Advanced Technologies Adoption and Use by US Firms: Evidence from the Annual Business Survey
data: 2018 Annual Business Survey covering AI, cloud computing, robotics, and digitization of business information across US firms
findings: Cloud computing adoption is widespread but uneven: about 25% of US firms use cloud services for all of their IT functions. In the Information sector, roughly 89% of firms use cloud services versus 97% using basic digital information technologies. Cloud adoption rises with firm size, but among small firms (1-9 employees) it is far higher for young firms (74%, 0-5 years old) than for old firms (58%, 21+ years old), with billing and security the most commonly cloud-hosted functions. Adoption of more advanced technologies (AI, robotics) remains far rarer and concentrated among larger, older firms.
magnitude: First nationally representative US firm-level baseline showing AI adoption clusters with cloud computing and robotics across all sectors

design: Staggered rollout
findings: Document the presence of “technology-induced” trade in France between 1997 and 2007 and assess its impact on consumer welfare. The paper uses the staggered roll-out of broadband internet to estimate its causal effect on the importing behavior of affected firms. Using an event-study design, it finds that broadband expansion increases firm-level imports by around 25%. The effect on domestic sales is positive but smaller (5%), suggesting that the impact on trade is not limited to a scale effect. It further finds that the “sub-extensive” margin (number of products and sourcing countries per firm) is the main channel of adjustment. Broadband internet reduced the consumer price index by 2.22% and that the import-channel, i.e. the enhanced access to foreign goods that is allowed by broadband, accounts for about 33% of that effect.

design: Systematic literature review
title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on the Labour Market: What Do We Know So Far?
venue: OECD Social, Employment and Migration Working Papers No. 256
data: Synthesis of the empirical and theoretical literature on AI's employment, wage, and skill-demand effects as of 2021
findings: Surveys the then-nascent evidence base on AI's labor-market impact, concluding that aggregate employment effects were not yet detectable but AI was already reshaping job tasks and skill requirements. Identifies major evidence gaps, particularly on wage/inequality effects and developing-country labor markets, that subsequent generative-AI-era research (2023-2026) has begun to fill.
magnitude: Pre-ChatGPT baseline: literature review found no detectable aggregate employment effect from AI as of 2021, but clear task/skill reshaping

design: Theoretical model of firms as data-capital producers (buy vs. build) under privacy regulation
authors: Mehmet Canayaz, Ilja Kantorovitch, Roxana Mihet
title: Privacy Laws and the Value of Personal Data
data: Theoretical model calibrated with stylized facts on firm data holdings and M&A/data-acquisition patterns
findings: The model treats consumer data as a form of intangible capital that firms can either produce in-house or acquire externally, subject to regulatory and technical frictions. Privacy laws that raise the cost of acquiring external data are shown to favor firms that already hold large in-house data stocks (typically large incumbents), shifting the equilibrium toward in-house data production and potentially raising data-driven firms' market value relative to a world with freer data trading.
magnitude: Model shows privacy regulation that raises the cost of buying external data disproportionately benefits data-rich incumbents over data-poor challengers

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Use an OECD dataset that combines register data on labor market outcomes from 2012 to 2019 and employs a longitudinal approach to assess the relationship between digital skills and labor market outcomes, finding that a one standard deviation increase in digital skills is associated with a 4-6% increase in hourly wages and a 10% higher likelihood of employment. The study highlights that the higher employment rate among those with at least basic digital skills is primarily due to increased labor force participation.

design: household-randomized controlled trial providing smartphones to women
authors: Philip Roessler, Peter Carroll, Festo Myamba, Constantine Jahari, Bertha Kilama, Daniel Nielson
title: The economic impact of mobile phone ownership: Results from a randomized controlled trial in Tanzania
venue: CSAE Working Paper Series, University of Oxford (WPS 2021-05)
data: Household panel RCT in which smartphones were randomly assigned to women in low-income households
findings: Randomly providing smartphones to women raised household annual consumption per capita by 20% relative to control over a 13-month period, with the gains operating through women's control and use of the device. However, by endline only 34% of smartphone recipients still possessed their handset, showing that ownership of this productive asset was tenuous for women in low-income households.
magnitude: Smartphone provision to women raised household consumption per capita by 20%, but only 34% still had the phone at endline

design: Natural experiment: debit cards issued to existing cash-transfer bank-account holders
authors: Pierre Bachas, Paul Gertler, Sean Higgins, Enrique Seira
title: How Debit Cards Enable the Poor to Save More
data: Administrative banking records of Prospera (Oportunidades) cash-transfer beneficiaries before/after debit-card issuance
findings: Before receiving debit cards, only 13% of cash-transfer beneficiaries held any savings in their bank accounts; this jumped to 29% immediately after card issuance and to 87% two years later. Beneficiaries accumulated a savings stock equal to about 2% of annual income after two years, driven by lower transaction and monitoring costs of accessing the account.
magnitude: Savings-account usage rose from 13% to 87% of beneficiaries within two years of debit-card issuance

design: Cross-sectional association
findings: Analyze the impact of digital skills (proficiency levels, including basic and advanced competencies in information, communication, content creation, and problem-solving) and internet usage on wages and salaries in EU member states. It employs factor analysis to condense variables related to internet access and digital skills. There is a significant strong correlation (Pearson coefficient = 0.685, p < 0.01) between digital proficiency and Internet usage component score and wages and salaries. It highlights that countries with higher digital proficiency scores tend to have higher wages. The study emphasizes the importance of digital skills for labor market performance, especially during the pandemic, which accelerated the shift towards online activities. The study identifies digital proficiency and internet usage as key components influencing labor market outcomes. It suggests that digital skills enhance employability and productivity, leading to higher wages and better job opportunities.

design: Difference-in-differences comparing EEA vs. non-EEA OECD networks' interconnection behavior around GDPR implementation
authors: Ran Zhuo, Bradley Huffaker, kc claffy, Shane Greenstein
title: The impact of the General Data Protection Regulation on internet interconnection
venue: Telecommunications Policy, Vol. 45(2) (also circulated as NBER Working Paper 26481)
data: Global network interconnection agreement data (CAIDA), IP-address-level interconnection points
findings: GDPR had precisely zero measurable short-run effect on the number and type of interconnection agreements or on IP-level interconnection points between EEA and non-EEA networks, and only economically small effects on network entry and customer counts. The authors conclude there was no visible short-run consequence of GDPR at the internet interconnection layer, despite the law's substantial compliance costs for application firms.
magnitude: GDPR shows a precisely-zero effect on interconnection agreement counts between EEA and non-EEA networks

design: randomized field experiment offering subscriptions to counter-attitudinal news outlets on Facebook
title: Social Media, News Consumption, and Polarization: Evidence from a Field Experiment
data: Randomized offers of subscriptions to conservative or liberal news outlets on Facebook, with tracked exposure, consumption, and attitude outcomes
findings: Random assignment to follow counter-attitudinal news outlets on Facebook increased users' exposure to and consumption of cross-cutting news and modestly reduced negative attitudes toward the opposing political party, showing that social-media algorithms (which limit exposure to counter-attitudinal content) contribute to polarization by restricting -- rather than causing -- exposure to opposing views.
magnitude: Nudging users toward counter-attitudinal news on Facebook increased cross-cutting news exposure and modestly reduced affective polarization

design: Descriptive analysis
title: Digital Jobs: a deep-dive
venue: Digital Skills & Jobs Platform (European Commission), Insights
findings: Uses qualitative analysis to explore the impact of digitization on the labor market, focusing on the classification and characteristics of digital jobs. The study identifies a growing demand for digital skills across all job categories. It categorizes digital jobs into ICT-intensive, ICT-dependent, and ICT-enhanced jobs, showing how digitization is transforming traditional roles. The study suggests that digital skills improve efficiency, productivity, and innovation within firms. It highlights the role of digital skills in enabling new forms of work, such as remote and hybrid jobs, and facilitating the integration of digital technologies into traditional industries. In 2021, there were 9 million ICT specialists in Europe, representing 4.3% of total employment. Moreover, online job ads mention the ability to use digital tools for collaboration and productivity, as the highest (19%) specific skill required, compared to programming computer systems at 5.8% and setting up computer systems at 4.6%.

design: updated systematic review of epidemiological studies
authors: Sarker M. Parvez, Farjana Jahan, Marie-Noel Brune, Julia F. Gorman, Musarrat J.
title: Health consequences of exposure to e-waste: an updated systematic review
countries: China, Ghana, India, and other informal e-waste recycling sites
data: Synthesis of 108 references on biomarkers and health outcomes among e-waste-exposed populations, updating Grant et al. (2013, The Lancet Global Health)
findings: Finds consistent evidence that exposure to e-waste toxicants (lead, mercury, cadmium, brominated flame retardants, dioxins) among informal recyclers and nearby residents is associated with adverse birth outcomes, DNA damage, thyroid dysfunction, and altered lung function, with children in informal e-waste recycling communities facing disproportionately high exposure levels compared with unexposed populations.
magnitude: Synthesizes 108 references linking informal e-waste recycling to adverse child health outcomes including birth defects and impaired lung function

design: Two-year randomized evaluation of a voice-based ICT agricultural advisory service (Avaaj Otalo)
title: 'Mobile'izing Agricultural Advice: Technology Adoption, Diffusion and Sustainability
data: RCT of a voice-based mobile agricultural advisory service for smallholder cotton and cumin farmers in Gujarat, India
findings: Demand for the mobile advisory service was high, and farmers trusted and acted on the advice: practice changes raised yields by 8.6% for cotton (in the subgroup receiving reminder calls) and by 28% for cumin. Farmers offered the service subsequently relied less on traditional, informal sources of agricultural advice, indicating real substitution rather than pure supplementation.
magnitude: Voice-based mobile agricultural advice raised cumin yields 28% and cotton yields 8.6% (with reminders)

design: Event study (stock returns, sales growth) around cyberattack disclosures
authors: Shinichi Kamiya, Jun-Koo Kang, Jungmin Kim, Andreas Milidonis, René M. Stulz
title: Risk Management, Firm Reputation, and the Impact of Successful Cyberattacks on Target Firms
venue: Journal of Financial Economics (NBER Working Paper 24409)
countries: Not specified in verified abstract; cross-country listed-firm sample
data: Firm-level data on disclosed cyberattacks matched to stock returns, sales growth, leverage, and CEO compensation for publicly traded target firms
findings: After a breach of customers' personal data, the average attacked firm loses 1.1% of its market value (about $607 million at mean equity value) and experiences a 3.2 percentage-point drop in year-on-year sales growth. Attacks on financial data are the most damaging to equity value and credit ratings. Firms with weaker board risk oversight and firms hit by repeat attacks suffer significantly larger losses, and targeted firms subsequently cut CEO risk-taking incentives and strengthen risk management.
magnitude: Average cyberattack on personal data costs a target firm 1.1% of market value and 3.2pp of sales growth

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Found that a 1 percentage point increase in internet penetration is associated with a 0.05-0.37 percent growth in real GDP per capita growth in Sub-Saharan Africa.

design: World Bank flagship report chapter synthesizing global data-governance institutions and policy
title: Institutions for Data Governance: Building Trust Through Collective Action (Chapter 8)
venue: World Development Report 2021: Data for Better Lives
countries: Global, with emphasis on low- and middle-income countries
data: Cross-country synthesis of data-protection laws, cross-border data-flow regimes, and open-data policies, drawing on World Bank, OECD, and academic sources
findings: The WDR 2021 argues that the value of data for development is only realized when supported by trusted institutions for data governance: it documents that as of 2020 fewer than half of developing countries had modern data-protection laws, and that fragmented, trust-deficient data governance (rather than lack of data per se) is the binding constraint on using data for development outcomes such as service delivery, poverty targeting, and firm productivity. It calls for an integrated national data governance framework balancing data use, protection, and cross-border flow.
magnitude: Fewer than half of developing countries had a modern data-protection law as of the report's writing, identified as a key constraint on safe data reuse for development

design: Quasi-experimental
findings: Examined the employment effects of subsidized broadband internet for low-income Americans using a triple differences approach. The study focused on Comcast's Internet Essentials program, which offers discounted broadband to eligible low-income families. The availability of Internet Essentials increased the employment rate by 0.9 percentage points, decreased the probability of unemployment by 0.5 to 0.6 percentage points, and raised income by $147 annually. These effects are driven by greater labor force participation and reduced job search frictions due to improved internet access. The program's impact on employment is partly attributed to the convenience and efficiency of searching for jobs from home, which is crucial for low-income individuals who may face time and location constraints.

design: Empirical analysis of compute requirements and institutional origin of published deep-learning research
title: The De-democratization of AI: Deep Learning and the Compute Divide in Artificial Intelligence Research
countries: Cross-country comparison of AI research institutions
data: Bibliometric analysis of compute-intensive deep learning papers and the institutional affiliations (corporate vs. academic, elite vs. non-elite) of their authors
findings: The paper documents and names the 'compute divide': as deep learning research has grown more compute-intensive, participation has concentrated among large technology firms and elite, well-resourced universities, crowding out non-elite academic institutions and researchers in lower-resource settings. The authors argue this concentration of compute access risks embedding bias and reducing diversity of perspectives in frontier AI research -- an early and now widely-cited diagnosis of the dynamic later termed the global 'compute divide' between the Compute North and Compute South.
magnitude: Origin paper documenting how rising compute intensity concentrated deep learning research among big tech and elite universities

design: Quasi-experimental
findings: Found that ICT use significantly increased CO2 emissions in 21 Sub-Saharan African countries from 1996 to 2014 using an extended STIRPAT model. A 1% increase in internet and mobile phone penetration resulted in 0.03% rises in CO2 emissions. The study also confirmed the Environmental Kuznets Curve, indicating an inverted U-shaped relationship between economic growth and CO2 emissions.

design: Randomized experiment
findings: Analyze a large field experiment and the nationwide scale-up of a reform to India's workfare program. Advance payments were replaced by "just-in-time" payments, triggered by e-invoicing, making it easier to detect misreporting. Leakages went down: program expenditures dropped by 24 percent, while employment slightly increased; there were fewer fake households in the official database; and program officials' personal wealth fell by 10 percent. However, payment delays increased. The nationwide scale-up resulted in a persistent 19 percent reduction in program expenditure.

design: Structural network-demand model with counterfactual subsidy-targeting simulation, estimated on nationwide transaction-level digital traces
title: The Effect of Network Adoption Subsidies: Evidence from Digital Traces in Rwanda
data: 5.3 billion transaction records from Rwanda's dominant mobile network operator
findings: Studies a real handset/subscription-adoption subsidy program covering roughly 8% of the rural handset stock, finding that subsidized connections are used about as much as ordinary retail purchases. Because of network externalities, 73-76% of the additional operator revenue generated by the subsidy program comes from non-recipients who benefit from having more contacts on-network, a spillover the paper uses to evaluate alternative subsidy-targeting rules.
magnitude: 73-76% of the revenue generated by a rural handset-adoption subsidy comes from spillovers to non-recipients rather than the subsidized users themselves

design: Predictive modeling of loan default from mobile phone usage metadata, validated out-of-sample
title: Behavior Revealed in Mobile Phone Usage Predicts Credit Repayment
venue: World Bank Economic Review (also World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 9074)
countries: Unnamed South American country (telecom operator data)
data: Call-detail-record behavioral features from a telecom operator matched to actual loan repayment outcomes from a lender
findings: Behavioral signatures embedded in mobile phone usage (e.g., calling patterns, mobility, social network structure) predict loan default with accuracy comparable to models built on formal credit-bureau and financial-history data. This matters for financial inclusion because a large share of borrowers in developing countries lack a formal credit history but do have a mobile phone.
magnitude: Mobile-phone behavioral data predicts loan default about as well as traditional credit-bureau data, without requiring a credit history

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Finds that digitalization drives global value chain fragmentation rather than reshoring, based on qualitative data from interviews. Automation, while increasing productivity in low-wage countries like China, makes reshoring unfeasible due to high costs and labor market dynamics. Digital platforms and modular production enhance coordination and customization, with examples like Adidas's Speedfactory shifting production to Asia for cost benefits. On-demand production and advanced logistics systems further support global sourcing, especially in low-transport-cost industries, through AI-based predictive analytics

design: Quasi-experimental
findings: Examine the role of an online reputation mechanism in international trade by exploring T-shirt exports on Alibaba. Exploiting rich transaction data and features of search and rating algorithms, the paper shows that exporters displaying a superior reputation perform significantly better than peers with nearly identical true ratings and observables, and the value of reputation rises with the level of information friction and the specificity of information. The paper develops a dynamic reputation model with heterogeneous cross-country information friction to quantify the effect of the reputation mechanism and find a 20% increase in aggregate exports fueled by a market reallocation towards superstars.

design: Production-function estimation with a control function for endogenous productivity (Ackerberg-Caves-Frazer)
title: The effects of digital-technology adoption on productivity and factor demand: firm-level evidence from developing countries
venue: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 9333
data: World Bank Enterprise Surveys, manufacturing firms in 82 developing economies
findings: Estimates the productivity return to the most basic digital tools, which is where most firms in developing countries actually are. Adopting email raises measured total factor productivity for 67.3 percent of firms, with a probability-adjusted median premium of 1.6 percent; adopting a business website raises it for 54.6 percent of firms, with a median premium of 2.2 percent. Both exceed the productivity premium associated with learning by exporting. Digital adoption is on average both labour- and capital-augmenting, so it does not show up as straightforward labour substitution.
magnitude: Website adoption raises TFP for 54.6% of firms, median premium 2.2%

design: Shift-share/instrumental-variables using cross-country industry robot exposure by commuting zone
title: Robots and Jobs: Evidence from US Labor Markets
venue: Journal of Political Economy (NBER Working Paper 23285)
data: US commuting-zone panel; robot exposure instrumented using robot adoption in the same industries in other (European) countries
findings: One additional robot per thousand workers reduces the employment-to-population ratio by about 0.2 percentage points and wages by about 0.42%. On average, one new industrial robot entering a local labor market coincides with the loss of about 5.6 jobs. Commuting zones more exposed to robots after 1990 show no differential pre-trends, and the effect is distinguishable from other capital/IT measures.
magnitude: 1 robot per 1,000 workers reduces employment-population ratio by 0.2pp and wages by 0.42%

design: review of quasi-experimental and experimental studies on internet/social media and politics
authors: Ekaterina Zhuravskaya, Maria Petrova, Ruben Enikolopov
title: Political Effects of the Internet and Social Media
data: Synthesis of natural experiments and RCTs on internet/social media penetration and voting, protest, polarization, and trust in institutions
findings: Reviews evidence that the internet and social media can both empower citizens against authoritarian regimes (facilitating protest coordination and exposing corruption) and fuel polarization, populism, and erosion of trust in democracies, concluding that effects depend heavily on the pre-existing media environment, degree of censorship, and platform design rather than internet access alone.
magnitude: Synthesizes evidence that internet/social media effects on politics are highly context-dependent, cutting both toward empowerment and toward polarization

design: Field experiment randomizing access to and incentives for digital payroll (mobile-money) accounts among factory workers
authors: Emily Breza, Martin Kanz, Leora F. Klapper
title: Learning to Navigate a New Financial Technology: Evidence from Payroll Accounts
venue: Journal of Finance (forthcoming); NBER Working Paper 28249
data: Field experiment with largely unbanked garment-factory workers randomized into digital payroll-account treatment arms
findings: Introducing digital payroll accounts to financially inexperienced garment workers led to increased account usage and accelerated 'learning by doing' about the new financial technology, with treated workers better able to avoid common pitfalls (e.g., unnecessary fees, mistrust-driven full withdrawals) as they gained experience using digital wage payments.
magnitude: Digital payroll accounts accelerated learning and safer usage among first-time users of formal finance

design: bottom-up global compute-instance and efficiency modeling
authors: Eric Masanet, Arman Shehabi, Nuoa Lei, Sarah Smith, Jonathan Koomey
title: Recalibrating global data center energy-use estimates
data: Bottom-up model of global data centre compute instances, server/storage efficiency, and utilization/virtualization rates
findings: Despite compute instances rising roughly 550% between 2010 and 2018, global data centre energy use grew only about 6% over the same period and held at approximately 1% of global electricity consumption, because efficiency gains from hyperscale/cloud consolidation, better cooling, and server virtualization offset most of the demand growth. The authors caution that continued efficiency gains are not guaranteed absent supportive policy.
magnitude: Data centers held near ~1% of global electricity in 2018 despite a ~550% rise in compute instances since 2010

design: randomized four-week Facebook deactivation experiment around the 2018 US midterm election
authors: Hunt Allcott, Luca Braghieri, Sarah Eichmeyer, Matthew Gentzkow
title: The Welfare Effects of Social Media
period: Four weeks around the 2018 midterm election
data: Randomized controlled trial (n≈2,844) in which treated Facebook users deactivated their accounts for four weeks, with surveys and behavioral follow-up
findings: Deactivating Facebook for four weeks increased subjective well-being, reduced factual news knowledge, and reduced political polarization, while increasing offline activities such as watching TV alone and socializing with family and friends. The study finds a large persistent reduction in Facebook use even after the experiment ended and that deactivation reduced users' own valuation of the platform, suggesting standard consumer-surplus metrics overstate Facebook's welfare contribution.
magnitude: Four weeks without Facebook raised subjective well-being and produced a persistent post-experiment reduction in use

design: Before/after case study with ISP surveys and traffic/latency measurement at two African IXPs
authors: Internet Society (research conducted with Analysys Mason)
title: Anchoring the African Internet Ecosystem: Lessons from Kenya and Nigeria's Internet Exchange Points Growth (update of the 2012 Assessment of the Impact of Internet Exchange Points)
data: ISP surveys and traffic/latency measurements at KIXP (Kenya) and IXPN (Nigeria)
findings: KIXP cut domestic latency from 200-600ms to 2-10ms and saved local ISPs nearly USD 1.5 million per year in international connectivity costs when first studied in 2012; by 2020 those annual savings had roughly quadrupled to about USD 6 million. IXPN generated close to USD 1 million per year in savings for Nigerian operators. Locally exchanged internet traffic in these countries rose from about 30% to 70% of total traffic between 2012 and 2020.
magnitude: IXP adoption cut Kenya's cross-border latency from 200-600ms to 2-10ms and quadrupled ISP cost savings to about $6 million/year by 2020

design: Structural model
findings: Based on data for 139 countries between 2010-2017 and using a simultaneous equations model, ITU (2020) found that overall a 10 percentage point increase in fixed broadband penetration is associated with a 0.77% increase in GDP per capita. The effect is 0% for countries with a GDP per capita below USD 12000, 0.58% for countries with GDP per capita between USD12000-22000, and 1.4% for countries with GDP per capita above USD 22000. A 10 percentage point increase of mobile broadband penetration is associated with a 1.5% increase in GDP per capita. The effect is 1.98% for countries with a GDP per capita below USD 12000, 1.76% for countries with GDP per capita between USD12000-22000, and 0% for countries with GDP per capita above USD 22000. Fixed broadband has greater contribution in developed countries with high penetration of fixed broadband, reflecting the return to scale effect. Mobile broadband generates greater economic dividend in countries and regions with low levels of economic development and low mobile penetration, reflecting the diminishing returns effect. This contribution diminishes in countries and regions with higher levels of penetration and development.

design: Quasi-experimental
findings: Koski and Valmari 2020 use extensive firm-level data on European and US companies from 2014–2018 to explore the short-term impacts of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) on European companies’ financial performance. The empirical analysis suggests that the costs of the GDPR during the first year of its implementation were substantial, at least for some European companies. The profit margins of the data-intensive firms increased, on average, by approximately 1.7 to 3.4 percentage points less than the profit margins of their US counterparts. The European data-intensive SMEs were the most disadvantaged group regarding their post-GDPR profit developments, while the large European data-intensive companies’ short-term post-GDPR profit margins dropped relatively less. They do not find any statistically significant difference in the profit margin developments of the very large European and US companies. This finding is consistent with the view that the very large, multinational US companies that often have European customers and deal with the personal data of EU citizens also faced substantial costs when they needed to comply with the GDPR.

design: RCT comparing vocational (classroom) training, firm-based (apprenticeship) training, and a control group
authors: Livia Alfonsi, Oriana Bandiera, Vittorio Bassi, Robin Burgess, Imran Rasul, Munshi Sulaiman, Anna Vitali
title: Tackling Youth Unemployment: Evidence from a Labor Market Experiment in Uganda
data: RCT randomly assigning unemployed youth to vocational training, firm-based training placements, or control, tracked over 4 years
findings: Both vocational and firm-based training raised employment and earnings relative to control, but through different channels: vocational training built skills and boosted formal-sector entry, while firm-based training worked mainly by improving firms' screening/matching to worker ability, with firms retaining the more able trainees. Earnings effects grew over the 4-year horizon rather than fading, contrary to the typical ALMP fade-out pattern.
magnitude: Both vocational and firm-based training raised youth earnings over 4 years, via distinct skill-building vs. matching channels

design: Continent-wide panel event-study (mobile signal coverage x protest incidence, 1998-2012)
title: Liberation Technology: Mobile Phones and Political Mobilization in Africa
data: Geo-referenced mobile phone signal coverage data plus geo-referenced protest event data across the African continent
findings: Mobile coverage increases the probability of protest participation, but only during periods of negative economic shocks (e.g., poor rainfall or growth downturns), consistent with mobile phones acting as a coordination technology deployed when latent grievances already exist rather than as an independent driver of unrest.
magnitude: Mobile coverage raises protest incidence specifically during economic downturns -- a conditional coordination-technology effect, not an unconditional mobilization effect

design: Instrumental variables
findings: Examines the relationship between access to broadband internet and household welfare between 2011 and 2018 by integrating the latest two rounds of household budget surveys with data on the location of fiber-optic transmission nodes and coverage maps of third-generation (3G) mobile technology. Results show that 3G coverage is associated with a 14 percent increase in total consumption and a 10 percent decline in extreme poverty. These results are robust to controlling for spatial characteristics and access to complementary digital infrastructure, as well as to an instrumental variable approach that relies on distance to 3G coverage in neighboring areas. These effects are larger among households in urban areas and households headed by men or younger cohorts. Although in the same direction, welfare effects of proximity to fixed broadband infrastructure are not statistically significant.

design: Patent-text-to-job-task overlap exposure measure with historical extrapolation
title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on the Labor Market
data: Text-overlap measure between AI/software/robot patent texts and O*NET occupational task descriptions
findings: Occupations historically most exposed to software and robot patents experienced relative declines in employment and wages. Unlike software and robots (which targeted low- and middle-skill tasks), AI patents disproportionately target high-skill, highly-educated occupations. Extrapolating historical substitution patterns, the paper projects AI will compress 90:10 wage inequality without much affecting incomes at the very top.
magnitude: AI patents concentrate on high-skill tasks; projected to narrow 90:10 wage inequality while leaving top 1% incomes largely unaffected

design: Firm-level panel combining survey and registry data, decomposing the productivity premium of digital adopters into direct and sectoral-spillover components
title: Digital Technology Adoption, Productivity Gains in Adopting Firms and Sectoral Spill-Overs: Firm-Level Evidence from Estonia
venue: OECD Economics Department Working Paper No. 1638
data: Firm-level dataset combining Statistics Estonia survey and registry data on digital technology (including ERP systems) adoption
findings: Firms adopting digital technologies show a consistently positive and sizeable labor-productivity premium over non-adopters across different technology types, including ERP systems, with additional positive productivity spillovers to other firms in the same sector, especially in manufacturing and industries with high automation potential.
magnitude: Digital technology adopters (including ERP users) show a consistently positive productivity premium, plus sectoral spillovers

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Digital platforms dominate in controlling data and creating value, approx. 90% of the market capitalization of the of the top 70 digital platforms is held by firms from the United States and China. Developing countries may face challenges in creating and capturing value in the digital economy due to factors like limited resources, skills, and infrastructure. (OECD, 2020)

design: RCT providing mobile-money accounts and encouragement to urban micro-entrepreneurs
authors: Shilpa Aggarwal, Valentina Brailovskaya, Jonathan Robinson
title: Cashing In (and Out): Experimental Evidence on the Effects of Mobile Money in Malawi
data: RCT among urban micro-entrepreneurs randomized into mobile-money account access/encouragement
findings: Among treated micro-entrepreneurs, 56% opened a mobile-money account and 32% reported using it to save, with average mobile-money balances of roughly $5, demonstrating meaningful but partial and modest-scale take-up of savings functionality when mobile money is actively introduced to previously unbanked small business owners.
magnitude: 56% of encouraged microentrepreneurs opened mobile-money accounts; 32% used them to save (avg. balance ~$5)

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Examined the role of digital capital in the rise of superstar firms from 1990 to 2016 using Hall’s Quantity Revelation Theorem. Digital capital, which accounted for at least 25% of firms' assets by 2016, is highly concentrated in a few superstar firms, predicting productivity increases three years ahead. Prices peaked during the dot-com boom in 2000, with the concentration of digital capital in top firms rising significantly over time, contributing greatly to their market value.

design: Natural experiment exploiting discrepancies between employer- and employee-reported wages under a hybrid paper/digital payroll-tax system
authors: Todd Kumler, Eric Verhoogen, Judith Frías
title: Enlisting Employees in Improving Payroll-Tax Compliance: Evidence from Mexico
data: Matched employer-employee administrative social-security records comparing self-reported and employer-reported wages
findings: Exploiting a reform that let workers verify their own wage records against employer reports, the paper shows that enlisting employees as a digital third-party check on payroll reporting increased reported wages for previously underreporting firms, illustrating how digitizing employee-facing verification channels can improve payroll-tax compliance beyond what employer-side reporting alone achieves.
magnitude: Employee-verifiable digital wage records raised reported payroll wages at underreporting firms

design: Structural model of network-goods demand with peer effects, estimated on near-census call-detail-record (CDR) data
title: The Adoption of Network Goods: Evidence from the Spread of Mobile Phones in Rwanda
data: Near-census panel of call-detail records (CDRs) from Rwanda's dominant mobile operator, used to estimate a structural model of phone adoption with social-network externalities
findings: Estimates a structural demand model in which the value of adopting a mobile phone depends on how many of an individual's social contacts have already adopted (a network externality). Counterfactual simulations show adoption diffuses much more slowly without these network effects, and that policies subsidizing highly-connected 'hub' individuals generate substantially larger network-wide diffusion spillovers than random or income-targeted subsidies.
magnitude: Structural estimates show network externalities are central to mobile-phone diffusion; subsidizing well-connected 'hub' users produces much larger adoption spillovers than untargeted subsidies

design: Continent-wide infrastructure-gap and investment-needs diagnostic
authors: Broadband Commission Working Group on Broadband for All (World Bank Group)
title: Connecting Africa through broadband: a strategy for doubling connectivity by 2021 and reaching universal access by 2030
data: Operator and regulator infrastructure inventories, Africa IXP Association records, coverage and investment modelling
findings: The clearest statement of how thin Africa's interconnection layer is. Forty-two percent of African countries had no internet exchange point at all, and only about 44 active IXPs served 32 countries, meaning most domestic traffic was routed through international hubs at international transit prices. About 830 million Africans remained without access to broadband of 10 Mbps or more. Reaching universal access by 2030 was costed at roughly 1.1 billion new users and about $100 billion in additional investment.
magnitude: 42% of African countries have no IXP; only 44 IXPs serve the continent; ~$100 billion investment gap to 2030
cite: Broadband Commission Working Group on Broadband (2019)

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Address the productivity paradox where AI advancements have not yet translated into significant productivity growth, noting a decline from 2.8% (1995-2004) to 1.3% (2005-2016). They attribute this lag to the time needed for complementary investments and organizational changes. Additionally, current metrics may not fully capture AI’s benefits​​.

design: Task-based decomposition of aggregate employment trends into displacement vs. reinstatement effects
title: Automation and New Tasks: How Technology Displaces and Reinstates Labor
venue: Journal of Economic Perspectives (NBER Working Paper 25684)
data: Decomposition of US employment and labor-share trends into displacement vs. reinstatement effects using task-content and occupation data
findings: The slowdown in US employment growth over the last three decades is attributed to an acceleration of the displacement effect (especially in manufacturing), a weakening reinstatement effect from new task creation, and slower overall productivity growth than in earlier periods. The framework implies automation not accompanied by comparable new-task creation will reduce labor demand and the labor share.
magnitude: Recent decades show an accelerating displacement effect and weakening reinstatement effect relative to the mid-20th-century pattern

design: Difference-in-differences
findings: Analyze the impact of internet penetration on exports across Chinese provinces from 1999 to 2007. Using a difference-in-differences approach to exploit variations in internet penetration, they find that a 10-percentage point increase in internet penetration leads to a 2.5% increase in exports per firm. Additionally, firms engaged in export activities increased by 1.8%. The positive impact is driven by better matching between buyers and sellers, reduced information asymmetries, and more efficient supply chain management. Notably, internet access boosted exports even before major e-commerce platforms like Alibaba emerged, suggesting significant reductions in trade costs and increase in virtual visibility​​.

design: Difference-in-differences
findings: Goldberg, Johnson and Shriver 2019 examine the impact of the GDPR on European web traffic and E-commerce sales using web analytics data from a diverse set of 1508 firms that use the Adobe Analytics platform. Using a difference-in-differences approach, the paper shows that recorded pageviews and recorded revenues fall by about 10% for EU users after the GDPR’s enforcement deadline. The extensive margin drives these changes as a user’s average time on site and average page views per visit stay constant.

design: Prospective diagnostic-accuracy validation study vs. expert manual grading
authors: Gulshan, V., Rajan, R.P., Widner, K., Wu, D., Wubbels, P., Rhodes, T., Whitehouse, K., Coram, M., Corrado, G., Kim, R.,…
title: Performance of a Deep-Learning Algorithm vs Manual Grading for Detecting Diabetic Retinopathy in India
data: 3,049 patients with diabetes screened at two Indian eye hospitals (Aravind Eye Hospital, Sankara Nethralaya), automated deep-learning grading vs. trained human graders, adjudicated by retina specialist panels
findings: The automated deep-learning system achieved sensitivity of 88.9% and specificity of 92.2% (AUC 0.963) at Aravind Eye Hospital, and sensitivity of 92.1% and specificity of 95.2% (AUC 0.980) at Sankara Nethralaya, generalizing well to Indian patient populations. Performance was comparable to or exceeded manual grading for referable diabetic retinopathy and macular edema, supporting AI-based screening in settings with limited numbers of retina specialists.
magnitude: AI screening achieved 89-92% sensitivity and 92-95% specificity for diabetic retinopathy detection in Indian patients (AUC up to 0.98)

design: Difference-in-differences (staggered submarine-cable arrival + terrestrial network maps)
title: The Arrival of Fast Internet and Employment in Africa
data: Submarine internet cable landing dates and terrestrial fiber backbone maps matched to household/labor-force survey and firm-census data across 12 African countries
findings: Found that the arrival of fast speed internet cables in Africa – supported by the WBG in 20+ countries – has already had a significant impact on firm productivity, exports, and job creation, especially in higher skill occupations. When fast Internet becomes available, the probability that an individual is employed increases by up to 13.2 percent, total employment per firm increases by up to 22 percent, and firm exports nearly quadruples.
magnitude: Employment probability rises by roughly 6.9-13.2 percentage points in the main cross-country samples (about +3.1pp in the South African firm/worker sample) after fast internet arrives

design: Diff-in-diff exploiting the introduction of consumer-receipt lottery tied to electronic sales reporting
title: Consumers as Tax Auditors? Evidence from an Anti-Tax Evasion Program in Brazil
data: Administrative data on over 1 million firms, 40 million individuals, and 2.7 billion electronically-reported receipts (Nota Fiscal Paulista program)
findings: The Nota Fiscal Paulista program gave consumers lottery-ticket incentives to demand electronically-verifiable receipts embedding their ID number, letting the tax authority cross-check reported sales. Firms' reported sales rose by at least 21% over four years, and despite the cost of rewards and increased reported expenses, net tax revenue rose by 9.3%.
magnitude: Consumer-verified e-receipts raised firm reported sales 21% and net tax revenue 9.3%

design: Randomized controlled trial of after-school computer-adaptive learning centers
authors: Karthik Muralidharan, Abhijeet Singh, Alejandro J. Ganimian
title: Disrupting Education? Experimental Evidence on Technology-Aided Instruction in India
data: RCT of the Mindspark computer-adaptive learning software in after-school centers in urban Delhi
findings: After 4.5 months, the program raised math and Hindi test scores by 0.37 and 0.23 standard deviations respectively, with the largest gains for students who were furthest behind grade level, showing the adaptive software successfully personalized instruction to each student's actual learning level rather than the grade-level curriculum.
magnitude: Adaptive computer-assisted learning raised math scores 0.37 SD in 4.5 months, largest gains for lagging students

design: Structural dynamic labor-supply model estimated on high-frequency administrative driver data
authors: M. Keith Chen, Judith A. Chevalier, Peter E. Rossi, Emily Oehlsen
title: The Value of Flexible Work: Evidence from Uber Drivers
data: High-frequency administrative data on Uber driver shifts, wages, and surge pricing, used to estimate a dynamic labor-supply model
findings: Drivers' ability to flexibly choose when and how much to work is estimated to be worth more than twice the surplus they would obtain under a comparable but inflexible taxi-style shift arrangement, because flexibility lets drivers concentrate hours in high-wage periods without the commitment costs of a fixed schedule.
magnitude: Real-time work flexibility roughly doubles driver surplus versus an inflexible shift arrangement

design: Quasi-experimental
findings: And Bessone et al. (2023) find no significant improvements in educational outcomes from home or mobile internet in Peru and Brazil, respectively—Malamud et al. (2019) find gains in digital proficiency, but home internet was used for entertainment rather than learning.

design: Analysis of digital (M-Shwari) loan take-up and household shock resilience
authors: Prashant Bharadwaj, William Jack, Tavneet Suri
title: Fintech and Household Resilience to Shocks: Evidence from Digital Loans in Kenya
venue: NBER Working Paper 25604; Journal of Development Economics
data: Household panel data tracking uptake of M-Shwari (mobile-money-linked digital savings/credit product) and exposure to income shocks
findings: M-Shwari, a digital bank product bundling a savings account with algorithmically-underwritten short-term mobile loans, expanded credit access to previously underserved borrowers and improved households' ability to maintain consumption and cope with negative income shocks relative to households without access to the product.
magnitude: Access to algorithmic digital credit (M-Shwari) improved household resilience to income shocks

design: synthesis of randomized evaluations of digital agricultural-extension services
authors: Raissa Fabregas, Michael Kremer, Frank Schilbach
title: Realizing the potential of digital development: The case of agricultural advice
data: Meta-analytic synthesis of randomized controlled trials of mobile-phone and digital agricultural extension/advisory services
findings: Digital delivery of agricultural information and advice (SMS, voice calls, video) raised measured crop yields by about 4% on average and increased the odds of recommended technology adoption by about 22% across reviewed trials, illustrating how precision/digital agriculture can raise input-use efficiency. However, demand for and willingness to pay for these services remains low among farmers, which the authors identify as the binding constraint on scaling impact.
magnitude: Digital agricultural advice raised yields by ~4% and technology-adoption odds by ~22% across reviewed RCTs

design: Cross-sectional association
findings: Examined the returns to technological talent and investments in AI. The study found that an additional engineer correlated with an $854,000 increase in market value. AI skills significantly correlated with market value, particularly post the TensorFlow launch, which led to a 4-7% increase in market value for AI-using firms. Firms outside the top quintile of AI use experienced growth of approximately $3.56 million for a 1% increase in AI skill, with mixed evidence on the causal value of engineers overall.

design: Retrospective quasi-experimental analysis of hospital operational data around a critical-infrastructure ransomware attack
authors: Saira Ghafur, Sarah Kristensen, Kate Honeyford, Guy Martin, Ara Darzi, Paul Aylin
title: A Retrospective Impact Analysis of the WannaCry Cyberattack on the NHS
data: NHS hospital trust operational records (cancelled appointments, A&E diversions, IT system downtime) for trusts infected by WannaCry ransomware
findings: The May 2017 WannaCry ransomware attack disrupted computer systems across at least 80 NHS trusts in England, forcing cancelled appointments and ambulance/A&E diversions. Widely-cited UK Department of Health follow-up accounting (reported contemporaneously in Computer Fraud & Security, 2018) put the total cost to the NHS at approximately £92 million, split between costs during the attack (lost output) and IT clean-up/upgrade costs afterward.
magnitude: WannaCry ransomware attack on the NHS (May 2017) cost an estimated £92 million and disrupted care across 80+ hospital trusts

design: Quasi-experimental
findings: Studies the effects of firms’ investments in information and communication technologies (ICT) on their demand for female and skilled workers. Using the gradual liberalization of the broadband Internet sector across provinces from 2006 to 2009 as a source of exogenous variation to identify the causal impacts of ICT, the paper finds evidence from the country’s comprehensive enterprise survey data that firms’ adoption of broadband Internet and other related ICT increased their relative demand for female and college-educated workers. The effect of ICT on firms’ female employment is particularly strong among the college-educated workers, and is stronger in industries that are more dependent on highly manual and physical tasks. These results suggest that ICT can lower gender inequality in the labor market by shifting the labor demand from highly manual, routine tasks in which men have a comparative advantage toward more nonroutine, interactive tasks in which women hold a comparative advantage. However, the effect of ICT is weaker in industries relying more on complex and interactive tasks, suggesting that gender differences in education may have limited female labor supply for the most innovative industries that require highly technical skills to complement ICT.

design: Task-based theoretical framework (displacement vs. reinstatement effects)
title: Artificial Intelligence, Automation and Work
venue: NBER Working Paper 24196 (in The Economics of Artificial Intelligence: An Agenda)
data: Theoretical task-based model; no new dataset
findings: Formalizes the tension between a 'displacement effect' (automation substitutes for labor in existing tasks, raising output per worker faster than wages and cutting labor's income share) and a countervailing 'reinstatement effect' from new labor-intensive tasks. Argues the net labor-market impact of AI-driven automation depends on whether enough new tasks are created, and highlights skill mismatches and rapid adoption speed as frictions that slow beneficial adjustment.
magnitude: Conceptual: net effect on labor's income share depends on displacement vs. reinstatement effects, not automation intensity alone

design: Hedonic price index construction using quarterly AWS pricing data
authors: David M. Byrne, Carol Corrado, Daniel E. Sichel
title: The Rise of Cloud Computing: Minding Your P's, Q's and K's
data: Quarterly Amazon Web Services (AWS) pricing data for compute, database, and storage services
findings: Cloud service hedonic price indexes fell substantially over 2009-2016, with the rate of decline accelerating to double-digit annual rates starting in early 2014 across all three product categories (compute, database, storage). Cloud provider capital expenditure on IT equipment expanded sharply over this period even though official U.S. National Income and Product Accounts showed comparatively weak IT equipment investment, pointing to mismeasurement of cloud-related investment in official statistics.
magnitude: Cloud computing prices fell at double-digit annual rates from 2014-2016, even as official statistics understated the associated investment boom

design: Panel analysis exploiting village-level rainfall shocks and heterogeneous mobile-money access
title: Mobile Money and Risk Sharing Against Village Shocks
data: Household panel data linked to village-level rainfall shocks and mobile-money access/usage
findings: Households without access to mobile money experienced significant consumption shortfalls following village-level (rainfall) shocks, while households with mobile-money access were able to smooth consumption through remittances from geographically-dispersed risk-sharing networks, highlighting mobile money's role in extending informal insurance beyond spatially-correlated local risk-sharing groups.
magnitude: Mobile-money access enabled full consumption smoothing against village rainfall shocks; non-users' consumption fell

design: Structural model
findings: Provide evidence on online trade and spatial consumption inequality. The paper finds that online trade is less hindered by distance relative to offline trade, and residents from smaller and more remote cities spend a larger fraction of their income online. The paper then builds a multi-region general equilibrium model to quantify the impacts of e-commerce on domestic trade and welfare. It finds that although it partially crowds out inter-city trade originally taking place offline, the emergence of e-commerce increases the aggregate domestic trade. The welfare gains from e-commerce are 1.6% on average, and are about 30% larger for cities in the smallest population and market potential quintiles.

design: Cross-country industry panel with instrumental variables for robot adoption
title: Robots at Work
venue: Review of Economics and Statistics, Vol. 100(5), pp. 753-768
data: Panel of industrial robot adoption across 17 countries, 1993-2007, using instruments based on robots' comparative task advantage
findings: Increased robot use raised labor productivity and total factor productivity and lowered output prices, contributing about 0.36 percentage points to annual labor-productivity growth on average across the sample. Robots had no significant effect on total hours worked, but reduced the employment share of low-skilled workers, indicating a compositional rather than aggregate displacement effect.
magnitude: Robot adoption added ~0.36 percentage points to annual labor productivity growth across 17 countries

design: Demand-elasticity model calibrated to historical automation episodes
title: AI and Jobs: The Role of Demand
data: Historical case studies of employment through automation episodes in the textile, steel, and automotive industries
findings: A demand-based model explains historical employment patterns: employment grew for over a century during rapid automation in these industries because demand was highly elastic, then declined in recent decades as demand became inelastic (saturated). The paper argues AI's aggregate employment effects will hinge on the elasticity of demand in AI-exposed sectors, not on automation intensity alone.
magnitude: No single statistic; core claim is that demand elasticity, not automation intensity, determined whether historical automation raised or cut industry employment

design: Gravity-model analysis of online-outsourcing contract-flow data from digital labor platforms
authors: John J. Horton, William R. Kerr, Christopher Stanton
title: Digital Labor Markets and Global Talent Flows
venue: NBER / High-Skilled Migration to the United States and its Economic Consequences (University of Chicago Press)
data: Transaction-level data from online labor platforms (e.g., oDesk/Upwork), analyzed with gravity-model methods for cross-border contracting flows
findings: Online labor platforms substitute in part for physical high-skilled migration by enabling cross-border hiring without relocation; contract flows follow gravity-model patterns shaped by shared language, prior migration corridors, and time-zone overlap, and diaspora ties measurably increase outsourcing flows between specific origin-destination country pairs (e.g., India-US on oDesk).
magnitude: Diaspora and migration ties significantly predict online-outsourcing contract flows between countries

design: Natural experiment: debit cards distributed to cash-transfer recipients, distance-to-bank analysis
authors: Pierre Bachas, Paul Gertler, Sean Higgins, Enrique Seira
title: Digital Financial Services Go a Long Way: Transaction Costs and Financial Inclusion
data: Administrative and geospatial data on cash-transfer beneficiaries' distance to nearest access point for their bank account
findings: Issuing debit cards to Prospera cash-transfer beneficiaries who could previously only withdraw funds in person at a bank branch cut the median distance to access their account from 4.8 km to 1.3 km, sharply lowering the transaction costs of using formal financial services in rural Mexico.
magnitude: Debit cards cut beneficiaries' median distance to access their account from 4.8 km to 1.3 km

design: Quasi-experimental analysis of individual customer transaction panel around a retailer data breach
authors: Ramkumar Janakiraman, Joon Ho Lim, Rishika Rishika
title: The Effect of a Data Breach Announcement on Customer Behavior: Evidence from a Multichannel Retailer
period: Around a major US multichannel retailer's data breach announ…
data: Individual-level purchase transaction data (online and offline channels) for customers of a large multichannel retailer before and after a publicized data breach
findings: Customer response to a data breach announcement is heterogeneous: some customers reduce spending and channel engagement (particularly online, the breached channel) after the announcement, while the overall effect on retailer revenue depends on whether affected customers shift toward offline channels rather than exit entirely. The study shows data breaches impose a customer-trust cost distinct from and additional to direct remediation costs.
magnitude: Data breach announcements shift affected customers' channel mix and reduce engagement in the breached (online) channel

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Raul L. Katz (2018) summarized the impact of the broadband internet on employment based on the literature. Broadband contributes to the creation of jobs in certain industries and geographies, while also being a key factor in capital-labor substitution under certain conditions. First, broadband construction programs create direct, indirect, and induced jobs under attractive multipliers. Second, deployment of broadband in emerging countries enables them to attract employment from industrialized economies. Third, broadband Internet in advanced economies leads to the emergence of businesses that were previously nonexistent. Fourth, broadband enables businesses to redeploy functions in different geographies to benefit from the availability of wider labor pools or lower factor costs; this leads in turn to job creation in certain regions. Fifth, firms can rely on broadband to deploy distribution channels in unserved remote geographies, leading to additional job creation.

design: Measurement study of Netflix Open Connect CDN server deployment and peering relationships across worldwide IXPs
authors: Timm Böttger, Félix Cuadrado, Gareth Tyson, Ignacio Castro, Steve Uhlig
title: Open Connect Everywhere: A Glimpse at the Internet Ecosystem through the Lens of the Netflix CDN
venue: ACM SIGCOMM Computer Communication Review, Vol. 48(1), pp. 28-34
data: Measurement of Netflix Open Connect CDN cache placement and peering relationships across global IXPs
findings: The worldwide IXP substrate is the main cornerstone underpinning Netflix's global CDN deployment strategy, with the company embedding caching servers directly within ISPs and at IXPs rather than relying on centralized hosting or paid transit. This illustrates how CDN/IXP co-location localizes content delivery and reduces the long-haul transit costs that hyperscale content firms and local ISPs would otherwise bear.
magnitude: IXPs serve as the 'corner stone' of Netflix's globally distributed CDN infrastructure, minimizing reliance on paid transit

design: RCT with randomized allocation of bootcamp slots (Medellin), plus qualitative case studies (Beirut, Nairobi)
authors: World Bank (Solutions for Youth Employment / Mastercard Foundation initiative)
title: Coding Bootcamps for Youth Employment: Evidence from Colombia, Lebanon, and Kenya
region: Latin America & Caribbean; Middle East; Sub-Saharan Africa
data: RCT with randomized allocation of coding-bootcamp slots in Medellin, Colombia, complemented by qualitative studies of bootcamps in Beirut and Nairobi
findings: The bootcamps combine intensive socio-emotional and technical (coding) skills training designed for rapid job placement, run as short, employer-linked 'skills accelerators.' The publicly available summary emphasizes program design lessons over pooled quantitative impact estimates; it remains one of the only RCT-evaluated coding-bootcamp models for youth employment in an LMIC setting.
magnitude: One of few RCT-evaluated coding-bootcamp models for youth employment in an LMIC (Medellin, Colombia)

design: Theoretical growth model with Baumol-style task bottlenecks
authors: Aghion, P., Jones, B.F., Jones, C.I.
title: Artificial Intelligence and Economic Growth
venue: NBER Working Paper 23928 (also in 'The Economics of Artificial Intelligence: An Agenda', 2019)
data: No empirical data; theoretical growth model built on Baumol's cost-disease logic applied to automation
findings: The paper frames AI as the latest wave in a 200-year automation process and shows that aggregate growth can remain constrained by tasks that are essential but hard to automate or improve (Baumol bottlenecks), even as AI dramatically raises productivity in automatable tasks. The framework is used to discuss how AI could affect the labor/capital income split and revives debates about technological 'singularities,' without providing single-point growth forecasts.
magnitude: Theoretical result: growth can stay bottlenecked by hard-to-automate essential tasks even amid rapid AI-driven automation elsewhere

design: RCT, 318 rural primary schools
authors: Cristia, Ibarraran, Cueto, Santiago, and Severin
title: Technology and Child Development: Evidence from the One Laptop per Child Program
data: Randomized rollout of OLPC XO laptops across 318 rural primary schools; student/teacher surveys and cognitive/achievement tests
findings: The program raised the computer-to-student ratio from 0.12 to 1.18 and sharply increased computer use both at school and at home. Despite this large increase in access and use, there is no evidence of effects on math or language test scores after 15 months, though there is some evidence of gains in general cognitive skills (abstract reasoning).
magnitude: Computers-per-student rose from 0.12 to 1.18; zero effect on math/language test scores despite the large access increase

design: Administrative-data and household-survey assessment of a nationwide digital land-regularization program
authors: Daniel Ayalew Ali, Klaus Deininger, Marguerite Duponchel
title: New Ways to Assess and Enhance Land Registry Sustainability: Evidence from Rwanda
data: Administrative records from Rwanda's digital Land Administration Information System merged with household surveys
findings: Rwanda's nationwide digital land-regularization program (creating a digital register of over 11 million parcels) improved gender equity in land documentation and expanded credit-market access, and decentralizing subsequent transaction-registration services to the local level significantly reduced informal (unregistered) land transactions. However, persistently high informality in rural areas raises concerns about the long-run sustainability of the digital registry absent continued investment in decentralized service delivery.
magnitude: Decentralized digital registry services significantly cut informal land transactions, though rural sustainability risks remain

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Use new individual-level survey data from India to evaluate how digital identification systems - particularly Aadhaar - have facilitated financial inclusion for rural and agricultural households. The study focuses on India’s flagship Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY), a government-led financial inclusion initiative that leverages Aadhaar to simplify and reduce the cost of opening bank accounts. The data show that account ownership has risen sharply, especially among women and poor adults, because of PMJDY’s streamlined application process and Aadhaar-enabled identification. Despite these improvements, the report finds that people still face informal costs—including document preparation, travel, and time lost—when applying for an account. These barriers remain more pronounced for women, rural residents, and individuals with lower education levels. The findings highlight the importance of designing inclusive and accessible account-opening mechanisms and suggest targeted policy measures to further reduce transaction costs and encourage both account ownership and usage.

design: Household survey of biometric ration authentication compliance and exclusion
authors: Jean Drèze, Nazar Khalid, Reetika Khera, Anmol Somanchi
title: Aadhaar and Food Security in Jharkhand: Pain without Gain?
data: Household survey of ~1,000 households across 32 villages in Jharkhand, following mandatory Aadhaar-based biometric authentication (ABBA) for ration shops
findings: In areas where biometric authentication was required for every ration sale, exclusion errors reached about 20%; in one gram panchayat (Tirla), 40 of 225 sampled households reported being deprived of rations for a month or more since ABBA became compulsory. Failures stemmed from fingerprint mismatches, poor connectivity, and incomplete Aadhaar 'seeding' of ration cards, with costs falling disproportionately on the elderly and manual laborers.
magnitude: Exclusion errors of roughly 20% in villages with mandatory biometric ration authentication

design: Instrumental variables
findings: Using an instrumental variables strategy that exploits cross-state variation in supply side constraints to residential broadband Internet access, Lisa J. Dettling (2017) find that exogenously determined high-speed Internet usage leads to a 4.1 percentage point increase in labor force participation for married women. There is no corresponding effect on single women or men. Among married women, the largest increases in participation are found among college-educated women with children. Supplemental analyses suggest that Internet use for telework and time saving in home production explain the increase in participation. The results suggest home Internet facilitates work-family balance.

design: Diff-in-differences using phase-wise policy rollout across districts plus its unexpected nationwide termination, with an original black-market audit survey
title: Curbing Leakage in Public Programs: Evidence from India's Direct Benefit Transfer Policy
venue: Working Paper, Michigan State University / International Growth Centre
data: 23.2 million LPG refill transactions from 3.79 million beneficiary households across 509 districts; distributor-level sales data from 3,341 distributors; original black-market audit survey of LPG delivery agents and small businesses in 89 districts
findings: Requiring Aadhaar/bank-verified Direct Benefit Transfer (DBTL) before releasing LPG cooking-fuel subsidies reduced subsidized ('domestic') fuel purchases by 11-14%, consistent with eliminating fraudulent 'ghost' beneficiary accounts. When the policy was unexpectedly terminated, domestic fuel sales reverted to control-district levels and black-market fuel prices fell by 13-20%, while commercial-sector (tax-paying) fuel purchases fell 6-9% as diverted subsidized fuel flowed back into the black market -- confirming the reform's effect on both formal and informal markets.
magnitude: Digital verification of subsidy recipients cut diverted fuel purchases 11-14% and moved black-market prices 13-20%

design: Literature review of the economics of mobile money
title: Mobile Money
data: Synthesis of the empirical literature on mobile-money adoption, risk-sharing, savings, and poverty impacts
findings: Surveys the rapid diffusion of mobile money since Kenya's 2007 M-Pesa launch and the accumulated evidence that it lowers the transaction costs of remittances and risk-sharing, increases savings, and -- per Suri and Jack (2016) -- reduced poverty in Kenya by about 2 percentage points, while noting more limited and mixed evidence on impacts in other countries with different agent-network density and regulatory environments.
magnitude: Synthesizes evidence that mobile money reduced Kenyan poverty by about 2 percentage points via lower transaction costs

design: Cross-country comparative analysis (countries with vs. without Universal Access/Service Funds)
title: The Impact of Universal Service Funds on Fixed-Broadband Deployment and Internet Adoption in Asia and the Pacific
data: Cross-country panel comparing fixed-broadband and internet-adoption trajectories in countries with versus without Universal Access/Service Funds (UASFs) across Asia-Pacific
findings: Countries that established Universal Access and Service Funds targeting broadband/internet expansion do not, on average, show better fixed-broadband or internet-adoption growth than countries without such funds, a result attributed to weaknesses in fund design, governance, and slow or incomplete disbursement rather than the policy instrument being inherently ineffective; some individual, well-implemented country programs did successfully connect underserved rural areas.
magnitude: No significant average improvement in broadband/internet growth from having a Universal Service Fund versus not, across Asia-Pacific -- effectiveness hinges on implementation design

design: Literature review synthesizing theoretical and empirical economics of privacy
authors: Alessandro Acquisti, Curtis Taylor, Liad Wagman
title: The Economics of Privacy
data: Synthesis of theoretical and empirical economics-of-privacy literature, spanning consumer valuation of privacy, price discrimination, data as an asset, and privacy regulation
findings: The review documents that consumers' stated valuations of privacy are highly context-dependent and manipulable by framing (the gap between willingness-to-pay to protect data and willingness-to-accept to disclose it), that data can act as a source of both efficiency (matching, price discrimination that can increase output) and inefficiency/consumer harm, and that welfare effects of privacy regulation are theoretically ambiguous and depend on market structure and the nature of data externalities across consumers.
magnitude: Establishes that measured privacy valuations vary by an order of magnitude depending on elicitation framing (willingness-to-pay vs. willingness-to-accept)

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Arroyo Prieto and Valenduc (2016) examine the impact of digital skills (computer and internet skills) on the labor market opportunities for low-skilled women. The study, conducted within the framework of ICT training initiatives by NGOs, uses a qualitative analysis to assess how these skills influence the employability of this demographic. Covering the period of rapid digitalization in the economy, the paper finds that while digital skills are essential, they alone do not significantly improve the labor market position of low-skilled women. The study emphasizes that broader gender equality measures and increased job opportunities are necessary to close the employment gap.

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: The European Commission (2016) study is based on a survey conducted among 7,800 workplaces in six EU member states, representing a wide range of economic sectors. It uses quantitative and qualitative data to assess digital skills (ability to use digital technologies effectively, including basic, advanced, and specialist skills) requirements and gaps which highlight the need for digital skills training to increase economic growth. 15% of workplaces report digital skills gaps, especially larger firms, suggesting that digital skills are crucial for improving productivity, efficiency, and business performance. Rather than studying the effect of digital skills on economic growth, it identifies the lack of digital skills as a barrier to technological adoption and economic growth.

design: Conceptual framework and case-based synthesis of open government data business models
authors: Fatemeh Ahmadi Zeleti, Adegboyega Ojo, Edward Curry
title: Exploring the Economic Value of Open Government Data
countries: Case studies drawn from multiple OECD countries
data: Case-study analysis of firms and business models built on open government data releases
findings: Develops a taxonomy of five open-data business archetypes (suppliers, aggregators, enrichers, application developers, and enablers) and documents case examples of firms built substantially on reusing open government data, some reaching billion-dollar valuations. The paper is a conceptual/case-based contribution rather than a causal econometric estimate, illustrating the mechanisms through which open data can seed private-sector entrepreneurship, while noting that rigorous causal estimates of open data's productivity effects remain scarce relative to industry-consultancy projections (e.g., McKinsey Global Institute's oft-cited $3-5 trillion/year global estimate).
magnitude: Identifies five distinct open-data business models and documents billion-dollar firms built on reusing open government data, though notes a scarcity of causal (vs. consultancy-projected) productivity estimates

design: randomized comparison of cash vs. mobile-money transfer delivery mechanisms
authors: Jenny C. Aker, Rachid Boumnijel, Amanda McClelland, Niall Tierney
title: Payment Mechanisms and Anti-Poverty Programs: Evidence from a Mobile Money Cash Transfer Experiment in Niger
period: Post-2009-2010 Sahel food-crisis humanitarian transfer progr…
data: Village-randomized experiment comparing cash, mobile-money, and mobile-money-plus-training transfer arms
