findings: In a randomized humanitarian cash-transfer program following the Sahel food crisis, delivering transfers via mobile money rather than cash raised household and child dietary diversity by 9%-16%, reduced travel time and cost of collecting transfers, and gave recipients (especially women) more control over spending, partly because mobile-money payments were less visible and thus harder for other household/village members to claim.
magnitude: Mobile-money delivery of humanitarian transfers raised child dietary diversity by 9%-16% versus cash delivery

design: RCT, phased rollout of biometric Smartcard payments across 296 sub-districts
authors: Karthik Muralidharan, Paul Niehaus, Sandip Sukhtankar
title: Building State Capacity: Evidence from Biometric Smartcards in India
data: Administrative NREGS/SSP payment records; household survey of ~8,000 households in 8 districts; AEA RCT registry AEARCTR-0001417
findings: Biometrically-authenticated Smartcard payments for NREGS workfare and SSP pensions cut leakage by 41% and 47% respectively, saving an estimated $38.5 million/year (NREGS) and $3.2 million/year (SSP). Beneficiaries collected payments 20% faster (22 fewer minutes) and were paid 6-10 days sooner, with NREGS program participation rising 17% and no reduction in access. Adoption remained incomplete, reaching only 67% (79%) of villages for NREGS (SSP).
magnitude: NREGS leakage fell 41% and payments arrived 6-10 days faster with no loss of access

design: Quasi-experimental
findings: Compare the effect of geographic distance on eBay and total international trade flows. The paper considers the same 61 countries and basket of goods for both types of transactions. It finds the effect of distance to be on average 65% smaller on eBay. We argue this difference is due to a reduction in search costs; it increases with product differentiation and is higher when trade partners speak different languages, when corruption in the exporting country is high and when uncertainty avoidance is high in the importing country. Moreover, eBay’s seller‐rating technology further reduces the distance effect on eBay.

design: Natural experiment comparing e-procurement vs. manual tendering across Indian and Indonesian road contracts
authors: Sean Lewis-Faupel, Yusuf Neggers, Benjamin A. Olken, Rohini Pande
title: Can Electronic Procurement Improve Infrastructure Provision? Evidence From Public Works in India and Indonesia
venue: American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, 8(3), 258-283 (NBER WP 20344)
data: Engineering road-quality audits and procurement/contractor records from Indian and Indonesian public works agencies
findings: E-procurement did not reduce prices paid by government for public works, but was associated with higher-quality roads in India and fewer project delays in Indonesia. The main channel was selection: e-procurement broadened the pool of bidders, drawing more winning contractors from outside the local region and raising average contractor quality.
magnitude: No price effect from e-procurement, but measurably higher road quality (India) and fewer delays (Indonesia)

design: Long-difference analysis exploiting geographic variation in M-Pesa agent-network expansion
title: The Long-Run Poverty and Gender Impacts of Mobile Money
data: Panel household survey data tracking M-Pesa mobile-money agent access across Kenya
findings: Use a quasi-experimental design leveraging the staggered rollout of M-PESA agents across Kenya to estimate the long-run impacts of mobile money access on household welfare. Through analyzing the longitudinal household survey data collected between 2008 and 2014, the study finds that access to M-PESA increased per capita consumption and lifted an estimated 194,000 households (roughly 2% of all Kenyan households) out of extreme poverty. The poverty reduction effect was especially pronounced among female-headed households, which experienced a 9.2% reduction in extreme poverty. Moreover, M-PESA access enabled occupational shifts, with approximately 185,000 women transitioning from agriculture into business or retail work. The study provides strong causal evidence that mobile money can improve financial resilience, facilitate economic mobility, and reduce poverty - especially for women - by lowering transaction costs and enabling better management of financial shocks.
magnitude: M-Pesa access lifted roughly 2% of Kenyan households (about 194,000-196,000) out of extreme poverty

design: Descriptive analysis
authors: Ajay Agrawal, John Horton, Nicola Lacetera and Elizabeth Lyons
title: Digitization and the Contract Labor Market: A Research Agenda
venue: In A. Goldfarb, S. Greenstein and C. Tucker (eds.), Economic Analysis of the Digital Economy, University of Chicago Press / NBER, April 2015, pp. 219-250 (NBER Working Paper 19525, October 2013)
findings: Analyze data from online labor platforms, oDesk to study the contract labor market's dynamics, focusing on the effects of digitization. Key findings include an over 800% increase in employers and a 1,000% increase in contractors between 2009 and 2013. The quarterly wage bill surged by 900%, from $10 million to nearly $100 million. Digitization lowered transaction costs, enhanced matching efficiency, and enabled global labor access. The study also observes the "superstar effect," where top performers capture a larger market share, and discusses digitization's impact on firm boundaries by facilitating outsourcing. Key mechanisms include reduced search and communication costs, improved matching efficiency, and the ability to access a global pool of labor. The paper also notes the role of digital platforms in providing standardized information to reduce information asymmetries.

design: Difference-in-differences (mobile coverage rollout x producer-price panel)
title: Mobile Phone Coverage and Producer Markets: Evidence from West Africa
data: Producer-level price data for cowpea and other crops across Nigerien markets matched with mobile-coverage rollout data
findings: Mobile phone coverage reduces the spatial dispersion of producer prices by about 6% for cowpea, a semi-perishable commodity, with effects strongest in remote markets and during certain seasons; effects are smaller or insignificant for less perishable/storable crops, suggesting the channel runs mainly through reduced search costs and spoilage-related waste.
magnitude: -6% spatial producer-price dispersion for cowpea after mobile coverage, strongest in remote markets

design: RCT, ~1,000 laptops distributed for home use
authors: Beuermann, Cristia, Cueto, Malamud, and Cruz-Aguayo
title: One Laptop per Child at Home: Short-Term Impacts from a Randomized Experiment in Peru
data: RCT distributing approximately 1,000 OLPC XO laptops for home use to primary-school children in Lima; household and school surveys
findings: Take-home laptops substantially increase children's computer use at home and improve some cognitive skills (verbal fluency), but there is no evidence of impacts on math or language academic achievement, nor on school effort or grade repetition, in the short run.
magnitude: Large increase in home computer use; no short-run effect on math/language test scores

design: Regression-discontinuity/threshold analysis around VAT third-party information reporting and audit-threat letters
title: No Taxation without Information: Deterrence and Self-Enforcement in the Value Added Tax
data: Administrative VAT records and a randomized audit-threat letter experiment covering over 400,000 Chilean firms
findings: The VAT's paper trail on transactions between firms generates a self-enforcing 'third-party reporting' effect: audit-threat letters had much larger deterrent effects on reported sales for transactions without a cross-verifiable paper trail (i.e., final consumer sales) than for business-to-business transactions already covered by electronic invoice matching, showing that digitized information trails substitute for costly audits.
magnitude: Digital third-party information on B2B transactions made audit threats far less necessary than for unverified consumer sales

design: Randomized controlled trial of work-from-home assignment within a single large firm
authors: Nicholas Bloom, James Liang, John Roberts, Zhichun Jenny Ying
title: Does Working from Home Work? Evidence from a Chinese Experiment
data: RCT at CTrip (16,000-employee Chinese travel agency): call-center volunteers randomly assigned to work from home vs. office for 9 months
findings: Working from home raised performance by 13%, split between a 9% gain from working more minutes per shift (fewer breaks/sick days) and a 4% gain from handling more calls per minute in a quieter environment. When employees were later allowed to choose, over half switched arrangements and performance gains almost doubled to 22% due to better self-selection, though promotion rates conditional on performance fell for home workers.
magnitude: Working from home raised call-center performance 13% in the RCT, rising to 22% once workers could self-select

design: Network measurement study using RIPE Atlas probes and controlled BGP route announcements (selective BGP announcements across upstream-only, IXP-only, and combined scenarios)
title: Is It Really Worth Peering at IXPs? A Comparative Study
data: Approximately 150 RIPE Atlas probes and controlled BGP announcements from three Italian ISPs (Mc-link, Seeweb, Unidata) measuring paths via two Italian IXPs (MIX, NaMeX)
findings: About 70% of probes using IXPs achieved average round-trip times of 30ms or less, versus only 20% of probes not using IXPs; for one major target, 50% of probes reached it within 15ms via IXPs versus just 30% via upstream transit. Roughly 80% of non-IXP paths were forced to traverse a non-Italian autonomous system (AS3356) even for purely domestic traffic, versus zero IXP paths, confirming that peering keeps domestic traffic local and reduces latency, hop count, packet loss, and jitter -- with the largest gains accruing to smaller, customer-class networks.
magnitude: IXP peering raises the share of connections with round-trip latency under 30ms from 20% to 70%, and eliminates the need for domestic traffic to route through foreign networks

design: Empirical analysis of intrusion detection/honeypot data linking vulnerability disclosure policy to attack diffusion
title: Information Disclosure and the Diffusion of Information Security Attacks
period: Not precisely specified in verified abstract
data: Intrusion detection system and honeypot data on attack volumes linked to the timing and completeness of security vulnerability disclosures
findings: The paper (building on the authors' earlier work on 'The Impact of Immediate Disclosure on Attack Diffusion and Volume') shows that public disclosure of security vulnerabilities affects how quickly and widely attacks exploiting those vulnerabilities diffuse across the internet, informing the central policy tradeoff in coordinated vulnerability disclosure and disclosure-timing regulation: transparency for defenders versus a roadmap for attackers.
magnitude: Timing and completeness of vulnerability disclosure systematically shapes the speed and volume of subsequent attack diffusion

design: Descriptive analysis
authors: Martin H. Thelle, Bruno Basalisco, Niels Christian Fredslund, Tine Jeppesen, Jacek Przybyszewski and Eva R. Sunesen
title: The economic impact of Google's data centre in Belgium
venue: Copenhagen Economics, study prepared for Google, June 2015, 37 pp.
findings: Assessed the economic impact of Google's data center in St. Ghislain near Mons from 2007 to 2014 using an input-output model. The study found that the data center contributed an average of €110 million per year to GDP, totaling €900 million over the period. Additionally, the employment impact averaged 1,500 full-time equivalent jobs annually.

design: Structural model
findings: Use a macroeconomic model to simulate the impact of digital structural reforms across different sectors. It evaluates reforms in areas such as radio spectrum, professional e-skills (competencies required to effectively use digital technologies in professional settings), eCommerce, and fixed broadband. Digital structural reforms can significantly boost GDP by improving productivity and efficiency. For example, reforms in professional e-skills are estimated to increase GDP by 0.1% to 0.3% in the long run. The paper identifies mechanisms such as increased labor productivity, enhanced innovation, and improved market efficiency as pathways through which digital reforms impact economic growth.

design: Computable general equilibrium (GTAP) modeling of data localization's economic effects across seven countries
authors: Matthias Bauer, Hosuk Lee-Makiyama, Erik van der Marel, Bert Verschelde
title: The Costs of Data Localisation: Friendly Fire in the War on Terror (methodology later published as "A Methodology to Estimate the Costs of Data Regulations," International Economics, 2016)
countries: Brazil, China, European Union, India, Indonesia, South Korea, Vietnam
period: 2014 analysis (GTAP baseline calibrated to mid-2010s trade/i…
data: A proxy index of data-localization/regulation barriers by country, fed into a GTAP computable general equilibrium trade model to simulate GDP, investment, and welfare effects
findings: Data localization measures produce negative GDP effects in every country studied: GDP falls by an estimated 0.1% (India) to 1.7% (Vietnam), with China at -1.1% and the EU at -0.4%. Domestic investment falls even more sharply (e.g., -4.2% in Brazil, -3.9% in the EU, -1.8% in China). Aggregate welfare losses reach an estimated $63 billion for China and $193 billion for the EU, equivalent to 11-20% of the average monthly salary per worker across the countries studied. The authors conclude that any security or industrial-policy benefits of localization are too small to outweigh these output and welfare losses.
magnitude: Data localization is estimated to cut GDP by 0.1-1.7% and domestic investment by up to 4.2% across 7 major economies, with welfare losses up to $193bn (EU) and $63bn (China)

design: Triple-difference (sector x firm-fixed-effects x time) around staggered mandatory adoption of electronic billing machines
authors: Nada Eissa, Andrew Zeitlin, Saahil Karpe, Sally Murray
title: Incidence and Impact of Electronic Billing Machines for VAT in Rwanda
data: Universe of quarterly VAT payments (2012q1-2014q3) for 9,655 firms, merged with Electronic Billing Machine (EBM) registration/activation records; a 129-visit 'mystery shopper' audit of Kigali retailers
findings: EBM adoption reached 77.8% of active VAT taxpayers by 2014q3 and raised firms' VAT payments by an average of 6.5%, with larger effects in computing/printing, construction and retail. A mystery-shopper audit found that, unprompted, only about 21% of small transactions received an EBM receipt, but simply asking for a receipt raised the likelihood of receiving one by 42 percentage points, pointing to incomplete utilization even among adopting firms as a key remaining compliance gap.
magnitude: EBM adoption raised VAT payments 6.5% on average, but unprompted receipt issuance was only 21%

design: Difference-in-differences exploiting staggered geographic rollout of mobile-money agents
title: Risk Sharing and Transactions Costs: Evidence from Kenya's Mobile Money Revolution
data: Household panel surveys tracking M-Pesa access, remittances and consumption around idiosyncratic income shocks
findings: Explore the impact of reduced transaction costs on risk sharing by estimating the effects of a mobile money innovation on consumption in Kenya. In their panel sample, adoption of mobile money increased from 43 to 70 percent. The paper finds that, while shocks reduce consumption by 7 percent for nonusers, the consumption of user households is unaffected. The mechanisms underlying these consumption effects are increases in remittances received and the diversity of senders. The paper reports robustness checks supporting these results and use the four-fold expansion of the mobile money agent network as a source of exogenous variation in access to the innovation.
magnitude: Mobile-money users fully absorbed income shocks via remittances; non-users' consumption fell

design: Cost-accounting synthesis across categories of cybercrime (direct losses, indirect losses, defense expenditure)
authors: Ross Anderson, Chris Barton, Rainer Böhme, Richard Clayton, Michel J.G. van Eeten, Michael Levi, Tyler Moore, Stefan Sav…
title: Measuring the Cost of Cybercrime
venue: The Economics of Information Security and Privacy (Springer)
data: Synthesis and re-estimation of cost figures across categories of cybercrime (e.g., online banking fraud, fake antivirus, patent-medicine scams, cybercrime infrastructure) drawing on industry, law-enforcement, and survey data
findings: The foundational study in this literature argues that societies systematically misallocate cybercrime-fighting resources: expenditure on anticipation/defense (antivirus, compliance) for many categories of 'traditional' crimes migrated online exceeds the direct losses those crimes cause, while genuinely new cybercrimes (e.g., large-scale card fraud infrastructure) impose the largest direct losses and receive comparatively little law-enforcement resource. The authors recommend shifting spending from purely defensive measures toward international law-enforcement response and takedown capacity.
magnitude: Indirect and defense costs of cybercrime (antivirus, compliance) exceed direct losses for many traditional crimes migrated online, while a few large-scale cybercrime categories drive most direct losses

design: RCT (adult-education program combined with mobile-phone literacy training, "Project ABC")
title: Can Mobile Phones Improve Learning? Evidence from a Field Experiment in Niger
data: RCT among adult-literacy students in Nigerien villages, randomizing a mobile-phone-based literacy/numeracy curriculum ("Project ABC") against the standard curriculum
findings: Adding basic mobile-phone use (writing texts, navigating phone menus) to an adult literacy curriculum raises writing and math test scores by about 0.19-0.26 standard deviations relative to the standard curriculum, with effects concentrated among women, who also report using their new skills to send/receive text messages more after the program.
magnitude: +0.19-0.26 SD on writing/math test scores from adding mobile-phone literacy training to adult education, Niger

design: Panel fixed-effects analysis (cross-country, Sub-Saharan African mobile markets)
title: Implications of Mandatory Registration of Mobile Phone Users in Africa
data: Panel of Sub-Saharan African mobile-telephony markets around the timing of mandatory SIM-registration mandates (many introduced from 2006 onward)
findings: Countries that impose mandatory SIM-card registration (tying prepaid SIM purchase to personal ID documentation) subsequently experience slower mobile-subscription penetration growth, likely reflecting the added cost, documentation burden, and privacy/surveillance concerns imposed on new subscribers, with knock-on implications for market competition.
magnitude: Mandatory SIM registration is associated with slower mobile-penetration growth across Sub-Saharan African markets after 2006

design: Diff-in-differences exploiting staggered computerization of sub-registry offices
title: Going Digital: Credit Effects of Land Registry Computerization in India
data: Administrative data on credit disbursed and registered land transactions across 387 sub-registry offices
findings: Digitizing land registry offices, without changing the underlying legal information, produced a statistically significant but quantitatively modest increase in mortgage credit in urban areas, with no detectable effect in rural areas. The authors note that a contemporaneous cut in stamp duty had a much larger effect on credit than computerization alone, suggesting digitization's benefits are context- and complement-dependent.
magnitude: Computerized land registries raised urban mortgage credit modestly; no effect in rural areas

design: RCT introducing fingerprint-based borrower identification into a rural credit market
authors: Xavier Giné, Jessica Goldberg, Dean Yang
title: Credit Market Consequences of Improved Personal Identification: Field Experimental Evidence from Malawi
data: Randomized rollout of biometric fingerprinting technology among borrowers in a rural credit market with weak identity infrastructure
findings: Fingerprinting borrowers -- which allowed the lender to withhold future loans from past defaulters and reward good repayment history even when borrowers tried to reapply under different identities -- significantly increased loan repayment rates among borrowers with the highest ex-ante default risk. The intervention had an estimated benefit-cost ratio of 2.34, providing early evidence that biometric personal identification improves credit-market efficiency where formal ID and credit-bureau infrastructure is weak.
magnitude: Biometric fingerprinting of borrowers raised repayment among high-risk borrowers with a 2.34 benefit-cost ratio

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Studies the relationship between ICT skills and employment opportunities using data from the Turkish Statistical Institute, covering the period from 2007 to 2010. The study employs probit regression models to analyze the impact of basic, medium, and advanced ICT skills on the probability of being employed. The main findings indicate that possessing ICT skills increases the likelihood of employment by 20-30%, but this positive relationship is driven by workers who acquired these skills at work, highlighting endogeneity issues such as unobserved skill bias and reverse causality. There is no causal direction from ICT skills to employment.

design: Difference-in-differences exploiting the EU e-Privacy Directive's restriction on behavioral tracking
title: Privacy Regulation and Online Advertising
countries: European Union (vs. rest of world comparison)
period: Around the EU e-Privacy Directive's implementation (mid-2000…
data: Data on advertising effectiveness (stated purchase intent) for a large sample of display ad campaigns in the EU compared with non-EU markets, before and after the e-Privacy Directive restricted behaviorally targeted data use
findings: The EU's e-Privacy Directive, which restricted the collection and use of data for behavioral ad targeting, reduced advertising effectiveness by an average of about 65% in the EU relative to the rest of the world, with the loss concentrated among general-content publishers, simple display ads, smaller ad formats, and ads lacking rich interactive/video features that could otherwise compensate for the loss of targeting data.
magnitude: The EU e-Privacy Directive's restriction on behavioral tracking cut display-ad effectiveness by about 65% on average

design: Difference-in-differences using staggered state adoption of data breach notification laws
authors: Sasha Romanosky, Rahul Telang, Alessandro Acquisti
title: Do Data Breach Disclosure Laws Reduce Identity Theft?
venue: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management, 30(2): 256-286
data: Panel of FTC identity-theft complaint rates by U.S. state and year matched to the staggered timing of state data breach notification law adoption
findings: Using variation from the staggered rollout of state mandatory breach-notification laws, the study finds that such laws are associated with a reduction in identity theft, plausibly because notification prompts consumers to take protective action (e.g., monitoring accounts, replacing cards) after a breach. The paper is a foundational reference for the economics of breach-notification regulation, though the authors note the effect is difficult to estimate precisely and is likely modest relative to the total identity-theft problem.
magnitude: State mandatory data-breach notification laws are associated with a measurable reduction in identity theft rates, using 2002-2009 state panel data

design: Descriptive analysis of repeated household survey rounds
title: Mobile Money: The Economics of M-PESA
data: Repeated household surveys tracking M-PESA mobile-money adoption, agent networks, and usage patterns in Kenya
findings: The paper documents the rapid, broad-based adoption of M-PESA across income, wealth, gender, and location groups, and characterizes its main uses for savings, remittances, and as an emerging general-purpose payment instrument, alongside the liquidity/inventory-management challenges faced by cash agents.
magnitude: Foundational descriptive account of M-PESA's rapid diffusion across Kenyan society, 2008-2010

design: Difference-in-differences (staggered mobile-tower rollout x grain-market price panel)
title: Information from Markets Near and Far: Mobile Phones and Agricultural Markets in Niger
data: Market- and trader-level grain price data across Nigerien markets matched to mobile-phone tower rollout dates
findings: Introduction of mobile phone service between market pairs reduces grain price dispersion by 10-16%, with larger effects for market pairs that are farther apart and connected by poor-quality (dirt) roads, consistent with phones lowering traders' search and spatial-arbitrage costs.
magnitude: 10-16% reduction in inter-market grain price dispersion following mobile-phone coverage, Niger 2001-2006

design: Descriptive/review of early mobile-phone-and-development literature
title: Mobile Phones and Economic Development in Africa
data: Descriptive review of mobile-phone penetration trends and emerging microeconomic evidence (agricultural markets, financial services, job search) across Africa
findings: Documents the extraordinarily rapid diffusion of mobile phones across Africa in the 2000s (from near-zero to substantial penetration within a decade) and reviews early microeconomic evidence that mobile phones reduce information/search frictions in agricultural markets, expand access to financial services (mobile money), and improve efficiency in labor and product markets, while cautioning that rigorous causal evidence at the time remained limited to a handful of settings.
magnitude: Synthesizes early evidence that mobile telephony diffused faster in Africa than any prior technology, with documented market-efficiency gains but a still-thin causal evidence base as of 2010

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Use qualitative analysis of existing literature and case studies on government initiatives and policies. They find that e-government and social media increase transparency and reduce corruption by enhancing government accountability through openness, promoting citizen participation, creating new channels for reporting corruption, and facilitating easier monitoring of government activities. They suggest that these initiatives reduce bureaucratic barriers, create a more level playing field for businesses, and improve efficiency in government-business interactions.

design: Instrumental variables (terrain/topography instrument for cell-tower placement)
title: Cell Phones and Rural Labor Markets: Evidence from South Africa
venue: Proceedings of the German Development Economics Conference, Hannover 2010 (CSAE-affiliated working paper)
data: Geocoded mobile-network coverage data plus nationally representative labor-force survey data; topographic terrain data used as an instrument for tower placement
findings: Mobile phone coverage raises the local employment rate by about 15 percentage points, with most of the gain concentrated among women, especially those without heavy childcare burdens. New jobs are overwhelmingly wage employment, while agricultural employment falls substantially, especially for men.
magnitude: +15 percentage points in local employment rate after mobile coverage arrives, concentrated among women

design: Instrumental variables, Panel regression
findings: Using panel data of OECD countries during 1996-2007 and an instrumental variable model where pre-existing voice telephony cand cable TV networks predict broadband penetration, Czernich et al. (2009) found that a 10 percentage point increase in broadband penetration increases annual GDP per capita growth by 0.9-1.5 percentage points.

design: Structural model
findings: Examined the economic impact of cloud computing on business creation, employment, and output using a dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) model. The findings indicate that cloud computing could lead to the creation of hundreds of thousands of new small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), contributing up to 0.3% to the annual growth rate (in the medium run under fast adoption of cloud computing) and creating about a million new jobs in the European Union over five years. The reduction of fixed ICT costs to variable costs significantly lowers entry barriers, promoting business creation and competition.

design: Cross-sectional association
findings: Surveyed 454 people enrolled in programs provided by non-profits and public workforce-development organizations between 2007-2008, which combine ICT training with soft skills and employment support services. They find that after attending the training, the percentage of participants that received employment increased from 17% to 58%, implying higher levels of ICT skills being correlated to increased employment. Participants employed after the training experienced an average 20% increase in wages compared to overall pre-training earnings. Age also played a factor – the older the worker, the lower the increase in wages.

design: Cross-country comparative welfare/efficiency analysis of spectrum-allocation mechanisms across 28 mobile markets
title: A Welfare Analysis of Spectrum Allocation Policies
countries: 28 countries (mix of OECD and developing markets, incl. Latin America and Asia)
data: Cross-country comparison of spectrum-allocation mechanisms (auctions vs. administrative/beauty-contest assignment) and resulting bandwidth allocation/market structure across 28 mobile-telephone markets
findings: Countries that allocate more spectrum bandwidth to licensed mobile operators and achieve more competitive market structures generate efficiency gains in output markets (lower prices, higher penetration) that generally exceed the direct fiscal gains governments capture from spectrum-license auctions, implying that a narrow focus on auction revenue can be welfare-reducing relative to prioritizing bandwidth allocation and competition.
magnitude: Efficiency gains from greater spectrum allocation plus competitive market structure generally dominate government revenue gains from license auctions, across 28 countries

design: Structural model
findings: Using data in 15 European Union countries during 2003-2006 and a simultaneous structural econometric model, Koutroumpis (2009) estimates that a 10 percentage point increase in broadband penetration is associated with a 0.26-0.85% increase in GDP. The effect is even larger when countries already have a critical mass of internet users.

design: Panel regression, Cross-sectional association
findings: Using panel data of 120 countries during 1980-2006, Qiang, Rossotto, and Kimura (2009) documented a robust and noticeable association between broadband access and GDP per capita growth: each 10 percentage point increase in broadband penetration is associated with a 1.21 percentage point increase in per capita GDP growth in high-income countries. For developing countries, the magnitude is similar - about a 1.38 percentage point increase for each 10 percent increase in penetration.

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Estimates the effects of broadband penetration on output and employment, in the aggregate and by sector, using US state level data during 2003-05. The paper found that for every 1 percentage point increase in broadband penetration in a state, employment is projected to increase by 0.2-0.3 percent per year. Employment in manufacturing and services industries is positively related to broadband penetration.

design: Natural experiment (staggered mobile-phone tower rollout along the Kerala coast)
title: The Digital Provide: Information (Technology), Market Performance, and Welfare in the South Indian Fisheries Sector
data: Weekly survey data on fish prices, sales, and catch from fishermen and wholesalers at multiple Kerala markets/landing beaches
findings: As mobile coverage spreads along the Kerala coast, fishermen begin checking prices across markets before landing their catch, and the share selling outside their home market jumps from zero to about 35%. Price dispersion for identical fish types across same-day markets collapses, waste from unsold catch is eliminated, and both fishermen profits and consumer welfare rise, consistent with the Law of One Price holding once phones remove the search friction.
magnitude: Out-of-home-market sales rise from 0% to ~35%; price dispersion and catch waste both collapse toward zero after phone adoption

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Finds that China's ICT-driven transformation from the mid-1990s to 2006 significantly improved telecommunications infrastructure and IT industry growth, contributing to GDP. E-government initiatives like Golden Tax enhanced public service efficiency, but challenges remain, including the urban-rural digital divide and ICT skill shortages.

design: Quasi-experimental
findings: Show that gravity holds in the case of digital goods consumed over the Internet that have no trading costs. Therefore trade costs cannot fully account for the effects of distance on trade. In particular, the paper shows that Americans are more likely to visit websites from nearby countries, even controlling for language, income, immigrant stock, etc. This effect only holds for taste-dependent digital products, such as music, games, and pornography. For these, a 1% increase in physical distance reduces website visits by 3.25%. For non-taste-dependent products, such as software, distance has no statistical effect.

design: Synthesis of a theoretical model (Auriol and Picard 2002) and an empirical cross-country panel analysis (Auriol and Tuske 2005: random-effects probit, 153 countries, 1985-2003)
title: Telecommunication Reforms in Developing Countries
countries: 153 developing/transition countries (panel); case studies of China and Vietnam
data: ITU, World Development Indicators, and privatization/PPI panel data across 153 developing and transition countries
findings: Synthesizing theory and cross-country panel evidence, argues telecom privatization is associated with roughly 50% employment cuts and a 38% decline in output on average, alongside a 42% gain in labor productivity, but with no clear consumer benefit; recommends liberalizing mobile/internet segments while keeping fixed-line incumbents more tightly regulated. Highlights China and Vietnam -- which paired a public fixed-line monopoly with competitive, lightly-regulated mobile entry -- as having the world's largest teledensity-rank improvements from 1990-2000 (China rising from 159th to 95th; Vietnam from 189th to 141st).
magnitude: Telecom privatization linked to ~50% employment cuts and 38% lower output despite a 42% labor-productivity gain; regulated-fixed-line-plus-competitive-mobile reformers (China, Vietnam) saw the world's largest 1990-2000 teledensity-rank gains

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Analyze the impact of computerization on U.S. labor market skills from the 1980s to the 1990s. The study shows that computerization increased demand for non-routine cognitive skills while reducing demand for routine manual and cognitive skills. Routine tasks, being more susceptible to automation, experienced decreased demand, whereas jobs requiring problem-solving and complex communication saw growth. Technological change is found to complement skilled labor, particularly in non-routine cognitive tasks, leading to wage polarization.

design: Descriptive analysis
findings: Examined the geographical agglomeration effects in the internet sector using data from the MIX-IXP in Milan from January 2000 to November 2002. The study utilized a probit model to estimate the likelihood of peering agreements between ISPs, considering factors like travel time between headquarters, maximum bandwidth, and the number of connections at other European IXPs. The findings indicated that shorter travel times between ISP headquarters, higher bandwidth, and fewer alternative European IXP connections significantly increased the likelihood of peering agreements.

design: Descriptive comparison of employment by age and occupational AI exposure in ADP payroll data, with firm-fixed-effect regressions as robustness; the authors state it is not a causal estimate
authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen
title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence
venue: Stanford Digital Economy Lab working paper (August 2026 version; updates the August 2025 paper)
data: Monthly ADP administrative payroll records for U.S. firms (3.5 to 5 million workers per month) by age group and detailed occupation; exposure from Eloundou et al. GPT-4 beta scores, with automation versus augmentation use classified from Anthropic Economic Index data
findings: This August 2026 update extends the ADP payroll panel to June 2026 and replaces the earlier headline of firm-shock-adjusted regression estimates (a 13% relative decline on July 2025 data, 16% on September 2025 data) with a simpler descriptive divergence measure. Employment of workers aged 22-25 in AI-exposed occupations now stands 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers, compared with 15% at the July 2025 vintage; in levels, employment of 22-25-year-olds in the two most exposed quintiles fell about 11% between November 2022 and June 2026, while it grew about 10% in the three least-exposed quintiles. Experienced workers show no comparable gap, the divergence works mainly through reduced hiring rather than separations and through employment rather than base pay, and it is concentrated in occupations where AI use substitutes for tasks (employment is flat or rising where use complements workers); the authors find no evidence of economy-wide displacement. Caveats: the authors stress these are descriptive facts, not causal estimates; the patterns attenuate when controlling for education, partly predate generative AI, and are more pronounced in the ADP sample than in national survey benchmarks.
magnitude: Employment of 22-25-year-olds in AI-exposed occupations is 19% below the level implied by less-exposed peers as of June 2026 (15% on July 2025 data); no comparable gap for experienced workers

design: Difference-in-differences, triple-difference and staggered event study comparing junior and senior employment at firms posting 'GenAI integrator' vacancies with non-adopting firms
authors: Seyed M. Hosseini and Guy Lichtinger
title: Generative AI as Seniority-Biased Technological Change: Evidence from U.S. Résumé and Job Posting Data
venue: SSRN working paper (first version August 2025; version of 6 May 2026)
data: U.S. LinkedIn résumé and job-posting data (Revelio Labs): about 65 million workers at more than 280,000 firms, 2015-2025, and almost 200 million job postings; 10,433 firms flagged as GenAI adopters by March 2025
findings: Firms are classed as GenAI adopters if they post at least one 'GenAI integrator' vacancy (10,433 firms by March 2025, 3.7% of firms but about 16% of employment). Adopters and non-adopters followed parallel junior-employment trends in 2015-2022; from 2023Q1 junior employment at adopters falls by about 9% after six quarters relative to non-adopters, while senior employment keeps rising. A triple-difference with firm-by-time and industry-by-time-by-seniority fixed effects gives the same drop, and the event study shows 8% after eight quarters. Junior employment in high-exposure occupations contracts roughly 7% relative to low-exposure occupations between 2022Q4 and 2025Q1, exposed tasks disappear from junior job postings, and the decline comes mainly from slower hiring rather than separations; juniors from mid-tier universities lose most. Caveats: adoption is proxied by integrator postings (silent adoption is missed), estimates are relative between firms rather than aggregate effects, and the authors suggest firms may be cutting hiring in anticipation of automation.
magnitude: Junior employment at GenAI-adopting firms about 9% lower than at non-adopters after six quarters; senior employment unaffected

design: Instrumented event study of foreign affiliates of multinationals that adopt generative AI (instrument: AI adoption by other multinationals headquartered in the same metropolitan area), matched to non-adopting affiliates
authors: Bharat Chandar and Bouke Klein Teeselink
title: How Does AI Change Labor Demand? Evidence from 41 Countries
venue: Stanford Digital Economy Lab working paper (20 September 2026)
countries: 41 countries, from the United States, Germany and Japan to Brazil, Turkey, South Africa, India, Indonesia and Egypt
data: Revelio Labs: 1.25 billion job postings and 154 million employment records for 395,638 affiliates in 41 countries (main sample 26,102 treated and 27,697 matched control affiliates), monthly
findings: Affiliates of AI-adopting multinationals (adoption inferred from generative-AI job ads) are matched to similar non-adopting affiliates in the same country and sector, with adoption instrumented by peer adoption near the parent's headquarters. By March 2026 the junior share of employment is 1.9 percentage points lower at treated affiliates, because senior employment is 6.7% higher while junior employment is 2.5% lower (not statistically significant); total employment is 3.3% higher (marginally significant). Adoption shifts demand toward the most-exposed seniors (5%) and away from the most-exposed juniors (2%). Re-estimating for 31 countries, the junior share falls in 23, significantly in seven including the United States, Brazil and Saudi Arabia (average decline 1.1 percentage points); junior losses are somewhat deeper in richer, more digitised economies, though most cross-country correlations are insignificant. Caveats: Revelio coverage is skewed to digitally attached multinational affiliates, so estimates may not represent domestic firms, and the productivity gains inferred from the model are modest and suggestive.
magnitude: Junior share of employment 1.9 percentage points lower at AI-adopting affiliates by March 2026 (average 1.1 points across 31 countries); senior employment +6.7%, total employment +3.3%

design: Difference-in-differences with continuous occupational GenAI exposure before and after ChatGPT, with industry-year (OEWS) or firm-year and MSA-year (Revelio) fixed effects and remote-work controls
authors: José Azar, Mireia Giné and Javier Sanz-Espín
title: The Wage Effects of Generative AI
venue: SSRN working paper (21 August 2026); previously circulated as 'AI Is Already Eroding Wages: Quasi-Experimental Evidence from Occupational Exposure'
period: Before and after ChatGPT (November 2022) to June 2026
data: BLS OEWS occupation-by-industry wages and employment (knowledge-intensive service industries); Revelio Labs job postings and matched employer-employee records through June 2026
findings: Moving from the 10th to the 90th percentile of GenAI exposure is associated with a 4.9% decline in median hourly wages in OEWS data (2025) with no statistically detectable employment change, and with declines of 8.71% in posted wages and 10.76% in starting wages in Revelio data (by 2026). Wage declines are largest for junior positions (about 7.5%, versus 3.2% for mid-level; not significant for senior) and appear across all age groups within junior positions. More exposed workers have a 3.0 percentage point lower separation rate (18.6% of the pre-period mean), driven by a 2.8-point fall in job-to-job transitions, with no change in moves into persistent non-employment; the wage elasticity of separation also falls, which the authors read as greater employer labor-market power. Results hold with controls for remote-work suitability and for industry, firm and MSA shocks. Caveats: exposure measures are imperfect and identification rests on the ChatGPT timing.
magnitude: 10th-to-90th percentile of GenAI exposure: -4.9% median hourly wages (OEWS), -8.71% posted wages and -10.76% starting wages (Revelio); no detectable employment change

design: Event-time difference-in-differences comparing initial employment and earnings of new bachelor's graduates across college-major AI-exposure deciles before and after ChatGPT
authors: Cody Orr, Lee C. Tucker and Lawrence Warren
title: Graduating into Disruption: Labor Market Outcomes for AI-Exposed College Majors
venue: U.S. Census Bureau Center for Economic Studies Working Paper CES-26-56 (September 2026)
period: Graduation cohorts 2016-2024; employment outcomes to Q3 2025
data: Census Post-Secondary Employment Outcomes linked to LEHD: 6,665,500 bachelor's graduate records (about 29% of U.S. bachelor's degrees, 2016-2024) from participating institutions; major-level exposure built from ACS occupations and Eloundou et al. scores
findings: The most AI-exposed decile of college majors (largely computer science, information systems and related fields) saw a 5 percentage point lower likelihood of employment in the quarter after graduation and about 13% lower full-quarter initial earnings after ChatGPT's introduction, relative to graduates of less-exposed majors (the bottom six exposure deciles for employment; regression-adjusted). The earnings loss is comparable to graduating into a large recession and attenuates to about 5% after two years. About half of the earnings decline reflects lower pay within industries and half a shift of graduates from high-paying sectors such as Information and professional services toward restaurants and retail, consistent with underemployment; job switching also rises. Caveats: the sample covers participating institutions only, exposure is assigned at major level from pre-ChatGPT occupation mixes, and effects are concentrated in the top decile.
magnitude: Most AI-exposed decile of majors: -5 percentage points in initial employment and -13% in initial earnings after ChatGPT (about -5% after two years)

design: Difference-in-differences style comparison of unemployment and monthly job-finding rates between highly exposed and unexposed occupations, using a new 'observed exposure' measure (O*NET tasks, Claude usage, LLM feasibility)
title: Labor market impacts of AI: A new measure and early evidence
period: CPS from 2016; post-ChatGPT from late 2022; Claude usage Aug-Nov 2025
data: Current Population Survey (unemployment by occupation; monthly job-finding of workers aged 22-25); O*NET tasks for about 800 occupations; Anthropic Economic Index Claude usage; Eloundou et al. feasibility scores; BLS 2024-2034 projections
findings: The 'observed exposure' measure counts a task only if it is feasible for LLMs and shows sufficient work-related Claude usage, weighting automated use fully and augmentative use half; coverage is far below feasibility (Claude covers 33% of Computer & Math tasks against 94% feasible). In a difference-in-differences framework the authors find no systematic rise in unemployment for highly exposed workers since late 2022: the change in the exposed-versus-unexposed gap is small and statistically insignificant, and differential increases of about 1 percentage point would be detectable. There is tentative evidence of slower hiring of 22-25-year-olds into exposed occupations (monthly job-finding rate down about 0.5 percentage points, a 14% drop against 2022, barely statistically significant; stable at about 2% a month in unexposed occupations; no such drop for workers over 25). Each 10-point rise in observed coverage is associated with 0.6 percentage points lower BLS-projected employment growth, which the authors call slight (the feasibility measure alone shows no such correlation). Caveats: young workers may be staying in jobs, switching, or returning to school instead.
magnitude: No significant rise in unemployment of exposed workers; job-finding rate of 22-25-year-olds into exposed occupations down about 14% (about 0.5 percentage points a month), barely significant

design: Descriptive dissimilarity index of the occupational mix (CPS) since ChatGPT versus the PC and internet eras, plus occupational exposure and usage shares from OpenAI and Anthropic data
authors: Martha Gimbel, Molly Kinder, Joshua Kendall and Maddie Lee
title: Evaluating the Impact of AI on the Labor Market: Current State of Affairs
venue: The Budget Lab at Yale (report, 1 October 2025)
period: November 2022 to July 2025 (33 months after ChatGPT)
data: Monthly CPS microdata (12-month moving averages) compared with 1984-1989, 1996-2002 and 2016-2019; OpenAI GPT exposure scores and Anthropic Economic Index usage by occupation
findings: The occupational mix has changed slightly faster than in earlier technology episodes but not markedly: the post-ChatGPT path is only about 1 percentage point above the internet-era path (the 1996-2002 shift was at most about 7 points), and much of the shift began in 2021, before generative AI. The shares of workers in low-, medium- and high-exposure occupations are stable at around 29%, 46% and 18%; unemployed workers come from occupations where about 25-35% of tasks are exposed regardless of unemployment duration; and the share of employment in occupations with high AI usage is stable at around 70% (automation) or 11% (augmentation), or 3% and 0% if unobserved tasks are assumed unused. Dissimilarity between recent graduates (ages 20-24) and workers aged 25-34 has risen slightly faster recently but stays in a 30-33% range since 2021. Caveats: exposure scores are theoretical or reflect one chatbot's users, CPS samples are small for graduates, and the analysis is descriptive and cannot identify AI effects.
magnitude: No discernible economy-wide disruption: occupational mix about 1 percentage point more different from November 2022 than on the internet-era path; worker shares by exposure group stable at about 29%/46%/18%

design: Synthetic difference-in-differences comparing top-tercile AI-exposed occupations with a weighted mix of bottom-tercile occupations around ChatGPT's release (Q4 2022)
authors: Martha Gimbel, Joshua Kendall and Ryan Nunn
title: What We Do and Don't Know About How AI is Affecting the Labor Market
venue: The Budget Lab at Yale (analysis, 7 May 2026)
period: Pre-period to Q3 2022; post-period Q4 2022 to Q1 2026
data: CPS microdata underlying the monthly jobs report: occupation employment shares (of the civilian population), log real hourly wages and unemployment rates; Budget Lab AI-exposure metric
findings: Synthetic difference-in-differences accommodates the persistent differences between exposed and unexposed occupations (exposed occupations employ more women and college graduates and, before the pandemic, were less cyclical). The estimated effect of AI exposure on employment shares and on log real hourly wages is close to zero and not statistically or economically significant in any quarter of the post-2022 window. Unemployment in exposed occupations shows a positive but statistically insignificant effect in the latest quarter (roughly half a percentage point for all workers, more for ages 16-34, as of Q1 2026). Caveats: exposure metrics are imperfect proxies that average over occupations that may gain or lose, LLM capabilities keep improving, remote-work trends correlate with exposure, and the CPS is underpowered for narrow groups such as 22-27-year-old graduates, so effects confined to those groups could be missed.
magnitude: No statistically or economically significant effect of AI exposure on employment or real hourly wages through Q1 2026; unemployment effect roughly half a percentage point, statistically insignificant

design: Event study of coder employment growth around ChatGPT (November 2022) with a novel control for industry-level shocks
authors: Leland D. Crane and Paul E. Soto
title: AI and Coder Employment: Compiling the Evidence
venue: Federal Reserve Board, FEDS Working Paper 2026-018 (March 2026)
period: Pre-ChatGPT trend versus November 2022 to late 2025
data: Monthly CPS employment of programming-intensive ('coder') occupations defined with O*NET (5.735 million coder jobs as the base), by industry
findings: Coder employment growth decelerated sharply after ChatGPT: it averaged about 4.8% a year beforehand (against 1.3% for total private employment) and is now about 3 percent a year lower, with growth flat or negative in coder-intensive industries (about 6% a year before). A novel control for industry-level shocks shows the slowdown is not explained by coders working in slowing industries, pointing to an occupation-specific shock around ChatGPT's introduction; the result survives dropping the Covid period or 2022-2023, and coder wages show no break in 2022. Coder employment still grows, but much more slowly than before 2022. Caveats: the authors caution against reading the 3% as a simple causal effect, since it omits AI's aggregate demand and price effects, changes in occupational task mix and reallocation of displaced coders.
magnitude: Annual coder employment growth about 3 percent lower than before ChatGPT (pre-ChatGPT trend about 4.8% a year)

design: Cell-level monthly employment indices by occupation, age and AI-exposure quintile since October 2022 (universe of private-sector jobs), validated against within-firm estimates from individual records
authors: Øystein Hernæs and Andreas R. Kostøl
title: Has AI Widened Employment Gaps? Tracking Early-Career Employment by Occupational Exposure in Norway
data: Norwegian employer-reported monthly register (A-ordningen/ARBLONN): about 3.1 million employment relationships a month, STYRK-08 occupations mapped to AI-exposure quintiles
findings: Since October 2022, the month before ChatGPT's release, employment in the most AI-exposed occupations has grown by 0.1 percent against 0.3 percent in the least exposed (an 'AI index' of -0.2), a gap tracked monthly on the public dashboard kiindeksen.no. Comparing young workers by complete exposure quintiles, the relative decline of the most exposed quintile is estimated as an imprecise zero; a 'canary' pattern of falling youth employment appears only for selected high-exposure occupations such as software development. Cell-level results agree broadly with within-firm estimates from individual records. Caveats: Norway is a high-AI-adoption setting, employment means paid payroll employment, cells with fewer than five observations are suppressed, and the exposure ranking rests on occupation-level indices.
magnitude: Employment since October 2022: +0.1% in the most AI-exposed versus +0.3% in the least-exposed occupations; relative decline for young workers in the most exposed quintile is an imprecise zero

design: Event study of firm employment relative to each firm's own 2021-22 trend, comparing 2023 first-time AI adopters with non-adopters within industry-by-month cells (authors do not claim causality)
authors: Simone Maria Bonin, Saman Darougheh and Andreas Kuchler
title: AI Adoption and Firm Size: Employment Effects in Monthly Administrative Data
venue: Danmarks Nationalbank Working Paper No. 223 (16 September 2026)
data: Statistics Denmark IT-usage survey with AI questions since 2022 (AI use among surveyed firms rose from 15% in 2023 to 43% in 2025), matched to a monthly employer-employee register recording every wage payment
findings: Firms that first used AI in 2023 fall behind their own pre-2023 employment path by about 6% two years later and about 11% by late 2025, relative to non-adopters. The gap comes entirely from adopters with fewer than 100 FTEs (about 16 log points below trend; large adopters stay on trend) and runs through reduced hiring rather than layoffs: the stock of workers with under two years' tenure is about 28 log points below trend and the workforce ages. Employment in AI-exposed occupations at adopters is about 25% below trend against 7% elsewhere, with sharper falls among young, university-educated workers, and wages do not respond. Aggregate effects are small: an exact decomposition attributes only about a quarter of employment shed in AI-exposed industries to adoption. Caveats: adoption is not randomly assigned and the authors do not claim causal effects; the 2023 cohort of adopters is an early, selected group.
magnitude: 2023 AI adopters 6% below their own employment trend after two years and 11% by late 2025; about 16 log points for firms under 100 FTEs, flat for larger firms

design: Difference-in-differences comparing job posts for automation-prone (writing, coding) versus manual-intensive freelance jobs before and after ChatGPT and image-generation releases
authors: Ozge Demirci, Jonas Hannane and Xinrong Zhu
title: Who Is AI Replacing? The Impact of Generative AI on Online Freelancing Platforms
data: Large data set of job posts and freelancer activity from a leading global online freelancing platform; Google Trends used for public awareness of ChatGPT
findings: Comparing automation-prone jobs related to writing and coding with jobs requiring manual-intensive skills, the number of job posts fell by 21% within eight months of ChatGPT's introduction, and posts related to image creation fell by 17% after image-generating AI tools arrived. The drop in posts raises competition among freelancers, while the remaining automation-prone jobs are more complex and offer higher pay. The decline is more pronounced where public awareness of ChatGPT's substitutability (Google Trends) is higher. Caveats: the evidence comes from a single platform's job posts, so it speaks to demand for freelancers rather than to workers' total earnings or to employment outside platforms.
magnitude: -21% job posts for automation-prone writing and coding jobs versus manual-intensive jobs within eight months of ChatGPT; -17% for image-creation posts

design: Reduced-form pricing of LLM-measured application customisation before and after ChatGPT, plus a structural model of costly signalling used for counterfactual equilibria
title: Making Talk Cheap: Generative AI and Labor Market Signaling
data: Freelancer.com fixed-price coding jobs: about 61,000 postings and 2.7 million applications from 212,000 workers, split at ChatGPT's release; LLM-based measure of how tailored each proposal is to its job post
findings: Before LLMs, employers paid for customised proposals (a one-standard-deviation higher signal raised the chance of being hired as much as a $26 lower bid); after mass adoption, including the platform's own AI proposal-writing tool introduced in April 2023, that premium disappeared and signals no longer predicted successful job completion. A structural signalling model is then used to remove written signals as a counterfactual: employers identify high-ability workers less well, so workers in the top ability quintile are hired 19% less often and those in the bottom quintile 14% more often than in the pre-LLM equilibrium. The counterfactual also implies a 5% fall in average wages, a 1.5% fall in the hiring rate per posted job, a 4% fall in worker surplus and a 1% fall in total surplus. Caveats: results come from fixed-price coding jobs on one platform, and the headline hiring effects are model-based counterfactuals, not observed outcomes.
magnitude: In the model-based counterfactual without written signals, top-quintile ability workers are hired 19% less often and bottom-quintile workers 14% more often; average wages -5%

design: Randomised field experiment: 7,137 knowledge workers (3,684 treated) at 66 large firms randomly given Microsoft 365 Copilot; six-month outcomes from Microsoft 365 telemetry, ITT and IV estimates
authors: Eleanor W. Dillon, Sonia Jaffe, Nicole Immorlica and Christopher T. Stanton
title: Shifting Work Patterns with Generative AI
countries: Multiple countries (most workers in the United States or Europe)
data: Microsoft 365 activity telemetry (email, meetings, documents) for 7,137 workers in 66 large, mostly multinational firms across industries; assignment staggered between September 2023 and April 2024
findings: Workers were randomly selected to receive a generative AI assistant built into Outlook, Teams, Word and other apps. Over 90% of treated workers used it at least once and weekly use settled at just under 40%, varying mainly by firm. In months 4-6, intention-to-treat estimates show 1.4 fewer hours a week in Outlook (a 12% reduction), and IV estimates imply 2 hours (17%) for users, who also consolidated email into fewer sessions and cut time in applications outside regular hours by about 0.25 hours a week (9%). There were no significant changes in total video-meeting time, in email threads replied to, Teams meetings attended or Word documents completed, so individual time savings did not shift the quantity or composition of tasks, and there were no negative spillovers on close coworkers. Caveats: outcomes are Office-activity measures rather than output quality or performance; the firms are very large early adopters; some authors work at Microsoft.
magnitude: Copilot access cut weekly Outlook email time by 1.4 hours (12%) in the ITT estimate and 2 hours (17%) for users; no detectable shift in tasks completed

design: Randomised controlled trial at the task level: 16 experienced open-source developers completed 246 real issues, each randomly assigned to allow or disallow early-2025 AI tools
authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Elizabeth Barnes and David Rein
title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
data: 246 tasks in mature open-source repositories where the 16 developers averaged 5 years of prior experience; AI condition mainly Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet
findings: Each task was randomly assigned to allow or disallow AI tools, and completion times were compared. Allowing AI increased completion time by 19%: the tools slowed the developers down. Before starting, developers predicted AI would cut completion time by 24%, and afterwards they still believed it had cut time by 20%; economics experts had predicted a 39% reduction and machine-learning experts 38%. The authors examine 20 properties of the setting that could explain the slowdown (such as project size, quality standards and prior AI experience) and say experimental artefacts cannot be fully ruled out but the slowdown is consistent across analyses. Caveats: only 16 developers working in mature repositories they know well, using early-2025 tools, so results need not generalise to other developers, settings or later models.
magnitude: Allowing AI increased task completion time by 19% (developers had expected a 24% reduction)

design: Descriptive analysis of ChatGPT consumer use: privacy-preserving LLM classification of about 1.1 million sampled conversations, growth of weekly users, name-based gender and country-income patterns
authors: Aaron Chatterji, Thomas Cunningham, David J. Deming, Zoe Hitzig, Christopher Ong, Carl Yan Shan and Kevin Wadman
title: How People Use ChatGPT
countries: Global (ChatGPT consumer users, countries with population above 1 million)
period: November 2022 to July 2025 (conversation sample May 2024 to July 2025)
data: OpenAI data on ChatGPT consumer plans: about 1.1 million sampled conversations (one message each) classified automatically, usage counts, and name-based gender classification of a uniform sample of 1.1 million accounts
findings: By July 2025 ChatGPT had 700 million users sending 18 billion messages a week, about 10% of the world's adult population. Early adopters were disproportionately male: about 80% of active users in the first months had typically masculine first names, but that share fell to 48% by June 2025, so the gender gap has narrowed dramatically and may have closed. Adoption between May 2024 and May 2025 grew disproportionately fast in low- and middle-income countries (GDP per capita of $10,000-40,000). Non-work messages grew faster than work messages, rising from 53% to more than 70% of usage; work use is more common among educated users in highly paid professional jobs; Practical Guidance, Seeking Information and Writing account for nearly 80% of conversations, and Writing dominates work tasks. Caveats: consumer plans only (no enterprise or API use), name-based gender inference, and a single provider's users.
magnitude: By July 2025 ChatGPT reached about 10% of the world's adult population; typically masculine names fell from about 80% to 48% of active users; non-work use rose from 53% to more than 70% of messages

design: Occupational AI-applicability scores built from LLM classification of 200,000 anonymised Bing Copilot conversations onto O*NET work activities, weighted by task completion and scope of impact
authors: Kiran Tomlinson, Sonia Jaffe, Will Wang, Scott Counts and Siddharth Suri
title: Working with AI: Measuring the Applicability of Generative AI to Occupations
venue: arXiv preprint 2507.07935 (v6, December 2025; first posted July 2025 as 'Working with AI: Measuring the Occupational Implications of Generative AI')
data: 200k anonymised, privacy-scrubbed U.S. English Microsoft Bing Copilot conversations; O*NET work activities; OEWS 2023 wages and employment; 2024 CPS wage, education and demographic data
findings: An LLM pipeline classifies, for each conversation, the O*NET work activities the user wants help with and those the AI itself performs, and combines them with task completion and scope-of-impact measures into an applicability score for each occupation. The most common and successful AI-assisted activities involve information work (gathering information, writing, teaching and explaining, advising), so applicability is widespread across sectors: scores are highest for media and communication workers (0.38) and services sales representatives (0.35), with computer occupations at 0.29. The score correlates at r = 0.73 with the Eloundou et al. predictions, but, unlike earlier work, its employment-weighted correlation with occupational wages is weak (r = 0.13) and applicability spans a broad range of education requirements. The method also predicts which occupations are more likely to delegate tasks to AI and which to use it to assist workflows. Caveats: it measures applicability from one chatbot's U.S. users, not employment or wage effects.
magnitude: Applicability scores correlate r = 0.73 with Eloundou et al. exposure but only r = 0.13 (employment-weighted) with occupational wages

design: Synthesis of 18 studies of generative-AI use (more than 140,000 individuals), platform user gender-share estimates and newly collected data on access-equalised usage
authors: Nicholas G. Otis, Solène Delecourt, Katelynn Cranney and Rembrand Koning
title: Global Evidence on Gender Gaps and Generative AI
venue: Harvard Business School Working Paper No. 25-023 (October 2024)
period: Studies and platform data up to 2024 (working paper dated October 2024)
data: 18 prior studies covering more than 140,000 individuals worldwide, estimates of the gender share of hundreds of millions of users on popular generative-AI platforms, and newly collected data
findings: Synthesising data from 18 studies covering more than 140,000 individuals worldwide, plus estimates of the gender share of hundreds of millions of users on popular platforms, the paper finds a gender gap in generative-AI use that is present in nearly all regions, sectors and occupations. Newly collected data show the gap persists even when access to the technology is equalised, so access alone does not explain it. Proposed explanations include lower familiarity and confidence among women and a greater tendency to see AI use in coursework or assignments as unethical or as cheating. The authors warn of a feedback loop: if women use these tools less, systems trained on usage data may under-sample women's preferences and needs, widening gaps in technology adoption and economic opportunity. Caveat: a working paper synthesising heterogeneous studies.
magnitude: Gender gap in generative-AI use found across nearly all regions, sectors and occupations (18 studies, more than 140,000 individuals) and persists when access is equalised

design: Difference-in-differences comparing occupations above and below median generative-AI exposure before and after ChatGPT, in household survey and administrative hiring data, with pre-trend, placebo and randomisation-inference checks
title: Early Labor-Market Responses to Generative AI in a Developing Country: Evidence from Brazil
venue: GovAI and University of São Paulo working paper (May 2026; preliminary)
data: PNAD Contínua household survey (5.7 million worker-quarter observations, 2017Q1-2024Q4) and CAGED administrative registry of formal hires and separations (13 million events, October 2020-December 2024, excluding April-September 2021)
findings: Using ChatGPT's November 2022 release as a timing shock, workers aged 16-21 in high-exposure occupations earn 4.7% less than otherwise-similar young workers in low-exposure occupations; this passes the linear pre-trends test, date placebos and randomisation inference. Two supporting estimates point the same way but do not clear every robustness check: young workers in high-exposure occupations are 1.5 percentage points less likely to be formally employed, and administrative hiring wages for young workers in those occupations fall 1.3% more, consistent with firms lowering entry-wage terms. Prime-age (30-54) and older (55+) workers show no differential movement in wages or formality. Unlike US and UK evidence, where effects concentrate on employment quantities for 22-25-year-olds, adjustment in Brazil runs through entry wages and contract terms for new young hires. Caveats: preliminary work; exposure scores are US task-based measures mapped to Brazilian occupations; high informality offers another adjustment margin.
magnitude: Workers aged 16-21 in high-exposure occupations earn 4.7% less than similar workers in low-exposure occupations after ChatGPT; formal employment 1.5 percentage points lower (weaker evidence); no differential effect for ages 30+

design: Mapping of the Felten et al. AI Occupational Exposure index to harmonised labor-force-survey microdata at 4-digit ISCO, with multivariate analysis of worker traits and household electricity access
authors: Gabriel Demombynes, Jörg Langbein and Michael Weber
title: The Exposure of Workers to Artificial Intelligence in Low- and Middle-Income Countries
venue: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11057 (February 2025)
countries: 25 countries (4 low-income, 12 lower-middle-income, 7 upper-middle-income, plus the United States and Chile)
data: Global Labor Database harmonised labor force surveys for 25 countries covering 3.5 billion people, about 3 million workers aged 15-64; household electricity access added to the data
findings: Exposure is measured as potential, not realised, effects and the regression is correlational. Mean exposure on a 0-100 scale is 49 in upper-middle-income, 44 in lower-middle-income and 37 in low-income countries, well below the high-income comparison countries, and high exposure covers just 12 percent of workers in low-income countries and 15 percent in lower-middle-income countries. Within countries, exposure is higher for women, urban workers and those with more education, with professionals about 56-66 index points more exposed than workers in elementary occupations. Lack of electricity limits effective exposure in low-income countries: using household electricity access (partly imputed), around 41 percent of occupations there lack electricity (5 percent in lower-middle-income countries), and 51 percent of rural workers in low-income countries are AI-exposed but without electricity (9 percent in urban areas). The authors conclude that AI's labor-market effects will be more limited in developing countries than in high-income ones, and that exposure signals potential augmentation or automation, not job loss; the electricity results are an upper bound.
magnitude: High AI exposure for 12% of workers in low-income and 15% in lower-middle-income countries; mean exposure index 37 (low-income) to 49 (upper-middle-income)

design: Model-based mapping of ILO-NASK GenAI occupational exposure to employment by income group, combined with observed or predicted worker internet access and PIAAC/STEP task-content data
authors: Paweł Gmyrek, Mariana Viollaz and Hernan Winkler
title: Disruption without Dividend? How the Digital Divide and Task Differences Split GenAI's Global Impact
countries: 135 countries for exposure (67% of global employment); 49 countries for internet-access analysis; 46 countries for task content
period: ILO-NASK 2025 exposure index with latest household and skills surveys
data: ILO-NASK GenAI exposure index (ISCO-08 4-digit); household and labour force survey microdata for 49 countries (43% of global employment) for internet access; PIAAC and STEP skills surveys for 46 countries for task content
findings: Exposure rises with income: about 32% of total employment in high-income economies is exposed to GenAI versus about 15% in low-income economies, a gap driven by automation-prone occupations such as clerical work while augmentation potential is spread more evenly across countries. The digital divide creates an asymmetry: workers in automation-vulnerable jobs usually have enough connectivity to be displaced even in low-income settings, whereas many jobs with augmentation potential lack it (in Mali 12% of jobs are exposed but only 10% of exposed workers have internet access, so 1.2% of workers hold jobs that are both exposed and usable), so disruption may arrive faster than productivity gains. Workers in developing countries perform substantially fewer non-routine analytical tasks even within highly exposed occupations, so standard exposure measures likely overstate GenAI's transformative potential there. Caveats: exposure shares are model-based estimates of potential, not observed employment effects.
magnitude: About 32% of employment exposed to GenAI in high-income versus about 15% in low-income economies; in Mali only 1.2% of workers hold jobs both exposed and connected

design: Labor-force-survey microdata combined with occupation-level AI exposure and complementarity scores
title: Artificial Intelligence and the Philippine Labor Market: Mapping Occupational Exposure and Complementarity
data: Philippine labor force survey microdata linked to occupational AI exposure and complementarity measures
findings: The paper links occupational AI exposure and complementarity scores to labor force survey microdata to describe who in the Philippines is exposed. About one third of workers are highly exposed to AI, and about 60% of those are also rated highly complementary, which points to potential productivity gains rather than displacement. The most exposed groups are college-educated, young, urban, female and well-paid workers in services, and business process outsourcing (BPO) has the highest share of jobs at risk of displacement. The authors argue that closing regulatory gaps, meeting infrastructure needs and reskilling the workforce are needed to capture the gains and limit harm. Caveats: exposure and complementarity are measures of potential, not observed job losses.
magnitude: About one third of Philippine workers highly exposed to AI, about 60% of them highly complementary; BPO has the highest share of jobs at risk of displacement

design: Pragmatic quality-improvement study with clinicians randomly assigned within clinic (1:1, blocks of 2) to an LLM clinical decision-support tool; independent physicians rated de-identified visit notes
authors: Robert Korom, Sarah Kiptinness, Najib Adan et al. (Penda Health, Nairobi County and OpenAI)
title: AI-based Clinical Decision Support for Primary Care: A Real-World Study
venue: arXiv preprint 2507.16947 (22 July 2025; not peer reviewed)
period: 30 January to 18 April 2025 (main period from 1 March 2025)
data: 106 clinicians (57 with AI Consult, 49 without) at 15 Penda Health clinics; 39,849 patient visits per the abstract (the text reports 20,589 AI-group and 18,990 non-AI-group visits); physician error ratings of de-identified notes, follow-up calls and a clinician survey
findings: Half of the clinicians in each Penda clinic were randomly given 'AI Consult', an LLM safety net in the electronic medical record that flags possible history, investigation, diagnosis and treatment errors with a green/yellow/red display. Independent physicians found significantly lower error rates in the AI group: relative risk reductions of 31.8% (95% CI 21.9-40.5) for history-taking, 10.3% (1.0-18.8) for investigations, 16.0% (6.9-24.2) for diagnosis and 12.7% (6.8-18.3) for treatment, which the authors project to about 22,102 fewer diagnostic and 28,880 fewer treatment errors a year at Penda's 400,000 annual visits. Effects were larger after an induction period with active deployment support. Patient-reported outcomes did not differ significantly: 3.8% of AI-group patients said in follow-up calls that they were not feeling better versus 4.3% in the non-AI group, and no case of patient harm was attributed to the tool. Caveats: outcomes are expert-rated documentation errors, not health outcomes; the study was funded by OpenAI, which took part in the analysis.
magnitude: 16.0% relative reduction in diagnostic errors and 12.7% in treatment errors for clinicians with the AI tool; no significant difference in patient-reported recovery (3.8% vs 4.3% not feeling better)

design: Pragmatic cluster-randomised trial, randomised by clinical officer (52 LLM-assisted, 51 control) across 16 primary care facilities; pre-specified primary outcome of expert-adjudicated 14-day treatment failure; intention-to-treat
authors: Ambrose Agweyu, Paul Mwaniki, Vaishnavi Menon, Robert Korom et al.
title: Generative AI-enabled clinical decision support system in primary care: a pragmatic, cluster-randomized trial
data: 9,691 patients enrolled and 9,347 encounters in the primary analysis under 103 clinical officers at 16 Penda Health facilities; follow-up for treatment failure within 14 days; 2,000 encounters reviewed for documentation quality
findings: Clinical officers were randomised to use the electronic medical record with or without LLM assistance. Treatment failure within 14 days occurred in 102 of 4,693 patients (2.2%) in the intervention arm and 94 of 4,654 (2.0%) in the control arm (adjusted odds ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.08, P = 0.13), so the primary outcome did not differ significantly; the pooled odds ratio across facilities was 0.76 (95% credible interval 0.50 to 1.12), or about five fewer treatment failures per 1,000 patients (credible interval includes zero). Secondary outcomes favoured the tool: appropriate diagnosis (aOR 1.74), comprehensive notes (1.68) and appropriate treatment plan (1.71) in 2,000 reviewed encounters. No serious adverse event was judged related to the intervention, and LLM cost was US$0.04 per patient. The authors conclude the assistance was safe but did not reduce treatment failure within 14 days and any benefit is probably modest.
magnitude: 14-day treatment failure 2.2% (LLM-assisted) vs 2.0% (control), adjusted odds ratio 0.77 (95% CI 0.55-1.08), not significant; documentation quality aOR 1.68-1.74
