design: Multi-country public opinion survey (mostly random telephone polling) on AI use and expectations, interpreted within a human development framework
title: Human Development Report 2025: A matter of choice: People and possibilities in the age of AI
countries: 21 countries across Human Development Index groups
data: UNDP Survey on AI and Human Development: more than 21,000 people in 21 countries and 36 languages, representing 63 percent of the world's population (random telephone polling; web in two countries)
findings: The report's survey finds AI use already substantial for about 20 percent of respondents at all Human Development Index levels, and at least two-thirds of respondents in low, medium and high HDI countries expect to use AI in education, health and work within one year. Expectations of augmentation (61 percent) just exceed those of automation (51 percent), the more people use AI the more confident they are that it will raise their productivity, and expectations in developing countries are particularly high. The report argues that development depends less on what AI can do than on how people reshape economies and societies to use it, and that for low-income and many middle-income countries the manufacturing-and-export pathways that created jobs at scale are narrowing. Caveats: the survey covers 21 countries and measures reported use and expectations, not realised effects.
magnitude: About 20 percent of respondents already use AI at every HDI level; at least two-thirds in low, medium and high HDI countries expect to use it in education, health and work within a year

design: Descriptive diffusion index: share of the working-age population using generative AI, built from aggregated Microsoft telemetry and adjusted for OS/device share, internet penetration and population
title: Global AI Diffusion Q1 2026: Trends and Insights
venue: Microsoft AI Economy Institute, AI Diffusion Report (May 2026)
countries: Global, by economy (Global North versus Global South comparison)
data: Aggregated, anonymised Microsoft telemetry on generative AI product use by people aged 15-64, adjusted to national device-market share, internet penetration and population
findings: Global AI use rose by 1.5 percentage points during the quarter, from 16.3% to 17.8% of the world's working-age population, and 26 economies now exceed 30%. The gap between the Global North and Global South keeps widening, with usage at 27.5% in the North and 15.4% in the South; the UAE leads at 70.1% and the United States ranks 21st at 31.3%, while adoption accelerated in Asia as AI capabilities improved in Asian languages. The report also notes that US software developer employment reached about 2.2 million in 2025 (up 8.5% year over year) and was about 4% higher in March 2026 than a year earlier. Caveats: the metric covers use of Microsoft-visible generative AI products and is an estimate, and the company says no single metric is perfect.
magnitude: Generative AI use at 27.5% of the working-age population in the Global North versus 15.4% in the Global South (March 2026); world 17.8%, up from 16.3% in the previous quarter

design: Descriptive analysis of one million sampled Claude.ai conversations by country and U.S. state, and one million first-party API transcripts, classified by task and automation versus augmentation
authors: Ruth Appel, Peter McCrory, Alex Tamkin, Michael Stern, Miles McCain and Tyler Neylon
title: Anthropic Economic Index Report: Uneven Geographic and Enterprise AI Adoption
countries: Global (Claude.ai users by country) and U.S. states
data: 1 million randomly sampled Claude.ai Free and Pro conversations (4-11 August 2025) and 1 million first-party API transcripts (August 2025)
findings: Claude usage is highly concentrated: the Anthropic AI Usage Index (usage share divided by working-age population share) is 7 in Israel, 4.57 in Singapore and 3.62 in the United States, against 0.48 in Bolivia, 0.36 in Indonesia, 0.27 in India and 0.2 in Nigeria, although India accounts for 7.2% of Claude.ai usage. A 1% rise in GDP per capita is associated with a 0.7% rise in Claude usage per capita, and coding is over half of usage in India versus about a third globally. After controlling for task mix, low-usage countries are more likely to delegate complete tasks, while high-usage countries lean toward augmentation. Enterprise API use is far more automation-oriented: 77% of API transcripts show automation patterns against about 50% on Claude.ai, and just under half of API traffic is computer and mathematical tasks. Caveats: the data cover one provider's users, not the whole population.
magnitude: Anthropic AI Usage Index: Israel 7, United States 3.62, India 0.27, Nigeria 0.2; a 1% rise in GDP per capita is associated with 0.7% higher usage per capita

design: Calibrated multi-region, three-sector global DSGE model (IMF GIMF) shocked with AI-driven TFP gains scaled by sectoral AI exposure, country AI preparedness and access to AI; high- and low-TFP baselines plus 'Limited AI Access' and…
authors: Cerutti, Garcia Pascual, Kido, Li, Melina, Mendes Tavares and Wingender
title: The Global Impact of AI: Mind the Gap
countries: Seven model regions: United States; EU and Switzerland; other advanced economies; China; emerging Asia and Central Asia; emerging Latin America, Middle East…
data: Employment-based sectoral AI exposure (Cazzaniga et al. 2024 index), IMF AI Preparedness Index, an AI-access measure, OECD Inter-Country Input-Output tables; benchmark TFP shocks bracketed by Acemoglu (2025) (low) and Aghion and Bunel (2024) (high)
findings: Scenario simulation in a calibrated model, not an estimate from outcome data: AI productivity shocks are scaled by each region's sectoral exposure, preparedness and access. Global TFP rises 2.4% (high-TFP scenario) or 0.8% (low) after ten years and world GDP rises nearly 4% (high) or 1.3% (low). Gains are uneven: after ten years GDP is 5.4% (high) / 1.8% (low) higher in the United States (the introduction cites 5.6% / 1.9%), 4.4% / 1.5% in the EU and Switzerland, and 2.7% / 0.9% in low-income countries, so advanced-economy growth effects are more than double those in low-income countries. If emerging markets and low-income countries lack access to AI technologies, their GDP gains fall by about 1 percentage point relative to baseline, and better preparedness narrows but does not close the gap. Results depend on the assumed benchmark TFP shocks and the model abstracts from within-country distribution.
magnitude: World GDP +1.3% (low) to nearly +4% (high) after ten years; advanced-economy growth effect more than double that of low-income countries

design: Acemoglu-style task-based TFP simulation for 31 European countries across 44 AI-exposure scenarios, with AI adoption predicted from reduced-form regressions on country and sector characteristics, plus a regulation counterfactual…
title: Artificial Intelligence and Productivity in Europe
data: Published task-level AI exposure estimates (44 scenarios), AI adoption rates calibrated to Svanberg et al. (2024) and regressed on European country/sector drivers, national occupation-regulation indicators, EU AI Act and data-privacy law mappings
findings: A simulation in the Acemoglu (2024) framework, not an estimate from observed outcomes. In the preferred scenario Europe-wide TFP gains are about 1.1% cumulatively over five years, almost 60% above Acemoglu's US estimate; the range across scenarios is wide. Gains are larger in higher-income countries, which have more value added in AI-exposed sectors such as finance and higher wages (the main predictor of AI adoption): Luxembourg gains about 2%, more than four times Romania. Assuming national occupational licensing and training requirements, data-privacy laws and the EU AI Act halve AI capability in the tasks, occupations and sectors they touch, combined regulation reduces Europe's gains by over 30%. The regulatory result is an assumption-driven counterfactual, not an evaluation of an enacted rule.
magnitude: About 1% cumulative TFP gain over five years for Europe; regulation could cut the gain by over 30%

design: Sectoral extension of Acemoglu's task-based micro-to-macro framework: micro-level AI productivity gains x sectoral task exposure x S-shaped adoption paths (slow, medium, fast) projected to 2034, with harmonised and imputed G7 adoption rates
title: Macroeconomic productivity gains from Artificial Intelligence in G7 economies
venue: OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers No. 41 (2025); see also SUERF Policy Brief No. 1283 (October 2025)
countries: Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, United Kingdom, United States
data: Micro-level experimental gains (conservative baseline of 30%, the average of the three most precisely estimated effects), Eloundou et al. (2024) task-level exposure, harmonised official firm-level AI adoption statistics (Canada, EU, US) with regression-imputed values for the UK and Japan
findings: Model-based projections, not measured effects. Across slow, medium and fast adoption scenarios, projected annual aggregate labour-productivity growth from AI is 0.4-1.3 percentage points in high-exposure countries such as the United States and United Kingdom, and 0.2-0.8 points in Italy and Japan (slow adoption 0.2-0.4 points; medium adoption with expanded capabilities 0.5-1; rapid adoption 0.8-1.3). Differences reflect the value-added share of the five most AI-exposed sectors (about one quarter in the US, 23% in the UK, around 15% in Japan, Italy and Germany) and 2034 adoption rates of 30-60% in the US, Canada, UK and Germany versus 15-50% in France, Italy and Japan. For scale, the authors cite an ICT contribution of 1-1.5 points a year to US labour-productivity growth in the mid-1990s. Harmonised adoption data are lacking, so adoption is partly imputed.
magnitude: 0.4-1.3 percentage points of extra annual labour-productivity growth in high-exposure G7 economies over ten years (0.2-0.8 in Italy and Japan)

design: Small-open-economy overlapping-generations model calibrated to 16 Asia-Pacific economies: AI adoption at scale is modelled as capital deepening (capital share rising at 2x, 5x or 10x the historical US rate), with adoption thresholds,…
title: AI and Economic Divergence in Asia
countries: 16 Asia-Pacific economies, including Singapore, Korea, Japan, Australia, India, the Philippines, Vietnam, Bangladesh, Cambodia and Nepal
data: Country calibration to latest macro and fiscal ratios: October 2024 WEO growth projections, Penn World Table 2019 TFP levels, World Bank education attainment for skill shares, global interest-rate paths from Benzell et al. (2021)
findings: Scenario analysis in a stylised model, not an empirical estimate; the 2x, 5x and 10x capital-share multiples are described by the authors as spanning a plausible-to-extreme range rather than a forecast. Advanced Asian economies adopt AI immediately, whereas emerging and developing economies (EMDEs) adopt later and, before adopting, grow about 0.5-0.6 percentage points a year more slowly than in a no-AI world in the mild and moderate scenarios because higher global capital costs depress investment (investment-to-GDP 5-6 pp lower); growth then recovers. In the long run AI adoption lifts annual growth by 0.5-1 pp in advanced Asian economies and by 0.2-0.8 pp in EMDEs, depending on the pace of AI progress. Structural reforms that raise the high-skilled labour share, labour productivity and capital productivity speed up EMDE adoption and amplify the growth gains. Within countries AI widens inequality across skill groups and across generations (asset-rich older households gain relative to younger workers), and redistribution mitigates this at an equity-efficiency cost.
magnitude: EMDEs grow about 0.5-0.6 pp a year slower before adopting; long-run AI growth boost of 0.5-1 pp a year in advanced Asia versus 0.2-0.8 pp in EMDEs

design: Asset-pricing identification mapped through a model: first-stage firm stock-return betas on an AI equity index (weekly, 2022-2025), second-stage cross-sectional regression on software-engineering payroll share, then Hulten-style GDP…
title: The Macroeconomic Effect of AI: Sizing the Software Engineering Channel
data: Weekly CRSP returns for about 1,850 US-listed firms that use software engineers as an input (software producers and the semiconductor supply chain excluded from the productivity estimate), ROBO Global AI index (THNQ), Fama-French factors, Revelio Labs software-engineer payroll shares
findings: The authors read financial markets' expectations of AI-driven software-engineering productivity off differential stock-return sensitivity to an AI index: a 1 percentage-point difference in a firm's software-engineer payroll share predicts a 1.24 basis-point larger return response to a one-point move in the AI index, robust to alternative factors and indexes and to an Oster coefficient-stability test. Through the model this implies that AI news from November 2022 to December 2025 raised the market's expected present value of software-engineering productivity by the equivalent of a permanent 32.6% increase, comparable to the 21-56% task-level speed-ups reported in experiments. The implied GDP level effect is 3.6% in the baseline and 6.5% when software engineering also raises R&D productivity; by mid-2026 the implied productivity and GDP effects had more than doubled relative to end-2025. These are market-implied expectations, not realised output, and depend on the model's substitution elasticities and on the AI index capturing AI news.
magnitude: Market-implied permanent +32.6% software-engineering productivity, equivalent to +3.6% GDP (+6.5% with R&D feedback), November 2022 - December 2025

design: Structured elicitation survey of five groups giving unconditional forecasts (2030, 2050) and forecasts conditional on slow, moderate and rapid AI-progress scenarios, with a variance decomposition of disagreement
authors: Karger, Kuusela, Abaluck, Bryan, Halperin, Jones, Murphy, Trammell, Reynolds, Mayland, Viswanathan, Mittal, Ceppas de Castro, Rosenberg and Tetlock
title: Forecasting the Economic Effects of AI
period: Survey fielded October 2025 - February 2026; forecasts to 2030 and 2050
data: Forecasts from 69 academic economists, 27 AI-industry employees, 25 AI-policy researchers, 38 superforecasters and 401 members of the public
findings: These are elicited beliefs, not estimates from outcome data. The median respondent in every group expects substantial AI capability gains by 2030, small demographic-driven declines in labour-force participation and 2.5% annual GDP growth, above the 2.0% medium-run and 1.7% long-run baselines of government and private forecasters. Conditional on a 'rapid' AI-progress scenario, experts forecast annualised GDP growth near 4% and labour-force participation falling from 62% to 55% by 2050, with roughly half of the fall (about 10 million jobs) attributed to AI; the economists' own rapid-scenario forecasts are 3.5% growth, 55.0% participation and an 80.0% wealth share for the top decile by 2050. A variance decomposition attributes expert disagreement mainly to different beliefs about the economic effects of highly capable AI rather than about the pace of progress. The economist sample is small (69 after filtering) and younger and more European than the sampling frame (results are reweighted).
magnitude: Median expert expects 2.5% annual US GDP growth (versus 2.0% in official baselines), rising to about 4% if AI progress is 'rapid'

design: Indicator dashboard from public and official series plus an accounting approximation of the AI buildout's contribution to quarterly GDP growth (software, data centres, power facilities, computers and peripherals, with net exports of…
title: The AI Buildout and the Economy: Publicly Available Data to Assess AI's Impact
venue: FEDS Notes, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (17 July 2026)
data: BEA national accounts, Census data-centre construction and Business Trends and Outlook Survey, SEC hyperscaler capex filings, Federal Reserve industrial production, BLS productivity, unemployment and JOLTS series, METR task horizons and Epoch AI GPU costs; accompanying XLSX of figure data
findings: The note proposes tracking indicators in three groups (capabilities and costs; investment and adoption; productivity and labour) and concludes the evidence is consistent with a buildout phase rather than broad-based displacement. Its GDP-contribution approximation (Figure 7) shows, in the accompanying data file, 2026Q1 contributions of +0.53 pp from software, +0.59 pp from computers and peripherals and +0.03 pp each from data centres and power facilities, offset by -0.45 pp from net exports of computers, peripherals and parts; in 2025Q4 the import drag (-0.61 pp) offset most of the gross contribution. High-AI-exposure sectors (information, finance, professional services) show faster labour-productivity growth than other sectors, but all groups' trends are similar over time, so micro-level gains are not yet visible in aggregates. There is no AI line item in the national accounts and the approximation rests on strong assumptions about categories and import shares.
magnitude: 2026Q1 contributions to annualized GDP growth: software +0.53 pp and computers and peripherals +0.59 pp, offset by -0.45 pp from net imports of computers and parts

design: Macro-accounting decomposition of US national accounts (expenditure and value-added approaches) combined with a stylised AI production chain and back-of-the-envelope estimates of future data-centre service output
title: Artificial intelligence and the US economy: an accounting perspective on investment and production
venue: Banca d'Italia, Questioni di Economia e Finanza (Occasional Papers) No. 1006 (March 2026); earlier preprint arXiv:2601.11196
data: BEA national accounts (investment, imports, GDP by industry), Trade Data Monitor server import data, hyperscaler capex disclosures
findings: Accounting evidence, not causal. Tech and AI-related capital spending clearly boosted US aggregate demand in the first three quarters of 2025: tech investment contributed 1.1, 1.1 and 0.5 percentage points to GDP growth in Q1-Q3 and purchases of computers and related equipment rose 104%, 62% and 46% (annualised), but imports of computers and peripherals surged +236%, +47% and +24%, so the contribution to GDP is more limited. On a value-added basis, computer and electronic products, data processing and computer-systems design contributed 0.5 pp (Q1) and 0.7 pp (Q2), around 40% of first-half growth. Simple calculations suggest services from new AI data centres could add to GDP on a scale comparable to investment to date, while short reinvestment cycles and uncertain demand are medium-term risks. Figures are version-sensitive: the January 2026 arXiv v1 reported import-purged tech-investment contributions of about 0.3, 0.6 and 0.2 pp.
magnitude: Tech investment added 1.1, 1.1 and 0.5 pp to US GDP growth in Q1-Q3 2025 before import offsets; computer and peripheral imports rose +236%, +47% and +24%

design: Instrumental-variable firm-level estimation: EU firms' AI adoption instrumented with the adoption rates of comparable US peers, using matched EIBIS-Orbis data
authors: Aldasoro, Gambacorta, Pal, Revoltella, Weiss and Wolski
title: AI adoption, productivity and employment: evidence from European firms
venue: BIS Working Paper 1325 (23 January 2026); also EIB Economics Working Paper 2026/02
countries: European Union (with United States peers as instrument)
data: EIB Investment Survey (EIBIS) matched to Orbis balance-sheet data for more than 12,000 non-financial firms in the EU and US
findings: The authors instrument EU firms' AI adoption with the adoption rates of comparable US peers to isolate exogenous technological exposure. AI adoption raises the level of labour productivity by 4%, driven by capital deepening rather than job losses: they find no adverse effect on firm-level employment, although longer-term effects remain uncertain. Productivity gains are unevenly distributed and concentrated in medium and large firms. AI-adopting firms are also more innovative and their workers earn higher wages, and complementary investment in software, data and workforce training is important for realising the gains.
magnitude: AI adoption raises labour productivity by 4% with no adverse effect on firm employment (IV, more than 12,000 EU and US firms)

design: Instrumental-variable (reported AI skills gap as instrument), selection-on-observables and plant fixed-effects estimates in linked Census establishment surveys (MOPS-ASM) and a firm panel (ABS-CMF), 2012-2022
title: The Rise of Industrial AI in America: Microfoundations of the Productivity J-curve(s)
venue: US Census Bureau Center for Economic Studies Working Paper CES-25-27 (April 2025); figures follow the revised December 2025 draft, with April 2025 values noted
period: AI use measured for 2017 and 2021; performance outcomes 2012-2022
data: 2021 Management and Organizational Practices Survey linked to the Annual Survey of Manufactures (about 28,500 establishments) and the 2018 Annual Business Survey linked to the Census of Manufactures (about 55,000 firms), with Census and IRS performance data
findings: About 23% of US manufacturing plants used some AI by 2021 (about 8% intensively). A one-standard-deviation higher AI-use index is associated with 1.33% lower TFP after controls; IV estimates, local to marginal adopters, imply productivity losses of roughly 44% in the December 2025 draft (about -60 percentage points in the April 2025 draft), and plant fixed effects show about a 2% short-run loss. AI use raises work-in-progress inventory, robot investment and labour shedding, consistent with adjustment costs; losses concentrate in older establishments, where abandoning structured management practices explains roughly half of the TFP loss (one-third in the April draft). Conditional on survival, early adopters grow faster over 2017-2021: one standard deviation more AI use is associated with about 2% higher labour-productivity growth among younger plants and 0.8% employment growth against a 1.5% sector-wide decline. The data cannot show when net returns turn positive, and the IV effect is not representative of infra-marginal adopters.
magnitude: J-curve: one-SD higher AI use linked to 1.33% lower TFP (OLS) and roughly 44% lower for marginal adopters (IV), followed by faster growth for surviving early adopters

design: Difference-in-differences with firm, sector-by-time and area-by-time fixed effects comparing AI adopters with firms calling AI 'not important' (pre-period 2016-2022, post-period 2023-2024), using survey data linked to balance-sheet and…
title: The economic impact of artificial intelligence: evidence from Italian firms
venue: Banca d'Italia, Questioni di Economia e Finanza (Occasional Papers) No. 1005 (March 2026)
data: Bank of Italy Survey on Inflation and Growth Expectations (industry and non-financial services firms with at least 50 employees, 2024Q3) linked to the Company Accounts Data System and INPS employer-employee records
findings: About 11% of Italian firms with 50+ employees reported using AI in 2024 and 28% planned to adopt within two years; adoption is concentrated in larger, more knowledge-intensive firms and those with higher labour costs. In the difference-in-differences design, AI adoption raises return on assets by about 0.5 pp, EBITDA over sales by 2.0 pp, value added per employee by about 5.2% and EBITDA per employee by 11.9%, with no significant increase in labour cost per employee. Total employment is unchanged but the white-collar share rises about 0.7 pp and the blue-collar share falls about 1.1 pp. Adopters also expect smaller increases in their own selling prices and lower 24- and 48-month inflation (roughly 0.25 and 0.33 pp). The survey does not record adoption dates, so the post-treatment window is assumed from external evidence, parallel trends fail for the apprentice outcome, and only larger firms are covered.
magnitude: AI adoption raises value added per employee by about 5.2% and EBITDA per employee by 11.9% with no significant change in total employment (DiD, Italian firms)

design: Randomised information-provision field experiment embedded in the ECB-European Commission SAFE survey: half of firms were told actual domestic and foreign (Germany, France, Italy) AI investment rates; 2SLS of own planned AI investment on…
authors: Baumann, Cullen, Faia, Ferrando, Perez-Truglia and Rariga
title: Innovation without borders? The geography of technological diffusion
venue: ECB Working Paper Series No 3246 (June 2026); also circulated as NBER Working Paper 35314
period: Fielded in the fourth quarter of 2025
data: About 3,300 firms in the Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises (SAFE); information treatment drawn from the earlier SAFE round on actual AI investment
findings: Firms substantially underestimated competitors' AI investment, on average by more than twenty percentage points, both domestically and abroad. Treated firms revised their expectations about peers' future AI investment and raised their own expected AI investment rate. A 1 percentage-point increase in the expected share of domestic peers investing in AI raises a firm's own expected AI investment rate by 0.570 pp, while the effect of expected foreign-peer investment is statistically insignificant, implying strong strategic complementarities within borders but not across them. The outcome is a stated planned share of investment, not realised spending, and the authors suggest informational frictions can slow AI diffusion independently of financial constraints.
magnitude: +1 pp expected domestic peers investing in AI raises a firm's own expected AI investment rate by 0.570 pp; foreign peers: no significant effect

design: Randomised information-provision field experiment embedded in the 2025 Bank of Italy INVIND survey: half of firms received a signal of comparable firms' adoption of AI and robotics; 2SLS reaction function of own intended adoption on…
authors: Cullen, Faia, Guglielminetti, Perez-Truglia and Rondinelli
title: The Innovation Race: Experimental Evidence on Advanced Technologies
data: About 3,000 firms in the Bank of Italy Survey of Industrial and Service Firms (INVIND), linked to administrative records; pre-registered (AEARCTR-0016177)
findings: Most firms underestimated competitors' adoption, with prior beliefs on average 24.5 pp below the signal, and treated firms updated their beliefs. The information raised intended robotics adoption by 6.5 pp (p=0.039; a 17.3% increase on baseline), and the 2SLS reaction function implies that a 1 pp rise in the expected share of competitors adopting advanced technologies raises intended robotics adoption by 0.732 pp by 2027. In contrast the authors find no significant effect on AI adoption plans, in the full sample or among firms with the largest underestimates, though low power means modest effects cannot be ruled out; they note high baseline AI use (about 28% of Italian firms in 2025 versus 23% for robotics) and experimental use as possible reasons. Outcomes are stated intentions, not realised adoption.
magnitude: +1 pp expected competitor adoption raises intended robotics adoption by 0.732 pp; no significant effect on AI adoption plans

design: Harmonised firm-level survey modules on AI use intensity, drivers, barriers, financing and expectations in two rounds of the ECB-European Commission SAFE, with regression associations controlling for size, sector and country
title: Adoption and investment in AI across the euro area: insights from harmonised firm-level data
countries: 12 euro area countries (adoption highest in the Netherlands, Finland and Austria; lowest in Italy and Ireland)
data: About 6,000 firms in the Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises (SAFE)
findings: About 70% of euro-area firms report some AI use but only 7% describe it as significant, a share similar across size classes; use exceeds 80% in the Netherlands, Finland and Austria and is below 65% in Italy and Ireland. Larger firms, firms founded around or after late 2022, technology-sector firms, and listed and venture-backed firms lead adoption; skill shortages, data-privacy concerns and system incompatibility are the main barriers, and AI is financed mainly from internal funds, grants and subsidised public loans. These are associations, not causal effects: significant users expect higher turnover growth and investment and own selling prices about 0.85 pp higher than non-users, there is no statistically significant productivity difference between users and non-users overall (positive only in technology sectors, using a survey-based productivity proxy), and no evidence of workforce reduction. A companion randomised information experiment (ECB WP 3246) is summarised in the paper.
magnitude: About 70% of euro-area firms use some AI but only 7% use it significantly; no overall productivity gap between users and non-users

design: Executive survey (CFO Survey panel plus supplemental samples) eliciting AI-attributed changes in labour productivity, revenue, employment and task mix, with a decomposition of implied gains into capital deepening and revenue-based TFP
authors: Baslandze, Edwards, Graham, McClure, Meyer, Sparks, Waddell and Weitz
title: Artificial Intelligence, Productivity, and the Workforce: Evidence from Corporate Executives
data: 603 responses from The CFO Survey (Duke University, Richmond Fed, Atlanta Fed) plus 145 from FEI, NASDAQ and alumni samples (nearly 750 executives; median firm 118 employees)
findings: Outcomes are self-reported attributions, not measured effects. More than half of firms have invested in AI, though many small firms are only starting in 2026. Executives report that AI raised labour productivity by 1.8% on average in 2025 and expect 3.0% in 2026, but the gain implied by observed revenue and employment changes is smaller (0.6% in 2025, 1.8% in 2026), which the authors read as a productivity paradox reflecting delayed revenue realisation. Implied 2025 gains are about 0.8% in high-skill services (especially finance) and about 0.4% in low-skill services, manufacturing and construction, and come mostly from revenue-based TFP rather than capital deepening. Aggregate employment is expected to fall by less than 0.4% in 2026 because of AI, with large firms expecting cuts and small firms modest gains, and routine clerical employment is expected to fall by more than 2 pp of the workforce over three years.
magnitude: Executives report AI raised labour productivity 1.8% in 2025 (3.0% expected in 2026), versus 0.6% (1.8%) implied by revenue per employee

design: Cross-country firm-level regressions with country, sector and size controls and an instrumental variable built from predetermined demographic cohort structure; AI and automation adopters identified by applying a large language model to…
title: Aging Economies and AI Adoption: Firm-Level Evidence from the World Bank Enterprise Surveys
data: World Bank Enterprise Surveys, 89,380 firms; 1,656 AI and automation adopters (1.9% of the sample; 221 explicit AI/ML firms)
findings: Adopters are identified by classifying firms' open-ended process-innovation descriptions with an LLM (about 550 more adopters than a keyword classifier; 96% agreement on a common subset). A ten-percentage-point rise in the old-age dependency ratio raises the probability of process adoption by about 0.6 pp after controlling for income, digital infrastructure, firm size, sector and region and time effects, and the IV estimate (based on the year-2000 cohort structure, after Acemoglu and Restrepo) is stronger than OLS. For the broad measure the effect is concentrated in manufacturing, large firms and developing economies; among firms explicitly mentioning AI the sector pattern reverses and services firms are more likely to adopt than manufacturers. Aging also predicts AI-enabled product development. Only 1.9% of firms are flagged as adopters and the flag depends on LLM classification of free text.
magnitude: +10 pp old-age dependency ratio raises firms' probability of AI/automation process adoption by about 0.6 pp (89,380 firms, 144 countries)

design: Event study of cumulative abnormal returns (primary window [0,+2]) around the 21 April 2021 EU AI Act proposal, interacting predetermined EU revenue share with pre-event AI-hiring growth (2015-2019)
title: Jurisdictional Capital and AI Regulation: Evidence from the EU AI Act
countries: United States (US-listed firms with EU revenue exposure); EU regulation
data: 771 US-listed firms: Lightcast AI job postings linked to Compustat, FactSet geographic revenue, CRSP daily returns
findings: EU market presence carried no general announcement premium (marginal effect near zero at average AI-hiring growth), but firms combining deeper EU revenue presence with faster pre-event AI-hiring growth earned higher announcement returns: a one-standard-deviation increase in AI-hiring growth raises the marginal effect of EU revenue share on the three-day abnormal return by 39.7 basis points, significant at 1% in every window. High-EU, high-AI firms lost 9 bp versus 58 bp for low-EU, high-AI firms, a 49 bp differential the authors translate into about $86 billion of shareholder value. The effect is stronger for high-risk AI and firms with prior compliance experience and is not explained by firm size, total foreign revenue or lobbying; EU-embedded AI-expanding firms also shift revenue toward the EU when peers are less embedded. It measures private valuation of regulatory experience, not the welfare effects of the Act.
magnitude: One-SD higher AI-hiring growth raises the EU-presence announcement return by 39.7 bp; about $86 billion of shareholder value for high-EU, high-AI firms

design: Triangulation of three public surveys with different units of analysis: Census Business Trends and Outlook Survey (firm-weighted), Real-Time Population Survey (individuals) and Atlanta Fed Survey of Business Uncertainty…
title: Monitoring AI Adoption in the US Economy
venue: FEDS Notes, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (3 April 2026)
data: Census Bureau BTOS (biweekly, from September 2023), Real-Time Population Survey (quarterly, from August 2024), Survey of Business Uncertainty (November 2025)
findings: About 18% of US firms had adopted AI by end-2025 in the BTOS, after a November 2025 question redesign that created a level break; before the redesign adoption had grown 68% (3.9 pp) in the year to September 2025 but decelerated in Q2 2025, and over 20% of firms expected to use AI in the first half of 2026. Work-related generative-AI use among individuals was about 41% in November 2025 (RPS, +9.7 pp year on year), while the SBU gives 78% employment-weighted AI adoption and 54% for LLMs. Differences mainly reflect unit of analysis and sampling, plus question framing and respondent type. Adoption rises with firm size, although very small firms adopt more than size alone would predict, and professional services (about 33%) and finance (about 30%) lead industries. Descriptive only: the BTOS question was redesigned in November 2025 (a level break), and headline adoption captures any use rather than intensity (the RPS puts daily generative-AI use at work at 12%).
magnitude: About 18% of US firms had adopted AI by end-2025 (BTOS), versus 78% employment-weighted (SBU) and 41% of workers using generative AI (RPS)

design: Extension of the WTO Global Trade Model with AI services (trade-cost reductions, task shifts from labour to AI, productivity gains) and four AI-uptake scenarios to 2040, plus a 2025 WTO-ICC firm survey and a new AI Trade Policy Openness…
title: World Trade Report 2025: Making trade and AI work together to the benefit of all
countries: Global, by high-, middle- and low-income economy groups
period: Projections to 2040; firm survey 2025; trade data 2023
data: WTO Global Trade Model simulations; WTO-ICC survey of firms; trade in AI-enabling goods (US$2.3 trillion in 2023); AI Trade Policy Openness Index (AI-TPOI) and IP/competition-policy counts
findings: Model-based scenarios plus descriptive evidence, not causal estimates. In the simulations global trade rises 34 to 37% by 2040 across scenarios (digitally deliverable services +42%) and global GDP rises 12 to 13%. In the benchmark scenario where low-income economies do not catch up in digital technology and infrastructure, incomes rise 14% in high-income, 11% in middle-income and 8% in low-income economies; closing half the digital-infrastructure gap lifts low-income gains to 11%, and adding broader AI adoption gives 15% (low-income) and 14% (middle-income). The skill premium falls 3 to 4% across scenarios while the rental rate of capital rises about 14 percentage points relative to wages. In the WTO-ICC survey 41% of small firms use AI versus over 60% of large firms, and fewer than one-third of firms in low- and lower-middle-income economies; the number of economies with at least one AI-related IP policy rose from 41 in 2017 to 140 in 2024.
magnitude: AI could raise global trade 34-37% and real GDP 12-13% by 2040; low-income economies gain 8% versus 14% for high-income economies if they do not catch up

design: LLM-based classification of HS10 product descriptions into AI-infrastructure categories applied to US customs trade data, with tariff analysis and a counterfactual accounting exercise for the goods trade deficit
title: Trade in AI-Related Products
venue: Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis Quarterly Review, Vol. 46, No. 1 (June 2026); also NBER Working Paper 35053
data: US HS10 import and export data, effective tariff rates, LLM-based product classification
findings: Descriptive classification and accounting, not causal. AI-related products (computer hardware plus electrical, networking, cooling and materials inputs, roughly half each) were 23% of all US imports through 2025, up from 15% in 2023; by March 2026 their trade was 73% above its 2023 level versus 3% for non-AI products, with divergence starting in early 2024, and Taiwan and Mexico each supply about a quarter of AI-related imports. The effective tariff on AI-related products was 4.5% versus 12.1% on other goods at the end of 2025 because exemptions covered about 69% of AI-related products by value. Exports grew 34.5% since 2023 but 46% are re-exports; if AI-related trade had grown like non-AI trade, the 2025 US goods deficit would have been nearly $194 billion (about 16%) smaller. The classification is LLM-generated and may misclassify products.
magnitude: AI-related products were 23% of US imports in 2025; without the AI boom the 2025 goods trade deficit would have been nearly $194 billion (about 16%) smaller

design: Capacity-constrained Ricardian trade model of AI compute services (training versus inference; latency as an iceberg trade cost; bilateral 'sovereignty premium' for distrust), calibrated across 85 countries
title: Cheap Energy Might Not Be Enough: A Trade Model of AI Compute Services
venue: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11426 (July 2026)
countries: 85 countries in the calibration (Kyrgyzstan lowest-cost; Malaysia, India and Brazil largest developing-country data-centre FDI recipients)
period: Static calibration with no time dimension (NVIDIA H100 as reference hardware)
data: Electricity prices (corrected for subsidies), climate-driven cooling overhead, construction costs, global GPU hardware prices, bilateral latency and trust frictions, data-centre FDI
findings: A calibrated model, not an estimate from observed compute trade. Hardware amortisation is roughly 90% of unit compute cost and is priced globally, so cross-country production-cost differences are only 12-20%, leaving little room for institutional frictions. Several energy-rich developing economies are among the lowest-cost producers under cost-recovery pricing, but once bilateral sovereignty (trust) premia are added, trust deficits with OECD buyers eliminate nearly all of their export potential. A 10-percentage-point cost-of-capital gap between OECD hyperscalers and locally financed developing-country operators adds about $0.29 per GPU-hour, roughly four times the electricity-cost spread among the top twenty producers. The author concludes that enforceable data governance, stable regulation, credible power contracts, access to finance and geopolitical alignment with buyers, rather than power prices, are the binding constraints; results depend on the calibrated frictions.
magnitude: Cross-country compute production costs differ by only 12-20%; a 10-pp financing-cost gap adds about $0.29 per GPU-hour, roughly four times the electricity-cost spread

design: Descriptive cross-country benchmarking of AI competitiveness using four composite indices (WIPO GII, IMF AI Preparedness Index, Stanford Global AI Vibrancy, Oxford Insights GAIRI) and indicators for compute, data centres, energy,…
title: The State of AI Competition in Advanced Economies
venue: FEDS Notes, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (6 October 2025)
countries: United States, China, European Union, United Kingdom, Germany, France, Japan, Canada, Italy, India
data: Epoch AI, Tony Blair Institute, Omdia, Top500, Stanford AI Index, OECD, Eurostat, EUKLEMS, IEA and national statistics
findings: The United States controls an estimated 74% of cumulative global high-end AI compute, China 14% and the EU 4.8%. Cumulative private AI investment over 2013-2024 exceeded $470 billion in the US versus roughly $50 billion across EU countries, $28 billion in the UK, $15 billion in Canada and $6 billion in Japan, and the US accounts for more than 75% of reported private VC in generative-AI start-ups. Data centres account for about 8.9% of average US energy use versus 4.8% in the EU and 2.3% in China, while China added 429 GW of net generation capacity in 2024, over 15 times the US addition. National statistics put firm AI adoption at 8.3-19.8% (US 9.4%, Canada 12.2%, Germany 19.8%) while the University of Melbourne/KPMG survey reports 50-89%, largely because private surveys over-represent large firms in AI-intensive sectors; Chinese compute and investment data are also opaque, so comparisons are indicative rather than precise.
magnitude: US holds an estimated 74% of global high-end AI compute versus 14% for China and 4.8% for the EU

design: General-equilibrium model with heterogeneous firms, variable (Kimball) markups, fixed AI-adoption costs and an AI-producing sector that uses data and energy, calibrated to US data; comparative statics for demand- and supply-driven AI…
title: Will AI Intensify or Weaken Market Competition?
venue: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco Working Paper 2026-15 (August 2026; authors label it an incomplete draft)
period: Calibrated to US data; adoption and concentration series 2010-2025
data: Calibration targets from US firm-level AI adoption (about 18% of businesses using AI in November 2025 - January 2026 in the Census BTOS, about 32% employment-weighted; about 17.5% of firms posting AI-skill jobs in Lightcast), industry concentration and markup series, GPU price decline
findings: A calibrated model, not an estimate from outcome data. As AI use rises from a low level large incumbent users gain market share, but once diffusion is wide, entry of smaller adopters erodes incumbents' share, so industry concentration is hump-shaped in AI adoption with a turning point at around 15% adoption; with US adoption at about 18%, the model implies concentration should fall as AI diffuses further, consistent with a post-2019 weakening in the observed correlation between AI use and concentration. The effect on the sales-weighted average markup depends on whether diffusion is driven by AI supply (markups rise) or demand factors such as lower adoption costs (non-monotonic); the persistently positive observed correlation between AI use and markups suggests supply-driven diffusion. A revenue subsidy of about 3% for AI adopters maximises welfare (gain of about 0.35% in consumption equivalent; about 4% and 0.4% if data complement AI), reflecting a tradeoff between aggregate productivity and markup distortions. Results rest on calibrated parameters and the paper is an incomplete draft.
magnitude: Concentration is hump-shaped in AI adoption with a turning point near 15% (US adoption about 18%); welfare-maximising subsidy to AI adopters about 3% of revenues

design: Analytical and conceptual assessment of foundation-model markets: cost structure (compute, data, talent), scale and scope economies, market tipping, vertical integration and competition-policy remedies
title: Concentrating intelligence: scaling and market structure in artificial intelligence
venue: Economic Policy 40(121): 225-256 (January 2025); earlier NBER Working Paper 33139 (November 2024)
data: Analytical paper
findings: Analytical rather than empirical. Foundation-model markets show technological features that drive intense competition among leading players today, but their cost structure, dominated by computing resources, data and talent, exhibits economies of scale and scope that could push the market toward greater concentration and possibly natural monopolies. The authors examine two competition concerns, the risk of market tipping and the effects of vertical integration, and assess policy remedies for keeping the market competitive. Looking ahead to more transformative AI systems, they argue that concentration could lead to an unprecedented accumulation of power, making competition policy a matter of broad societal concern.
magnitude: No estimate: argues that scale and scope economies in compute, data and talent could tip foundation-model markets toward concentration

design: Protein-level difference-in-differences: proteins with no experimental structure before AlphaFold2 (treated) versus proteins with one (control), around the July 2021 release of AlphaFold2 predicted structures
title: How Artificial Intelligence Shapes Science: Evidence from AlphaFold
period: AlphaFold2 release July 2021; outcomes observed about three years later
data: UniProt SwissProt (about 570,000 curated proteins, only 8% with an experimental structure before AlphaFold), Protein Data Bank experimental structures, curated protein literature, ChEMBL bioactivity records
findings: The release of hundreds of thousands of predicted structures was a large information shock for proteins without experimental structures and a negligible one for proteins that had them. The rate of experimental structure determination has stayed almost unchanged; researchers instead use predictions as templates that complement experiments. Basic research on previously unsolved proteins rose by 15 to 40% relative to solved proteins (the introduction reports 16 to 25%), shifting work toward less-studied proteins, and new papers on those proteins cite the AlphaFold papers disproportionately. There is no evidence yet of a corresponding rise in applied early-stage drug research (ChEMBL bioactivities), though estimates are noisy and effects may take longer to emerge. Evidence comes from one AI tool in one field.
magnitude: Basic research on previously unsolved proteins rose 15-40% relative to solved proteins after AlphaFold; no change in experimental structure output or early drug research

design: Heterogeneous-adoption difference-in-differences across districts around the mandated UPI integration of a fintech wallet (matching and distance-to-hub IV as robustness)
authors: Copestake, Kirti, Martinez Peria and Zeng
title: Integrating Fragmented Networks: Interoperability in Money and Payments
venue: IMF Working Paper WP/25/126 (June 2025; updated August 2026)
period: UPI data April 2016-September 2024; integration event falls inside this window…
data: Universe of UPI transactions (monthly, by payer app, payer bank branch and payee app; P2P and P2M), district-month totals from a major pre-existing fintech wallet, and NPCI ATM cash-withdrawal data (April 2016-December 2023) as a cash proxy, at district level
findings: Identification: a heterogeneous-adoption difference-in-differences compares districts that were more versus less fragmented ex ante between UPI and a large closed-loop wallet after an RBI directive made the two networks interoperable, with district and state-by-month fixed effects (robust to matching on observables and a distance-to-hub instrument; no differential pre-trends). Total peer-to-merchant (P2M) payment value per person rose by 8.3 rupees per month more in more fragmented districts, equal to 93% of those districts' pre-integration mean (125% of less fragmented districts' post-integration mean), driven mainly by more users, and digital payments rose relative to an ATM-withdrawal proxy for cash. Lending likely based on payment data also accelerated in the more fragmented districts. A model-based aggregation that assumes no gain in unfragmented districts implies interoperability raised total national digital-payment usage by over 50% in the year after integration, which the authors say probably understates the effect. Caveats: the cross-district design identifies only relative effects, so the headline number depends on model assumptions; the wallet is anonymised and the horizon is short.
magnitude: Model-based estimate: interoperability raised total digital payment usage by over 50 percent in the year after integration

design: Intention-to-treat triple-difference: Pix launch x pre-Pix municipal mobile penetration x small vs large establishments, on matched employer-employee data
title: Financial Technologies, Labor Markets, and Wage Inequality: Evidence from Instant Payment Systems
data: Matched employer-employee records on all formal workers and establishments (RAIS, Ministry of Labor), 2016-2024, at municipality level, combined with Central Bank of Brazil municipality-month Pix data, firm-registry (CNPJ) data on firm creation, bank-branch data and 2019 mobile penetration (3G+ devices per capita, ANATEL)
findings: Identification: an intention-to-treat triple-difference interacts Pix's nationwide November 2020 launch with pre-Pix municipal mobile-phone penetration (a strong predictor of Pix adoption) and with the greater payment frictions of small versus large establishments; event studies show no differential pre-trends. A one-standard-deviation higher pre-Pix mobile penetration raises wages in establishments with fewer than 20 workers by 0.4% relative to larger ones (0.8% in retail and 1.4% in services, no effect in wholesale or manufacturing), raises employment in micro establishments by 1.7%, and lowers the municipal wage Gini by about 1% of its sample mean, with gains concentrated in the lower half of the wage distribution. Effects are larger where low-skill labour is scarce and are consistent with lower payment frictions raising small-firm labour demand; aggregate business lending does not rise, and formalisation or wage reporting alone does not explain the results. Caveats: only formal employment is observed, estimates are relative intention-to-treat effects, and the aggregate gains from uniform adoption come from a calibrated monopsony model rather than from the data.
magnitude: One-SD higher pre-Pix mobile penetration raises wages in small relative to large establishments by 0.4% (0.8% in retail, 1.4% in services) and lowers the wage Gini by about 1 percent

design: Instrumental variables: municipal flood events after Pix's launch as exogenous shifters of local Pix usage, with municipality and time-by-flood-risk fixed effects
title: Payment Technology Complementarities and their Consequences in the Banking Sector: evidence from Brazil's Pix
venue: Banco Central do Brasil Working Paper Series No. 600 (September 2024)
data: Weekly municipality-level data on Pix, TED wire transfers, boleto payment slips, debit-card acceptance and other payment methods (2019-2022); individual- and firm-level credit-registry (SCR) and account-registry (CCS) data; official municipal flood-emergency declarations
findings: Identification: floods, which the authors show did not affect other payment methods or banking behaviour before Pix, trigger a sustained rise in Pix use afterwards (including remittances into flooded municipalities) and serve as an instrument for local Pix usage, with municipality and time-by-flood-risk fixed effects. A 1% increase in active Pix users raises payment-slip transactions by 5.7%, bank-wire transactions by 4.5% and the number of firms accepting debit cards by 1.2%, and raises first-time bank-account holders by 0.80%, new credit relationships by 0.45% and new bank relationships by 0.25%. After a flood, actively used bank accounts grow by more than 4% for individuals and 2% for firms; both traditional and digital banks gain (digital banks more in new accounts, traditional banks more in firm account activity). Caveat: the instrument identifies the effect of flood-induced Pix usage working partly through an informal-insurance channel, so the elasticities may not extend to Pix adoption driven by other factors.
magnitude: A 1% increase in active Pix users raises first-time bank-account opening by 0.80% and payment-slip transactions by 5.7%

design: IV for municipal Pix usage using the easing of COVID-19 restrictions before launch, plus a second IV from counterparty-bank payment timeouts
title: Payment Convenience and Competition for Deposits
venue: Working paper, draft of 21 September 2026 (SSRN 4176990); supersedes 'Instant Payment Systems and Competition for Deposits', which the author's CV lists as revise-and-resubmit at the Journal of…
data: Monthly Pix transaction values and user counts for Brazil's 5,570 municipalities (from November 2020), bank-by-municipality balance sheets for 119 commercial banks (ESTBAN, January 2020-November 2022), bank-level deposit rates, municipal GDP and demographics
findings: Identification: municipalities that eased COVID-19 restrictions earlier used Pix more at launch, which instruments Pix usage; a second instrument uses failures at counterparty banks that disrupt Pix payments, and placebo tests show effects only around the November 2020 launch. Checking and time deposits at small banks rise relative to large banks and local deposit concentration (HHI) falls; a doubling of Pix transaction value is associated with a 14-basis-point narrowing of the deposit-rate gap between small and large banks, and small banks also expand lending somewhat. The effects run through cheaper transfers and retail payments and are stronger in more banked areas, indicating reallocation across existing accounts rather than new account opening; a deposit-demand model gives an average welfare gain of $380 per quarter (model-dependent). Caveats: both instruments rest on exclusion restrictions, the data cover commercial banks only (not credit unions or fintechs), and the paper is an unpublished job-market paper.
magnitude: A doubling of Pix transaction value is associated with a 14-basis-point narrowing of the deposit-rate gap between small and large banks

design: Berry-style logit demand estimation for payment instruments with network effects and instrumented fees, plus consumer-surplus simulations
title: Adoption and welfare effects of payment innovations: the case of digital wallets in Peru
data: Monthly market shares (by value and number of transactions) for six digital payment instruments (Yape and Plin wallets, intra-bank transfers, ACH immediate and non-immediate transfers, debit and credit cards) and cash, with fee and feature attributes
findings: Method: a logit demand model in the spirit of Berry (1994) estimates adoption of Peru's Yape and Plin wallets, with cash as the outside good, network effects, and payee fees used as an instrument for payer fees; simulations then quantify the role of product features and consumer surplus. A PEN 0.01 (USD 0.003) rise in payer fees cuts wallet market share by 0.31 percentage points (debit cards and cash each gain 0.11 pp); removing 24/7 immediate transfers lowers wallet usage by 15.75 pp, discontinuing POS-terminal interoperability by 26.01 pp and eliminating QR-code payments by 4.45 pp. The simulated consumer-surplus gain per transaction from wallet availability among banked individuals rises from 0.5% in January 2019 to 68% by April 2024, partly reflecting network effects. Caveats: estimates cover banked users only, rest on market-level aggregates, and the welfare gains are model-based simulations.
magnitude: Discontinuing wallet interoperability with POS payments would cut digital-wallet usage by 26.01 percentage points; a PEN 0.01 payer fee cuts market share by 0.31 pp

design: Market- and firm-level randomised entry of non-financial microenterprises as mobile-money agents across 136 localities (control, +1 or +3 entrants)
title: Randomized Entry: The Equilibrium Effects of Entry in Digital Financial Markets
venue: NBER Working Paper 33134 (issued November 2024; revised October 2025)
period: Baseline March-May 2023; entry June-October 2023; endline April 2024; phone…
data: Market census and surveys in 136 localities across 13 districts (627 incumbent mobile-money vendors, 575 potential-entrant firms and 4,872 consumers at baseline), audit studies, trust games and provider administrative records
findings: Design: with MTN Mobile Money and GCB's G-Money, which had banned new vendors, localities were randomly assigned to no entry, one added vendor or three added vendors, drawn from local non-financial microenterprises upgraded to mobile-money agents; 170 entrants were established. Treated potential entrants were 25 percentage points more likely to be mobile-money vendors at endline; net vendor misconduct fell by 46% (entrants 29% lower than incumbents; incumbents in treated localities 35% lower than in control localities). Market-level price-cost markups for non-financial goods fell by 32%, household expenditure rose 16% and revenues of non-financial goods and services rose 20%, linked to a 15 percentage-point (26%) shift from cash to cashless payment and lower transaction costs. Effects are larger in high-entry localities and where firms compete closely, and treated and untreated firms' prices for non-financial goods moved in opposite directions, netting to no change in average prices. Caveat: working paper from one country, with entry induced by providers relaxing their own entry ban; exits are tracked only by phone survey at 16 months.
magnitude: Randomised entry cut net vendor misconduct by 46% and raised revenues of non-financial goods and services by 20%

design: Difference-in-differences between districts whose government lead bank joined UPI early vs late (matched within state), plus a within-district-quarter comparison of self-employed vs other households
title: Can Cashless Payments Spur Economic Growth?
venue: NBER conference draft (first draft February 2023; this draft July 2023; latest version found)
data: CMIE household panel of about 200,000 households in 500+ districts (income, business ownership, borrowing), merged with district-quarter UPI transaction volumes from PhonePe (from 2018)
findings: Identification: UPI adoption differed across districts because the district's government lead bank joined the platform early (29 banks signalled interest at the August 2016 launch) or late (by May 2017); early- and late-adopter districts in the same state with similar branch penetration, literacy and population show parallel pre-trends, and the demonetisation shock is absorbed with fixed effects. Early-adopter districts had about 15-20% higher digital payments, and their households had 7.5% higher income and 2.39% higher business ownership after UPI; in panel regressions the elasticity of household income to district digital payments is 0.09. Effects are stronger where bank branches are scarcer and for self-employed households (street vendors and hawkers), who shift borrowing from informal to formal sources, pointing to lower payment transaction costs and relaxed borrowing constraints. Caveats: conference draft not yet peer-reviewed, and the lead-bank timing is treated as as-good-as-random only conditional on matching.
magnitude: Households in early-UPI-adopter districts have 7.5% higher income post-UPI; income elasticity to district digital payments is 0.09

design: Regression discontinuity in time around the August 2014 VAT rebates on card payments, plus retail-vs-wholesale difference-in-differences on firm VAT filings
title: Electronic Payment Technology and Tax Compliance: Evidence from Uruguay's Financial Inclusion Reform
data: Transaction-level data on all electronic (card) transactions and monthly firm-level VAT declarations from the tax authority, 2006-2015
findings: Identification: a regression discontinuity in time using high-frequency card data around the August 2014 introduction of consumer VAT rebates for debit/credit card payments (cutting VAT payable on debit-card purchases by up to 40%), and a difference-in-differences comparing retailers (treated, historically less compliant) with wholesalers on VAT declarations. Rebates triggered an immediate 50% rise in the number of card transactions and a 30% rise in card volume, but POS terminals in use rose only 10%, driven by firms that already had one; a 2015 cut in the rebates did not reduce card use. The retail-versus-wholesale difference-in-differences effect on reported sales, output VAT and net VAT liability is close to zero and precisely estimated. The authors attribute the null to endogenous POS adoption and to electronic sales being under 30% of reported sales among POS firms. Caveat: figures are from the 2021 working-paper version; the null concerns firm-level reported VAT, not aggregate revenue.
magnitude: VAT rebates raised card transactions by 50% but had a near-zero effect on firms' reported sales and VAT liabilities

design: Randomised encouragement design (information plus an offer to open a Lipa na M-Pesa account) among 1,222 restaurants and pharmacies; ITT and IV estimates
authors: Dalton, Pamuk, Ramrattan, Uras and van Soest
title: Electronic Payment Technology and Business Finance: A Randomized, Controlled Trial with Mobile Money
data: Baseline and follow-up firm surveys plus mobile-loan outcomes for 1,222 SMEs in Nairobi (669 restaurants, 553 pharmacies); 615 firms assigned to treatment and 607 to control
findings: Design: when Safaricom launched Lipa na M-Pesa, a retail e-payment product, treated merchants were informed about it and offered an account opened on their behalf (41.5% accepted: 62% of restaurants, 21% of pharmacies), and intention-to-treat and IV effects are measured 16 months later. The technology raised access to mobile loans (both number and amount borrowed) by at least 50% (0.17 SD), plausibly because digital transaction records reduce information asymmetries. It had no effect on sales or profits, but reduced sales volatility and precautionary investment, especially for smaller firms, suggesting mobile loans help small firms absorb short-term shocks. Caveats: the gains are in short-term mobile credit rather than firm growth, and the sample is restaurants and pharmacies in Nairobi.
magnitude: E-payment technology increased access to mobile loans (number and amount) by at least 50% (0.17 SD), with no effect on sales or profits

design: Triple-difference using interview date relative to the 1 July 2021 levy x rural vs urban x survey wave 5 vs wave 4; household fixed effects in the panel subsample
title: The Impact of a Mobile Money Levy on Household Welfare: Evidence from Tanzania
venue: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11228 (October 2025)
period: Survey waves 2014/15 and 2020-22; levy effective 1 July 2021
data: Tanzania National Panel Survey (wave 5: 4,709 households interviewed December 2020-January 2022, 2,071 of them after July 2021, with a panel subsample linked to wave 4) plus high-frequency phone-survey data
findings: Identification: the levy raised the fee on a USD 18 transfer from about USD 0.50 to almost USD 1.20 (+140%) before a roughly 30% cut in September 2021; treatment is defined by whether a household was interviewed before or after 1 July 2021, interacted with rural residence and compared with the earlier survey wave. In the pooled cross-section, rural adult-equivalent food consumption was 9% lower (not significantly different from zero without controls) and rural households were 10 percentage points more likely to worry about food; in the panel subsample the consumption decline of rural households is about 18%, giving the paper's 10-18% range. Food insecurity rose but severe deficits did not, and quarter-by-quarter estimates point the expected way but are imprecise. Caveats: interview-timing identification could be confounded by contemporaneous rural shocks (the authors control for shocks and run robustness checks), and several triple-difference coefficients are statistically insignificant.
magnitude: Rural households' per capita food consumption fell by 10-18 percent after the mobile money levy

design: Randomised early-vs-late roll-out of digital value-voucher transfers to 2,409 female-headed households, with diversion audits and merchant checks
title: Can Digital Aid Deliver During Humanitarian Crises?
data: 2,409 very poor female-headed households identified by Community Development Councils in 16 neighbourhoods of Kabul, Herat and Mazar-i-Sharif; monthly phone surveys plus transaction data from the digital payments provider (including merchants serving beneficiaries)
findings: Design: households were randomly assigned to an early group (1,208 households paid November 2022-January 2023) or a late group (1,201 paid from January 2023), with the late group as counterfactual while the early group received 4,000 AFN (about USD 45) every two weeks for two months through an interoperable digital payments platform. 99.75% of recipients used the payments; a prespecified nutrition index rose by 0.5 SD and a mental and financial health index by 1.5 SD (working-paper version), and 80% of recipients would prefer digital aid to paying a 2.5% fee to receive cash. Rigorous checks found no evidence of diversion by beneficiaries, merchants or the Taliban, and conservative delivery costs are under 7 cents per dollar, about 10 cents below the WFP global figure for cash-based transfers. Caveats: a two-month programme measured by phone surveys in one fragile setting; policymakers and experts surveyed in the paper overestimated diversion risk and delivery costs.
magnitude: Digital transfers raised a nutrition index by 0.5 SD at delivery cost under 7 cents per dollar, with no evidence of diversion

design: Randomised mobile-money cash transfers (eight transfers vs one transfer to controls) with endline and two-year follow-up
authors: Karlan, Lowe, Osei, Osei-Akoto, Roth and Udry
title: Social protection and social distancing during the pandemic: Mobile money transfers in Ghana
period: COVID-19 pandemic, with follow-up two years after the last transfer
data: Randomised sample of low-income Ghanaian households receiving mobile-money transfers during the pandemic; survey outcomes on food expenditure, income, psychological well-being and social distancing
findings: Design: low-income households were randomly assigned to receive eight mobile-money transfers summing to roughly one month's income, while control households received one transfer; the effect of merely announcing upcoming transfers is also tested. The announcement alone had no effect, but once disbursed transfers raised contemporaneous food expenditure by 8% and income by 20% without affecting psychological well-being; over 40% of the transfers were spent on food, and there is suggestive evidence that transfers increased social distancing. The income gain did not persist: two years after the last transfer, effects on consumption and psychological well-being are negative. The authors summarise long-term effects as null or negative.
magnitude: Transfers raised food expenditure by 8% and income by 20% while paid, but two-year effects on consumption and psychological well-being were negative

design: Staggered difference-in-differences and event studies on country adoption of open-banking (customer data-sharing) policies, plus UK SME difference-in-differences using a GBP 25 million turnover eligibility cutoff
authors: Babina, Bahaj, Buchak, De Marco, Foulis, Gornall, Mazzola and Yu
title: Customer data access and fintech entry: Early evidence from open banking
venue: Journal of Financial Economics 169, 103950 (NBER Working Paper 32089; Bank of England Staff Working Paper 1,059)
countries: 168-country policy database (49 countries with key open-banking policies by October 2021); UK microdata
period: Fintech VC analysis 2011-2021 (VC data 2000-first half 2021); policies through…
data: Hand-collected open-banking policy database for the 168 largest countries (over 99% of world GDP), fintech venture-capital financings, UK FCA consumer survey and UK SME panel data
findings: Identification: staggered adoption of open-banking policies across countries in difference-in-differences and event-study designs (no pre-trends), and, for UK SMEs, a difference-in-differences exploiting that the commercial open-banking policy applied only to firms with turnover below GBP 25 million. After adoption, the number of VC-backed fintech financings rises by about a third and the amount invested doubles (working-paper figures), with increases across advice, credit, payments and regtech; consumer trust in sharing data with fintechs predicts which countries adopt. In the UK, eligible SMEs are more likely to form new lending relationships with non-bank lenders and pay less interest on them, but the gains accrue mainly to SMEs with prior lending relationships, at odds with financial-inclusion goals. A calibrated model finds open banking raises welfare when used for advice, while for credit it promotes entry but raises prices for costlier or privacy-conscious consumers. Caveat: the cross-country evidence is on fintech investment rather than household or firm outcomes, and the authors describe it as early evidence.
magnitude: After open-banking policy adoption, VC-backed fintech financings rose by about a third and the amount invested doubled (working-paper version)

design: Comparative case study of Pix, Sinpe Móvil and CoDi using transaction microdata, tracking adoption by municipal income
authors: Argente, Gonzalez Alvarez, Méndez and Van Patten
title: Drivers of Digital Payment Adoption: Lessons from Brazil, Costa Rica, and Mexico
period: Pix from November 2020; Sinpe Móvil from 2015 (data to 2024); CoDi from 2019
data: Transaction-level microdata and user characteristics for the three central-bank-linked P2P platforms, aggregated to municipality level, with Findex and central-bank adoption statistics
findings: Method: a descriptive comparison of three central-bank-linked peer-to-peer mobile payment platforms, tracking how adoption spreads from affluent early adopters to lower-income groups (the 'income gradient'); there is no causal identification. Pix reached 60% of Brazilian adults within a year, Costa Rica's Sinpe Móvil took five years to reach 40% adoption and reached 80% in 2024, whereas Mexico's CoDi stagnated at 2-3% of adults since its 2019 launch. Pix and Sinpe Móvil reached nearly all income segments within five years, with the lowest-income municipalities transacting at nearly the same rates as richer ones, aided by low adoption costs, network effects, coordinated supply-side integration and early awareness efforts; CoDi stayed low-use and mostly high-income. Conditional on income, internet speed and bank-account ownership explain regional gaps, and in Costa Rica the marginal adopter became increasingly female, less urban and lower-skilled. Caveat: three cases only, so the patterns are correlations bundling platform design with country context.
magnitude: Pix reached 60% of Brazilian adults within a year; Mexico's CoDi reached only 2-3% of adults since 2019

design: Policy insight synthesising 28 randomised evaluations of digital financial services (narrative review, not a meta-analysis)
authors: J-PAL (academic leads Emma Riley and Emily Breza; insight author Tyler Spencer)
title: Digital financial services to improve formalized access and inclusion
venue: J-PAL Policy Insight (suggested citation 2024; page updated June 2025)
countries: Kenya, Bangladesh, Mozambique, Malawi, Uganda, Niger, Ghana, Afghanistan (as cited on the page)
data: 28 randomised evaluations of digital financial services (mobile money, digital savings, digitised government payments, digital credit) in low- and middle-income countries
findings: Method: J-PAL's narrative synthesis of 28 randomised evaluations of digital financial services. Reported effects include Niger, where digital transfers cut per-transfer costs by 20% and halved recipients' round-trip travel distance (about 4 km to 2 km); Malawi, where microentrepreneurs' mobile-money deposits rose 55-80% in quantity and 67-83% in value; Uganda, where switching female borrowers' loan disbursements to mobile money raised business profits 15% and capital 11%; and Bangladesh, where migrants sent 30% more remittances and recipient households' consumption rose 7.5%. Risks and limits are documented too: in Kenya small digital-loan borrowers were 6.3 percentage points less likely to forgo expenses after a shock but with no effect on assets or consumption; in Malawi 62% of digital borrowers failed to repay on time and providers had misled them about late fees; violence in Afghanistan deterred mobile-money use, and agent roll-out in northern Uganda did not raise usage where baseline phone ownership was low. Caveat: a narrative synthesis of heterogeneous studies, so the effect sizes come from different contexts and are not directly comparable.
magnitude: Niger: digital transfers cut per-transfer costs by 20% and halved recipients' round-trip travel distance (about 4 km to 2 km)

design: Coarsened-exact-matched stacked difference-in-differences and event studies on staggered e-invoicing adoption and first audits
title: E-invoicing, tax audits and VAT compliance
venue: Journal of Development Economics 172, 103403 (BSE Working Paper 1454, July 2024)
data: Universe of Rwanda Revenue Authority VAT filings and audit records, 2012-2019 (39,176 firm-year observations; 112,472 in the stacked sample)
findings: Identification: a stacked difference-in-differences with coarsened exact matching on the tax authority's audit risk score exploits staggered e-invoicing (electronic billing machine) adoption and first audits, comparing treated taxpayers with never-treated ones. In the working-paper version, e-invoicing adoption alone raised annual net VAT declared by about US$11,000 per firm and an audit by about US$27,000, while audits of e-invoicing adopters raised it by about US$33,400: the compliance gain comes mostly from audits becoming more deterrent, not from firms becoming more compliant on their own. Firms also respond on other margins: output VAT rises, and e-invoicing adopters report less input VAT only when audited, while effects on non-taxable sales are imprecise. Caveat: the July 2024 working paper stresses that the net-VAT effect of e-invoicing per se is quantitatively limited because firms re-adjust expenses, whereas the journal abstract reports higher net VAT payments and more efficient audits overall.
magnitude: E-invoicing adoption raised net VAT declared by about US$11,000 per firm; audits of e-invoicing adopters raised it by about US$33,400 (working-paper version)

design: Synthetic difference-in-differences exploiting an April 2022 mandate that about 5,000 larger VAT firms integrate their systems directly with the e-invoicing platform (EFRIS)
authors: Lees, Jouste, Musoke and Okello Ayo
title: The panopticon taxman: the impact of e-invoicing on VAT compliance in Uganda
venue: UNU-WIDER Working Paper 2025/112 (December 2025); ICTD partner publication
period: VAT returns 2013-2023; main balanced monthly panel January 2021-June 2023
data: Uganda Revenue Authority administrative VAT returns (full panel about 45,000 firms) and a balanced monthly panel of 9,442 EFRIS-user firms
findings: Identification: because all VAT-registered firms had to adopt EFRIS at once, the authors exploit the April 2022 requirement that about 5,000 larger firms switch to system-to-system integration with the tax authority, using synthetic difference-in-differences against comparison firms because levels and trends diverge. Treated firms reduced reported purchases by 43% and raised reported VAT liabilities by nearly 150%, with effects growing over time; the increase comes mainly from lower input-VAT claims and a sharp fall in negative VAT balances carried forward. Reported sales fell by 39%, which the authors read as indicative evidence of sales suppression as firms shift to other evasion margins, and on average treated firms still had negative VAT liabilities by the end of the data. On the extensive margin, monthly VAT filers accelerated (many previously filing only corporate income tax), suggesting new VAT payers entered the net. Caveat: effects are relative to comparison firms and identified for larger firms only.
magnitude: Treated firms reduced reported purchases by 43%, raised reported VAT liabilities by nearly 150%, and cut reported sales by 39%

design: Difference-in-differences around a reform introducing a computerised real-time risk-analysis system that accepts or rejects VAT credit claims (with electronic filing)
title: Using computerized information to enforce VAT: Evidence from Pakistan
data: Administrative VAT filing data on firms' tax-credit claims
findings: Identification: difference-in-differences compares firms exposed to a reform that draws on information beyond the VAT paper trail and authorises a computerised risk-analysis system to accept or reject tax credits in real time with unexposed firms, in a setting with electronic filing. Credit claims declined by 50% in treated firms, with firm-level responses ranging from 30% to 90%, and approximately 10% of treated firms were fake firms created for missing-trader fraud. The lower-bound estimate of the increase in net VAT collection at the country level is 10%. The author concludes that traditional enforcement (cross-matching, audit and recovery) fails to deter evasion in developing countries whereas risk-based real-time enforcement is effective.
magnitude: VAT credit claims fell by 50% (30-90% across firms); lower-bound increase in country-level net VAT collection of 10%

design: Staggered-rollout difference-in-differences across waves of mandatory VAT e-invoicing (firms mandated 2014-2018), balanced firm panel
title: Digitalization to improve tax compliance: Evidence from VAT e-Invoicing in Peru
period: 2010-2017 (quarterly panel; mandatory roll-out in waves from 2014)
data: Confidential SUNAT administrative tax data (full dataset nearly 200,000 firms); balanced panel of about 53,000 mandated firms (about 85% of domestic VAT collections), 1,010,380 firm-quarters
findings: Identification: the staggered mandatory roll-out of VAT e-invoicing across firm waves is used as a quasi-experiment in a difference-in-differences design. E-invoicing raises reported firm sales, purchases and VAT liabilities by more than 5% in the first year after adoption. The effect is concentrated among small firms and in sectors with higher non-compliance, which the authors attribute to lower compliance costs and stronger deterrence. Existing stocks of VAT credits offset part of the gain in VAT collections, so complementary reforms are needed to realise the full revenue effect.
