Caveats: the panel excludes micro, informal and fraud-linked firms and firms entering or exiting, and the paper pre-dates 2024 (included as the flagship Latin American e-invoicing evaluation).
magnitude: E-invoicing raised reported sales, purchases and VAT liabilities by more than 5% in the first year after adoption

design: Staggered-rollout difference-in-differences across districts digitised in three phases (2011-2014), with stacked estimators and satellite and survey data separating tax-base from bureaucrat effects
title: Spillovers in State Capacity Building: Evidence from the Digitization of Land Records in Pakistan
data: Novel digitised administrative dataset on agricultural taxation in Punjab's 36 districts, a survey of local revenue bureaucrats (including 118 Qanungos), satellite vegetation data and farmer survey data
findings: Identification: difference-in-differences exploiting the staggered three-phase digitisation of Punjab's land records, with not-yet-digitised phase-3 districts as controls and stacked estimators robust to heterogeneous effects. Digitisation cut tax collection by 47% in phase 1-2 districts relative to phase 3 even though the tax base did not shrink (the effect on farm profits is positive but insignificant); bureaucrats issued lower tax demands and collected 35.4 percentage points less as a share of demand (about 66% of the pre-reform average). In the survey, 46% of bureaucrats said digitisation hurt tax collection, mostly through lost influence over taxpayers, and the share agreeing that citizens bribe for land titles fell from 48% to 33%. Caveat: causal estimates cover about two years after roll-out and later years are noisier, and the mechanism (loss of bureaucrats' leverage and bribe income) may not extend to settings where enforcement is already formalised.
magnitude: Land-records digitisation reduced agricultural tax collection by 47% in early-roll-out districts without a fall in the tax base

design: Staggered-rollout difference-in-differences (stacked estimator preferred, TWFE and IV versions, event studies) with treatment assigned at the phase level (2012-2014) across Punjab's 36 districts
title: Spillovers of Digitization
venue: Job market paper, KDI School of Public Policy and Management (undated draft citing 2026 work)
data: Ten administrative datasets incl. district-by-year agricultural credit (State Bank of Pakistan), 45,347 confidential anti-corruption incidents (restructured into a mouza-by-month panel), court cases, household survey data and land-tax records
findings: Identification: difference-in-differences (stacked, TWFE and IV, plus event studies) on the staggered phase-level roll-out of land-record digitisation in Punjab, with placebo checks on concurrent development budgets and pre-reform election returns. Digitisation raised the number of agricultural borrowers by roughly 19,000 (more than the sample mean) and lending by PKR 5-7 billion, concentrated among the smallest, previously collateral-constrained borrowers; recorded land-bureaucracy corruption incidents roughly tripled across complaints, enquiries, cases and convictions, which the author reads as better detection rather than more bribery. Land-case resolution improved and rental-market activity rose, while land purchases and sales were unchanged. Caveats: not peer-reviewed; the corruption outcome measures enforcement actions rather than bribery itself; and the same reform reduced agricultural tax collection in Aman-Rana and Minaudier (AER 2026).
magnitude: Land-record digitisation expanded agricultural lending by PKR 5-7 billion (about 19,000 more borrowers) and roughly tripled recorded land-related corruption cases

design: District-level randomised trial giving subdistrict managers, district principals, or both access to PayDash, an app tracking pending workfare payments, vs control
authors: Dodge, Neggers, Pande and Troyer Moore
title: From Delay to PayDay: Easing Bureaucrat Access to Implementation Information Strengthens Social Protection Delivery
data: 73 districts and 561 subdistricts with over 1,200 bureaucrats; 17.4 million MGNREGS worker attendance registers; app-usage analytics; bureaucrat posting records
findings: Design: PayDash is a mobile and web app that reads timestamps from the government's online work-verification and payment-processing system; districts were randomly assigned to control or to one of three treatments (managers, principals, or both receive it), and officials were encouraged but not compelled to use it. Treated districts processed worker payments 17% (1.4 days) faster, active worksites rose 23% and household days worked 10%, mostly in the agricultural lean season. Access for principals was as effective as for managers and giving it to both added nothing, indicating that managers' cost of acquiring information is the binding constraint; principal access also cut manager posting transfers by 24%, and processing-time gains were larger in high-workload districts (22% vs 12%). The authors estimate rural households' benefits exceed costs by more than 170 times and that PayDash strengthens capacity at a much lower cost than hiring staff. Caveat: NBER working paper covering two states and one programme.
magnitude: PayDash sped up payment processing by 17% and raised household work days by 10%; benefits exceed costs by more than 170 times

design: Cluster-randomised trial of biometric tracking devices in tuberculosis treatment centres (65 clusters; 34 treated, 31 control)
title: Biometric Monitoring, Service Delivery, and Misreporting: Evidence from Healthcare in India
venue: Review of Economics and Statistics 107(6), 1553-1572 (NBER Working Paper 26388)
period: Experiment lasted 12-14 months depending on state
data: 129 areas in urban slums grouped into 65 clusters served by the NGO OpASHA; 3,393 patients and 85 health workers in the impact evaluation, using surveys, random centre visits and hospital registers
findings: Design: the NGO randomised, at cluster level and stratified by city and health-worker type, the roll-out of biometric devices that record health-worker attendance and patient dose-taking and prompt follow-up when patients miss doses. Patients at biometric-equipped centres were 25% less likely to interrupt treatment, reflecting greater health-worker attendance and effort and better patient adherence. The technology also improved data quality by reducing overreported patient numbers in both NGO data and government registers and underreported treatment interruptions. Effects were sustained over time and did not reduce health-worker or patient satisfaction. Caveat: one NGO's tuberculosis programme in urban slums, with a modest number of clusters (65).
magnitude: Patients at biometric-equipped centres were 25% less likely to interrupt tuberculosis treatment

design: Coarsened exact matching of electronic vs paper tenders combined with procuring-entity and year fixed effects (two matching strategies), exploiting discretionary staggered e-GP adoption
authors: Blum, Datta, Fazekas, Samaddar and Siddique
title: Introducing E-Procurement in Bangladesh: The Promise of Efficiency and Openness
venue: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 10390 (April 2023)
period: FY2011-12 to FY2017-18 (e-GP roll-out from FY2012-13)
data: Electronic tenders of three public-works agencies (BWDB, LGED, RHD): 69,240 tenders across 185 district-level procuring entities, matched to a sample of 10,319 paper-based tenders, plus surveys of 600 procurement officials and 600 firms
findings: Identification: because procuring entities chose when and which tenders to move to e-GP, the authors match electronic and paper tenders with coarsened exact matching (within entities across years, and within years across entities with similar baseline values) and run fixed-effects regressions on tenders least exposed to spillovers. E-procurement increased the number of bidders by 1.6-2.2, cut the probability of a single bidder by 7.8-13.5 percentage points, raised winning discounts by 7.4-8.0 percentage points and shortened tendering time by 15.6-19.2 days. The authors estimate direct government savings of US$460-513 million in the analysed tenders and a GDP gain of 0.48-0.54% (US$1.4-1.6 billion in 2019) from indirect macro effects. Caveats: the design is non-experimental, low performance and rent-seeking may have been displaced to the still largely paper-based contract-implementation phase, and the savings and GDP figures are extrapolations.
magnitude: E-procurement raised the number of bidders by 1.6-2.2 and cut the probability of a single bidder by 7.8-13.5 percentage points

design: Pre/post OLS comparison of tender outcomes with time trend and entity/goods fixed effects (no control group; planned RDD abandoned after a density jump at the start date)
title: Examining the Impact of E-Procurement in Ukraine
venue: Center for Global Development Working Paper 511 (June 2019)
period: Pre-ProZorro data January 2014-July 2016; ProZorro piloted from February 2015…
data: Above-threshold (over UAH 200 thousand) one-lot competitive tenders from legacy portals and the ProZorro BI module: 78,038 observations in the baseline number-of-bids regression, 4,192 procuring entities
findings: Design: OLS regressions of number of bids, savings rate and time to contract on a ProZorro dummy, with a time trend, contract-value controls and (in later columns) entity and goods-type fixed effects, restricted to larger competitive tenders that were already fairly transparent; a regression-discontinuity design was abandoned because the density of tenders jumped at the ProZorro start date. The ProZorro dummy raises the savings rate (final versus estimated price) by 3.5-5.3 percentage points across specifications and shortens tender-to-contract time by about 5.5-6.4 days in four of five specifications, but its effect on the number of bids is small and insignificant once entity and goods fixed effects are added (and negative for repair services). The savings result loses significance when limited to cases where final price is below the estimate, and the reform at the same time banned awards above the estimated price and tightened time limits. Caveat: no control group, so ProZorro cannot be separated from concurrent reforms; the large rise in the share of procurement value tendered competitively (24.5% in 2015 to 70.3% in 2017, per earlier work the authors cite) is not captured.
magnitude: ProZorro dummy: savings rate higher by 3.5-5.3 percentage points and tender-to-contract time shorter by about 5.5-6.4 days; no robust effect on number of bids

design: Staggered difference-in-differences (Sun-Abraham interaction-weighted estimator); treated = country's first tower-sharing deal covering at least 1,000 towers; 107 deals
title: The Impact of Shared Telecom Infrastructure on Digital Connectivity and Inclusion
countries: Developing countries: 28 treated by a deal of at least 1,000 towers; deals recorded in 40 countries, including Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda, Brazil, India and Indonesia
data: Country-year panel of developing countries: 107 tower-sharing transactions in 2008-2020 (TowerXchange) matched to ITU ICT price baskets in PPP terms (mobile voice and data), GSMA mobile connections and HHI, and Gallup household internet access for rural and female-headed households (2010-2015)
findings: Staggered difference-in-differences (Sun-Abraham estimator) comparing developing countries from the year of their first tower-sharing deal covering at least 1,000 towers (28 treated countries; 107 deals in 2008-2020) with never-treated countries; event studies show no significant pre-trends. The PPP-adjusted mobile-price index falls by $1.60 from a 2010 mean of $3.16 (s.e. $1.10, so imprecise) and the data-price index by $1.00 per GB from a baseline of $3.41 (s.e. $0.29); mobile connections rise by 1,422 thousand (s.e. 385). The headline estimates put the gain in internet access at 4.7 percentage points for rural households and 3.6 percentage points for women-headed households. The results section is more nuanced: the women-headed gain is 3.2 points in the baseline and persists when early years are dropped, while the rural gain is concentrated in the transaction year and fades after two years. Market concentration (HHI) falls 5.3%, pointing to competition as the channel. Contract form matters more than size: sale-and-leaseback deals (54% of deals), where the seller stays as anchor tenant, cut voice tariffs by about 1.1 log points per minute while acquisitions (38%) show an insignificant increase, with no meaningful difference for data prices or connectivity; deals above about 2,000 towers add little. Preprint; the deals are voluntary commercial transactions, not mandated sharing.
magnitude: Data price -$1.00 per GB (baseline $3.41); internet access +4.7 percentage points for rural and +3.6 percentage points for women-headed households; HHI -5.3%

design: Operator-level staggered difference-in-differences (TWFE, Borusyak-Jaravel-Spiess and Callaway-Sant'Anna estimators, IV, randomisation tests) on 140 operators
title: To share or not to share? The impact of mobile network sharing for consumers and operators
data: Quarterly panel of 140 mobile operators: sharing agreements by type (Coleago database: passive, active, roaming, tower company), GSMA Intelligence coverage, ARPU, capex, EBITDA and HHI, Ookla download speeds (2011-2018)
findings: Operator fixed-effects difference-in-differences comparing operators that entered a sharing agreement with operators in countries with no sharing (baseline window: 5 years before to 2 years after the deal), checked with Borusyak-Jaravel-Spiess and Callaway-Sant'Anna estimators, an instrumental-variable specification and 3,000 random reassignments of treatment. Any sharing is associated with 3G coverage +1.6 pp, 4G coverage +5.6 pp, lower normalised capex (-23.2, p<0.05), market HHI -100 points and ARPU (the price proxy) -EUR 0.54 (p<0.1); average coverage gains are 2-9 pp depending on specification and deal type. Passive sharing drives capex savings, higher EBITDA margins, 3G coverage (+3.9 pp) and the ARPU fall (-EUR 1.63); active sharing drives 4G coverage (+5.3 pp), download speed (+4.7 Mbps) and data traffic; roaming raises coverage but lowers average speeds in the baseline (-2.9 Mbps); benefits are larger for smaller operators, while HHI rises when the largest operators (40%+ share) share. Caveats: price is proxied by ARPU, which also reflects usage; the instrument is weak (low first-stage F); the tower-company results are labelled indicative only; two authors work at the GSMA (the mobile operators' association).
magnitude: Any sharing: 4G coverage +5.6 pp and market HHI -100 points; passive sharing: ARPU -EUR 1.63 (baseline window, 5 years before to 2 years after the agreement)

design: Structural model of operator competition in prices and network quality, identified from the cost gap between shared and non-shared deployment, plus reduced-form fixed-effects regression on download speeds
title: Horizontal cooperation on investment: Evidence from mobile network sharing
venue: TSE Working Paper 20-1100 / CEPR Discussion Paper 14770 (preliminary draft, April 2020)
data: Czech mobile market: operator prices, Ookla download speeds (district-quarter-operator panel, 5,540 observations, Q1 2011-Q2 2019) and network deployment costs; geo-split sharing agreements between O2 and T-Mobile CZ signed 2013/2014
findings: Structural estimation of the effects of the 2013/14 geo-split network sharing agreements (2G/3G/4G) between O2 and T-Mobile Czech Republic against a counterfactual of independent deployment. The authors summarise that operator costs are roughly 40% lower with the agreements (counterfactual marginal costs of quantity are 40.4% higher for T-Mobile CZ and 33.6% higher for O2), prices are on average 14% lower, download speed on average 24% higher, and consumer surplus over four years EUR 1.8 billion larger; in the counterfactual prices would be 14.8%, 14.6% and 12.5% higher for T-Mobile CZ, O2 and Vodafone, and quarterly consumer surplus 5.9% lower (EUR 111.1 million). A reduced-form district-operator regression finds download speeds 21.7% higher after the agreements (20.6-35.2% across specifications). Caveats: preliminary draft with no journal version found; the authors worked for NERA on behalf of a mobile operator in the European Commission's case AT.40305 on this agreement; the counterfactual rests on assumed cost increases (including a 33% rise in Vodafone's costs without the deals), and a lab experiment by Krämer and Vogelsang (2016) suggests co-investment can facilitate collusion.
magnitude: Compared with independent deployment (authors' summary): costs roughly 40% lower, prices 14% lower, download speed 24% higher, and consumer surplus EUR 1.8 billion larger over four years

design: Difference-in-differences on operator-level cost data for 33 mobile operators (11 control operators); national roaming and other sharing types
title: Analyzing the Economic Effects of Past Mobile Network Sharing Deals for Future Network Deployment
data: Operator-level operating and capital expenditure for 33 mobile operators, 11 of them control operators without sharing deals
findings: Difference-in-differences analysis of 33 operators (11 controls) to measure the cost-reduction effect of mobile network sharing. The authors report a reduction in overall operating expenditure and short-term capital expenditure from national roaming. They argue that sharing becomes more viable and relevant in 5G deployment because additional spectrum bands raise the total cost of ownership of networks. Houngbonon et al. (2025) summarise this paper as finding national roaming cuts operating expenditure by 14% in the short run and 19% in the long run. Caveats: the outcomes are operator costs rather than prices or coverage.
magnitude: National roaming reduced overall operating expenditure and short-term capital expenditure (difference-in-differences, 33 operators incl. 11 controls); secondary source reports -14% (short run) and -19% (long run) opex

design: Fixed-effects and dynamic panel regressions of network investment on market competition, infrastructure sharing and their interaction
title: Market Competition, Infrastructure Sharing, and Network Investment in China's Mobile Telecommunications Industry
data: Panel data on China's mobile telecommunications industry (market competition, infrastructure sharing and network investment measures)
findings: Fixed-effects and dynamic panel models of the link between market competition, infrastructure sharing and network investment in China's mobile industry. Market competition has a significant positive effect on total industry network investment, but the interaction of competition and infrastructure sharing undermines network investment; the authors read this as operators shifting from facility-based to service-based competition when deep sharing and fierce competition coincide, weakening incentives to invest in advanced technology. They recommend supporting sharing but exercising caution with in-depth sharing. Caveat: panel regressions without a quasi-experimental shock.
magnitude: Competition raises total industry network investment, but the competition x infrastructure-sharing interaction reduces it

design: Laboratory experiment: duopoly network-competition game comparing co-investment, unilateral investment and duplicate investment
title: Co-Investments and Tacit Collusion in Regulated Network Industries: Experimental Evidence
data: Laboratory sessions with human participants playing a network-competition game
findings: Laboratory experiment motivated by regulators' recent permission for competing network operators to co-invest in infrastructure. Treatments compare co-investment with unilateral and duplicate investment. The main finding is that co-investment (cooperation at the infrastructure level) significantly facilitates tacit collusion at the retail level, which questions the positive consumer-surplus evaluation of co-investment in the theoretical literature. This contrasts with ex-post studies of real sharing agreements (e.g. Koutroumpis et al. 2023; Cojoc et al. 2020) that find lower prices. Caveat: a stylised game rather than a real market.
magnitude: Co-investment facilitated tacit collusion significantly relative to unilateral and duplicate investment

design: Difference-in-differences with coarsened exact matching of census tracts; Iowa's 2015 dig-once and permitting laws vs matched tracts in non-adopting states (eight specifications)
title: Do 'dig once' and permitting policies improve fiber availability?
period: Iowa laws passed 2015; outcomes after implementation
data: Census-tract fiber and fixed-wireless availability; treated and control tracts matched on pre-2015 demographics and broadband-availability trends
findings: Difference-in-differences on matched census tracts evaluating two Iowa laws passed in 2015: a dig-once requirement that state-funded construction notify local internet providers about buried conduit, and a permitting law requiring timely local responses to broadband equipment requests. Iowa's policies increased fiber broadband availability by 2.4%-6.6% across eight model specifications (varying regional controls, other broadband policies and federal funding) and had no detectable effect on fixed-wireless availability. Caveats: the two laws are bundled so their separate effects are not identified; a single treated state; the outcome is availability rather than take-up; figures as summarized by the Benton Institute.
magnitude: Iowa's dig-once and permitting policies increased fiber broadband availability by 2.4%-6.6%; no effect on fixed-wireless availability

design: Panel fixed effects (difference-in-differences type) plus control-function IV using an entry model, on local exchange data; effects of local loop unbundling and cable competition
title: Unbundling the Incumbent: Evidence from UK Broadband
venue: Journal of the European Economic Association 13(2): 330-362
data: Quarterly broadband lines by operator for over 5,500 BT local exchanges (Dec 2005-Dec 2009, from Ofcom), individual broadband speed tests (2009) and exchange-level demographics
findings: Evaluation of mandated wholesale access (local loop unbundling, LLU) in UK broadband using an entry model, panel fixed effects and a control-function approach. LLU entry rose strongly over 2005-2009 but raised broadband penetration only in the early years and no longer once the market matured, whereas it continued to raise service quality because entrants differentiate upward; exchanges with LLU entry have considerably higher average speed, entirely due to the entrants' lines, with no higher speed for BT customers. Inter-platform competition from unregulated cable raised both penetration and quality, including in recent years. Caveats: proprietary Ofcom data; funded by the Orange Innovation and Regulation Chair; the paper does not measure incumbent investment directly; single country.
magnitude: LLU entry raised broadband penetration only in the early years (no effect once the market matured) but kept raising speed; the speed gain came entirely from entrants' lines

design: Panel econometric model of incumbent and entrant investment with strategic interaction and endogenous regulation (70+ operators)
title: Regulation and Investment in Network Industries: Evidence from European Telecoms
countries: 20 EU member states (fixed-line markets; list not extracted)
data: Data set covering 70 fixed-line operators in 20 countries over 10 years
findings: Panel econometric model that allows different investment incentives for incumbents and entrants, strategic interaction between their investments, and endogenous regulation. Access regulation has a negative effect on both total industry investment and individual carrier investment, so promoting market entry through regulated access undermines incentives to invest in facilities-based competition. The authors also find a regulatory commitment problem: higher incumbent investment encourages the provision of regulated access. Caveats: fixed-line rather than mobile markets and a regulation index rather than a single reform.
magnitude: Access regulation reduced both total industry investment and individual carrier investment (70 fixed-line operators, 20 countries, 10 years)

design: Difference-in-differences, country-trend DiD and synthetic control on tariff price baskets, Austria vs ten EU countries with no merger or entry
title: Ex-post analysis of the merger between H3G Austria and Orange Austria
countries: Austria; controls: Belgium, Denmark, Finland, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Sweden
data: Quarterly tariff data (Tarifica) for the main brands in Austria and ten control countries, turned into smartphone-user and traditional-user price baskets (average of the four cheapest tariffs per operator brand), Q1 2011-Q4 2014
findings: Ex-post evaluation of the January 2013 four-to-three merger of Hutchison 3G (Drei) and Orange Austria, cleared by the European Commission in December 2012 with spectrum, national-roaming and MVNO-access commitments; the study measures price effects before the MVNO remedies became effective (data to November 2014). For the smartphone-user basket the long-run price effect is +30.1% (basic DiD, but the common-trend test fails), +90.2% (country-trend DiD) and +50.4% (synthetic control, significant only at 10% on the placebo test); the short-run effect is +24.2% with country trends and insignificant otherwise. For the traditional user (voice and SMS only) long-run effects are +27.6%, +31.3% and +22.3% with no short-run increase. Results hold when the October 2013 spectrum-auction costs are considered. Caveats: authored by the national regulator using a methodology developed with the European Commission and the Dutch regulator; few control countries (standard errors likely biased downward); list tariffs exclude handset subsidies.
magnitude: Long-run price rise of 50% (synthetic control) to 90% (country-trend DiD) for smartphone users and 22-31% for traditional users after the H3G/Orange merger, before MVNO remedies took effect

design: Synthetic control on the Czech Republic's 2013 MVNO market entry (the 2021 conference version used difference-in-differences against Slovakia and 13 EU countries)
title: The impact of mobile virtual network operators on the mobile telecommunications services market: The case of the Czech Republic
period: Q3 2010-Q4 2015 in the 2021 conference version; MVNO entry in 2013
data: National and cross-country mobile market data (call prices, operator ARPU, outgoing minutes)
findings: Evaluates the 2013 entry of MVNOs (which buy wholesale capacity from the three network operators) in the Czech Republic. The published synthetic-control analysis finds that MVNO entry led to a decrease in the price of calls and in operators' average monthly revenue per user (ARPU), with no significant effect on data prices or on consumption. The earlier 2021 conference version, using difference-in-differences with Slovakia and 13 EU countries as controls, reports call-price falls of 7.6% to 17.5% on average and an ARPU fall of 9% against the EU control group (insignificant against Slovakia); its minutes results fail the common-trend test. Caveats: single country and single entry event; the magnitudes are from the earlier conference version.
magnitude: MVNO entry lowered call prices and ARPU but not data prices or consumption (published); 2021 DiD version: call price -7.6% to -17.5%, ARPU -9% vs EU controls

design: Difference-in-differences with Rest-of-the-World roaming traffic as control; consumer-surplus bounds (Kang-Vasserman) and profit changes
authors: Canzian, Mazzarella, Ronchail, Verboven and Verzillo
title: Evaluating the impact of price caps - Evidence from the European roam-like-at-home regulation
countries: 28 EEA countries (Rest of the World as control)
data: Quarterly operator-level international roaming traffic and revenues (BEREC/European Commission questionnaires): 105 retail operators (84 MNOs, 21 MVNOs) and 87 wholesale MNOs, 2,100 retail and 1,740 wholesale observations
findings: Evaluates the EU roam-like-at-home (RLAH) regulation, which banned retail roaming surcharges within the EEA from June 2017 and tightened wholesale caps, using roaming traffic to the Rest of the World as control. Intra-EEA roaming volumes rose substantially, more for data than voice; wholesale revenues rose proportionately less than data volumes; MVNOs and operators in Central-East and South Europe saw larger traffic increases. Bounding demand curves, annual EEA consumer surplus rose by EUR 1.4-2 billion (about 80% from data, about EUR 1 billion from existing demand), retail profits fell by EUR 1.3 billion, wholesale profits rose by about EUR 300 million and annual total welfare rose by EUR 0.2-1 billion; no waterbed effect on domestic prices is detected. Caveats: only one pre-regulation quarter for the event study; welfare uses Commission marginal-cost estimates; EEA setting, not low-income countries (relevant to regional roaming integration).
magnitude: RLAH raised annual EEA consumer surplus by EUR 1.4-2 billion and total welfare by EUR 0.2-1 billion

design: Operator panel regressions with fixed effects and instrumental variables for spectrum price (short-term government debt in developing countries; non-auction assignments and regional prices in developed countries)
title: The impact of spectrum assignment policies on consumer welfare
data: Panel of 229 mobile operators in 64 countries: spectrum assignments and prices (GSMA Intelligence), 3G/4G population coverage, Ookla speeds and ITU price baskets/ARPU
findings: Panel estimates of how the amount, timing and cost of spectrum assignment affect coverage, network quality and consumer prices, instrumenting spectrum prices. Higher spectrum prices slowed 4G rollout in both developed and developing countries and 3G rollout in developing countries, and lowered network quality; in IV estimates a 1% rise in spectrum cost (USD PPP per MHz per capita per licence-year) lowers 4G coverage by 0.53 pp in developing countries and 0.16 pp in developed countries, and a delay of at least two years in releasing 4G spectrum goes with 11-16 pp lower 4G coverage. Higher spectrum prices are also associated with higher consumer prices in developing countries, but the authors say this needs further research to confirm robustness. Caveats: the magnitudes quoted are from the 2019 GSMA technical report version of the study; GSMA is the mobile operators' trade association; instruments may be imperfect.
magnitude: IV estimate: a 1% increase in spectrum cost lowers 4G coverage by 0.53 pp in developing countries (0.16 pp in developed); a 2+ year delay in 4G spectrum release goes with 11-16 pp lower 4G coverage (2019 technical report)

design: Structural model of price and infrastructure competition (demand for plans and data use, engineering-based download speeds, endogenous base-station investment) with merger and spectrum-allocation counterfactuals
title: Market Structure, Investment, and Technical Efficiencies in Mobile Telecommunications
data: French consumer data on subscriptions and data consumption by plan and commune for one operator (Orange Mobile, 2015), Ookla measured download speeds, ANFR base-station data and INSEE income data
findings: Structural estimation of a model in which operators choose prices and base-station investment and download speeds follow engineering relationships with economies of density and pooling. Equilibrium simulations show that prices fall as the number of firms rises but so do download speeds; in the published version consumer surplus is maximised at six symmetric firms, while fewer firms would raise total surplus and welfare for high-income consumers (low-income consumers prefer more firms). The framework also values spectrum allocation: the June 2024 working-paper version reports that the marginal social value of spectrum is about five times a single firm's willingness to pay, and that every two-operator merger in France reduces consumer surplus in the short run. Caveats: model-based counterfactuals for one country and one year; the working-paper version reported consumer surplus maximised at eight firms; research supported by Orange through the TSE Partnership foundation.
magnitude: Consumer surplus is maximised at six firms (working-paper version: eight); fewer firms would improve total surplus and high-income consumers' welfare

design: Semi-parametric treatment-effect estimators comparing countries that assigned 3G spectrum by auction with those using beauty contests, across seven market outcomes
title: The effects of spectrum allocation mechanisms on market outcomes: Auctions vs beauty contests
data: Cross-country data on seven mobile market outcomes after 3G spectrum was assigned by auction or beauty contest
findings: Compares seven market outcomes in 47 countries after mobile spectrum was allocated through auctions or beauty contests between 2000 and 2008, using two semi-parametric treatment-effect estimators. 3G mobile penetration in auctioning countries is 1.04%-8.95% lower than in beauty-contest countries. The authors conclude that auctions used to raise public revenue shift profits to the government but reduce consumer surplus, consistent with newer theory that auction-related selection and debt effects can harm aftermarket competition. Caveats: countries self-select the mechanism, and a study of 21 OECD countries (Park, Lee and Choi 2011, Information Economics and Policy 23(1)) finds no evidence of harm from 3G auctions.
magnitude: 3G penetration in auctioning countries is 1.04-8.95% lower than in beauty-contest countries

design: Panel regressions with country and time fixed effects and instrumental variables (interpretable as a staggered difference-in-differences of market structure) on operator-level prices and capex
title: Evaluating market consolidation in mobile communications
data: Unique panel of mobile operators' prices (usage baskets) and accounting information, including capex, across 33 OECD countries
findings: Panel estimates of how market concentration, driven by entry via licensing and exit via mergers, affect end-user prices and investment, with country and time fixed effects and instruments based on regulatory interventions. More concentrated markets lead to higher end-user prices and to higher investment per mobile operator, but the effect on total industry investment is not conclusive. Based on the estimates, a hypothetical symmetric 4-to-3 merger would raise consumers' bills by 16.3% on average and operator-level capex by 19.3%; for recent asymmetric 4-to-3 mergers among smaller European firms the CERRE summary reports bill increases of about 4-7% and capex per operator increases of 7.5-14%. Caveats: figures are from the April 2017 Economic Policy panel draft and CERRE summary; capex per operator is a proxy for investment; a previous version was written for CERRE.
magnitude: Hypothetical symmetric 4-to-3 merger: end-user bills +16.3% and capex per operator +19.3% on average; total industry investment effect inconclusive

design: Dynamic firm-level panel with instrumental-variable estimation (competition intensity based on the Lerner index in the 2014 conference version)
title: What level of competition intensity maximises investment in the wireless industry?
data: Firm-level panel data on wireless operators (capex, revenues, profits)
findings: Dynamic panel estimates with instrumental variables of the relationship between competition and investment in the wireless industry. The relationship is inverted-U shaped: the investment-maximising intensity of competition is reached when operators' gross profits represent 37 or 40 per cent of revenues, depending on whether capex is normalised by the number of subscribers; below these thresholds there is a trade-off between competition and investment. The authors also find a long-run effect of competition on investment that amplifies the short-run effect by a factor of 3-4. Caveat: the result is a statistical relationship across operators rather than the effect of a specific policy.
magnitude: Investment peaks when operators' gross profits are 37% or 40% of revenues (inverted-U); long-run effect of competition on investment 3-4 times the short-run effect

design: Structural oligopoly model of the French mobile market around Free Mobile's 2012 entry and the incumbents' fighting-brand launches, with welfare decomposition
title: Market Entry, Fighting Brands, and Tacit Collusion: Evidence from the French Mobile Telecommunications Market
data: French mobile services market data around the 2012 entry of Free Mobile, 2011-2014
findings: Empirical oligopoly model of the French mobile market before and after the new low-cost entrant Free Mobile and the introduction of fighting brands by the three incumbents. The incumbents' fighting-brand strategies are difficult to rationalise as unilateral best responses; they are consistent with a breakdown of tacit semi-collusion on restricting product variety, which became harder to sustain after entry because of stronger business-stealing incentives. Consumers gained considerably from the added variety and, to a lesser extent, from the incumbents' price responses: according to the AEA research summary, 50% of consumer gains came from the entrant's added variety, 32% from the incumbents' fighting brands and 18% from intensified price competition, and Free Mobile captured 20% of the market within a few years. Caveats: structural inference depends on the model's conduct assumptions; numbers quoted are from the AEA research summary of the paper; the episode is an entry event rather than a merger, so implications for merger control are indirect.
magnitude: Of consumer gains from the entry episode, 50% came from the entrant's added variety, 32% from fighting brands and 18% from intensified price competition (AEA summary)

design: Structural model of mobile phone adoption and use with network effects, tower investment and firm competition; counterfactual simulations of earlier entry and interconnection policy
title: Competition in network industries: Evidence from the Rwandan mobile phone network
data: 5.3 billion transaction records from the incumbent operator (over 88% market share) covering 1.5 million networked consumers, regulator's engineering cost data, and a consumer survey on switching costs
findings: Structural estimation of consumers' utility from adopting and using mobile phones, with firm tower-rollout and pricing equilibria, used to simulate competition policy. Granting the second, well-run competitor a licence in 2005 rather than at the end of 2009 would have lowered prices by 30-50% and increased the incumbent's incentive to build rural towers, raising net welfare by up to 38% (USD 112m or USD 153m), equivalent to about 1% of GDP; business stealing accounts for 80-88% of the incumbent's profit from rural towers. Lower interconnection fees lower prices and raise welfare but reduce the return on tower investment (building rural towers stays profitable across the range), and forcing free interconnection can lower incentives to invest. Caveats: counterfactual simulations conditional on the model; one country and one incumbent's data; figures are from the September 2021 working-paper revision.
magnitude: Earlier licensing of a second competitor would have cut prices 30-50% and raised welfare by up to 38% (about 1% of GDP)

design: Cross-country panel regressions of telecom sector performance on privatisation, competition and independent-regulator reforms, including policy interactions and reform sequencing
title: An assessment of telecommunications reform in developing countries
countries: 86 developing countries in Africa, Asia, the Middle East, and Latin America and the Caribbean
data: Panel of 86 developing countries: mainline penetration and productivity against reform indicators for privatisation, competition and independent regulation
findings: Cross-country panel analysis of how ownership and competition policies, their interaction and the regulatory framework affect telecom performance in developing countries. Both privatisation and competition lead to significant performance improvements; a comprehensive reform programme combining both with an independent regulator produced the largest gains, an 8 percent higher level of mainlines and a 21 percent higher level of productivity compared with years of partial or no reform. The sequence of reform matters: mainline penetration is lower if competition is introduced after privatisation rather than at the same time. Autonomous factors such as technological progress account for about 5 percent a year growth in teledensity and 9 percent in productivity over the period. Caveats: figures are from the 2002 working-paper version (World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 2909); fixed-line era data (before mobile dominance); reform indicators are endogenous.
magnitude: Comprehensive reform with an independent regulator: 8% higher mainlines and 21% higher productivity than years of partial or no reform

design: Dynamic country panel (Anderson-Hsiao IV and Arellano-Bond difference GMM) of new-network connections on state aid, with geographic Hausman-type and political-ideology instruments; cost-benefit using external GDP estimates
title: Effectiveness and Efficiency of State Aid for New Broadband Networks: Evidence from OECD Member States
venue: Economics of Innovation and New Technology 33(5): 672-700
data: Country-year panel for 32 OECD countries: state aid for new (fibre-based) broadband networks and share of households with new-network connections
findings: Panel instrumental-variable and GMM estimates of the effect of public subsidy programmes (state aid) on the deployment of fibre-based new broadband networks. State aid significantly increases new broadband network connections, by 22 percentage points of households in the short term and 39.3 percentage points in the long term (the 2021 working paper reported 22% and 39.2%). Comparing actual state-aid amounts with the estimated effect on GDP growth, the programmes are highly cost-efficient and break even after three years on average. The authors discuss improvements such as technology neutrality, consideration of mobile broadband and demand-side funding. Caveats: only 32 countries and aggregate subsidy measures; the cost-benefit step uses external estimates of the output effect of fibre networks; OECD context.
magnitude: State aid raises new broadband network connections by 22 pp of households in the short term and 39.3 pp in the long term; programmes break even after three years on average

design: Structural model of private fibre entry estimated on municipality data, used to simulate private entry without subsidies, plus evidence on the plan's effect on early fibre coverage
title: State aid for broadband and crowding out of private investment: Evidence from the French market
data: Fibre deployment data for more than 34,000 municipalities in mainland France, 2014-2019, and public subsidies disbursed under the Plan France Très Haut Débit
findings: Estimates a model of fibre entry and assesses whether private investment would have occurred in subsidised municipalities without state aid. In 36% of cases public subsidies went to municipalities where private entry would have occurred within three years, and about EUR 902 million of the EUR 2,203 million disbursed by the end of 2019 may have crowded out private investment; the French plan nevertheless accelerated fibre coverage in subsidised municipalities in the early stages of deployment. The earlier 2023 CESifo working-paper version framed the same exercise as 64-93% of subsidies going where private entry would not have occurred, with 'inefficient' subsidies costing EUR 243-902 million. Caveats: counterfactual entry is model-based; the French setting (high-income, dense fibre market) may not transfer to low-income countries.
magnitude: In 36% of cases subsidies went where private entry would have occurred within three years; about EUR 902 million of EUR 2,203 million may have crowded out private investment

design: School panel with school and year fixed effects exploiting variation in E-Rate subsidy rates (20-90%) across districts; second stage on test scores
title: The Impact of Internet Subsidies in Public Schools
data: Technology data for every public school in California 1996-2000 plus E-Rate application data and test scores
findings: Panel estimates of the effect of the US E-Rate subsidy, which covered 20%-90% of school spending on internet and communications from 1998, on Internet investment in California public schools. The subsidy significantly increased Internet investment: the implied first-dollar price elasticity of demand for Internet investment is between -0.4 and -1.1, greatest in urban schools and schools with large black and Hispanic student populations, and by the final sample year there were about 68% more Internet-connected classrooms per teacher than without the subsidy. The authors do not find significant effects of E-Rate on student performance, at least so far. Caveats: the 2002 NBER working-paper version reported an elasticity of -0.9 to -2.2 and about 66% more Internet classrooms; one state; test scores may respond only with a lag.
magnitude: First-dollar price elasticity of Internet investment between -0.4 and -1.1; about 68% more Internet-connected classrooms per teacher; no significant effect on student performance

design: County-level difference-in-differences and triple-difference (following Zuo 2021) comparing low-income counties well served by fixed broadband with underserved low-income counties, before and after ACP's January 2022 launch
title: Evaluating the Impact of the Affordable Connectivity Program
venue: USC Annenberg ARNIC, MEDIA Phase II report (May 2024)
data: FCC broadband deployment data, USAC ACP enrolment and ACS 1-year estimates: 237 counties (1,471 observations) in the double-difference and 1,921 counties (11,366 observations) in the triple-difference
findings: Because ACP had no state-level variation, the study uses low-income counties with fewer than half of locations served by fixed broadband (about 100 counties) as controls for low-income counties with adequate fixed supply. The average treatment effect on the share of households with broadband and a computer is +5.7 pp (s.e. 3.45, significant only at 10% with wild-bootstrap errors) in the double-difference and +9.8 pp (s.e. 3.07, p<0.01) in the triple-difference, about 7% of the 2021 adoption level in the conservative case. ACP uptake in December 2023 was 25.3% of households in underserved low-income counties versus 31.1% in other low-income counties. Caveats: preliminary, non-peer-reviewed policy report; only one post-treatment year (2022); intention-to-treat effects at county level using a median-income proxy for eligibility; the control group assumes supply constraints isolate ACP's effect.
magnitude: ACP raised the share of households with broadband and a PC by 6-10 pp (5.7 pp double-difference; 9.8 pp triple-difference) in well-served low-income counties relative to underserved ones

design: Programme analysis of India's Universal Service Obligation Fund: subsidy auctions, rural tower commissioning and rural teledensity trends
title: Role of Universal Service Obligation Fund in Rural Telecom Services: Lessons from the Indian Experience
venue: IIMA Working Paper 2009-06-03 (Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad)
data: USOF collection and disbursement data, reverse-auction outcomes for rural mobile infrastructure subsidies, tower commissioning status (DoT) and TRAI teledensity statistics to 2008-09
findings: Descriptive analysis of the outcomes of India's Universal Service Obligation Fund (USOF), especially its subsidised rural mobile deployment. Despite innovative reverse-auction design (winning subsidies in the Part A tender were 68.7% below the benchmark), the programme had little impact on rural teledensity: by September 2008 only 1,934 of 7,871 awarded towers (25%) had been commissioned, 13% for the state incumbent BSNL, while rural teledensity was 12.62% against 81.38% in urban areas in December 2008. Cost-reducing policies (revenue shares, duties, access deficit charge) and competition did more to raise rural penetration. Weak accountability between the state-owned incumbent and the fund administrator, no ring-fencing, poor project management and unenforced penalties are blamed; the authors estimate that raising rural teledensity by one percentage point needs nearly USD 1 billion, against nearly USD 3 billion unspent in the fund in September 2008. Caveats: working paper and programme analysis without a counterfactual or causal design.
magnitude: Only 25% of awarded USOF towers (1,934 of 7,871) were commissioned by September 2008; rural teledensity 12.62% vs urban 81.38% (December 2008)

design: Difference-in-differences on monthly tariffs comparing the former zero-rating providers (Telekom, Vodafone) with other providers around the July 2022 ban on marketing zero-rating options
title: Ökonometrische Analyse des Verbots von Zero Rating in Deutschland (Econometric analysis of the zero-rating ban in Germany)
venue: WIK Kurzstudie (WIK Wissenschaftliches Institut für Infrastruktur und Kommunikationsdienste), Bad Honnef, December 2024
period: May 2021-June 2023 (main specification; ban on new marketing from July 2022)
data: Monthly tariff data collected by WIK for 32 mobile network providers, grouped into three price classes
findings: After EU Court of Justice rulings (September 2021), Germany's regulator banned new marketing of Deutsche Telekom's StreamOn and Vodafone Pass zero-rating options from 1 July 2022. Difference-in-differences with other providers as comparison finds a significant rise in included data volumes of about 480 MB in price class 1 (up to EUR 29.99, possibly a lower bound), 3.5 GB in class 2 (EUR 29.99-39.99) and 14.1 GB in class 3 (above EUR 39.99). The authors compute thresholds below which former zero-rating customers gain and conclude that they were on average probably not worse off. Caveats: short study by a research institute; outcome is included data volume, not prices paid or usage; only two treated providers; WIK cites an RTR (2019) study of 11,000+ tariffs from 50+ operators in 15 EU countries that found no systematic effect of zero-rating on other tariff features.
magnitude: Included data volume rose by about 480 MB (price class 1), 3.5 GB (class 2) and 14.1 GB (class 3) after the zero-rating ban

design: Event study and difference-in-differences around Uganda's July 2018 mobile money tax, comparing users and districts in the top quartile of ATM density with the rest (differential response by availability of substitutes)
title: Mobile money tax: Financial inclusion versus financial development. Evidence using transaction-level data: The case of Uganda
venue: International Growth Centre (IGC) final report UGA-24179, May 2025
data: Universe of one of the two main mobile money operators' transactions (over 50 million in 2018; about 5.5 million active users before the tax, district known for about 1.5 million), Uganda National Panel Survey 2018/19 (5,000+ individuals), bank-district cash issuance (26 banks, 10 districts) and ATM withdrawal data
findings: Uganda introduced a 1% tax on all mobile money transactions in July 2018, quickly revised to 0.5% on withdrawals only. Transaction-level data show a drop in average mobile money balances and in transactions after the tax that did not recover after the revision, and the DiD shows that users in high-ATM-density districts reduced usage more than users in low-density districts: they transact 4% to 12% less after the tax, and survey respondents there are up to 9% less likely to use mobile money. Substitution towards banking agents, bank deposits, ATM withdrawals and cash is concentrated where banks are accessible (urban districts), leaving rural users with fewer options; the report links the volatile deposit inflows to banks shifting credit to safer borrowers. Caveats: the design identifies the differential response by ATM density, not the average effect of the tax; project report, not peer reviewed; the headline persistence and regressivity conclusions rest on descriptive time-series plus these differential estimates.
magnitude: High-ATM-density users transact 4%-12% less than low-density users after the tax; up to 9% less likely to use mobile money (survey)

design: Average effective tax rate (AETR) of a calibrated representative mobile operator ('TELCO') built from GSMA Intelligence data, including general taxes, special taxes and regulator fees, compared with a representative gold-mining plant and a…
title: The tax burden on mobile network operators in Africa
countries: 25 African countries (19 with a gold-mining comparator)
data: Representative operator constructed from the GSMA Intelligence database for 25 African countries; tax and regulatory-fee schedules; web application for replication
findings: Because country-level financial data are lacking, the authors build a representative operator and compute its average effective tax rate including special taxes and fees raised by the telecommunication regulator. The AETR varies widely, from 33 percent in Ethiopia to 118 percent in Niger. Special taxes and fees represent a large share of the AETR, illustrating taxation by regulation and a potential race to the top between the finance ministry and the regulator. The tax burden of the telecom sector is higher than that of the gold-mining sector in 15 of the 19 countries for which gold-mining data exist. Caveats: figures are from the FERDI working-paper version; a calibrated representative firm rather than observed firm tax payments; descriptive, with no estimate of effects on connectivity or revenue.
magnitude: Average effective tax rate on a representative mobile operator ranges from 33% (Ethiopia) to 118% (Niger); higher than for gold mining in 15 of 19 countries

design: Incidence analysis of platform fees and prices on Amazon around the introduction of national digital service taxes
title: Navigating the Amazon: The Incidence of Digital Service Taxes
venue: Working paper (WU Vienna research repository, published 12 June 2025)
countries: Countries with digital service taxes where Amazon operates
data: Data on Amazon (the largest online retailer): platform fees and seller prices around digital service tax introductions
findings: Studies who bears national digital service taxes (DSTs), which tax the revenue of large digital firms to indirectly tax profits earned in the market country, using Amazon data. On average Amazon increased its fees by roughly half the amount of the DST, and firms selling through Amazon have largely passed these higher fees on to consumers. Large digital firms thus bear only a small part of the tax burden, although the tax may still make them less competitive relative to brick-and-mortar rivals. Caveats: working paper; one platform.
magnitude: Amazon raised its fees by roughly half the amount of the digital service tax; sellers largely passed the fee increases on to consumers

design: Country panel regressions with fixed effects and instrumental variables (several panel estimators) on net neutrality regulation and fibre investment, motivated by a two-sided market model
title: Net neutrality and high-speed broadband networks: evidence from OECD countries
venue: European Journal of Law and Economics 55(3): 533-571
data: OECD country panel for 32 countries: fibre-optic (high-speed) broadband connections as the investment measure and net neutrality regulation indicators
findings: Estimates the causal impact of net neutrality regulation on new fibre investment by internet service providers, using a 32-country OECD panel and several panel techniques including instrumental variables. The authors find that net neutrality regulations exert a significant and strong negative impact on fibre investments, so strict rules clearly slow down the deployment of new fibre-based broadband connections. They stress that they cannot provide evidence on the overall welfare consequences of net neutrality. Caveat: the US evidence is contested, and one US study finding no investment effect (Hooton 2020, Telecommunications Policy) carries a journal expression of concern and was not used.
magnitude: Net neutrality regulation has a significant and strong negative impact on fibre investment

design: Bottom-up installed-base energy model with 2024-2028 scenarios and water and emissions accounting
authors: Shehabi, Smith, Hubbard, Newkirk, Lei, Siddik, Holecek, Koomey, Masanet and Sartor
title: 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report
venue: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report LBNL-2001637 (prepared for the US Department of Energy under the Energy Act of 2020)
data: Installed base of data-centre equipment reconstructed from shipment data, market-analyst and industry inputs (no facility-level metering); county-level water and emissions intensity factors by electricity balancing authority
findings: A bottom-up engineering model of the US data-centre equipment stock (not an econometric estimate), with post-2023 results shown as scenarios that vary GPU shipments, AI-server utilisation and cooling choices. Electricity use was about 60 TWh in 2014-2016, 76 TWh (1.9% of US electricity) in 2018 and 176 TWh (4.4%) in 2023, a compound annual growth rate of about 7% in 2014-18 and 18% in 2018-23. The 2028 scenario range is roughly 325-580 TWh, 6.7%-12.0% of forecast US electricity consumption (74-132 GW at 50% utilisation), i.e. 13%-27% annual growth. Direct water consumption was 66 billion litres in 2023 (21.2 billion in 2014), hyperscale facilities are projected to use 60-124 billion litres in 2028, and indirect water use through electricity is nearly 800 billion litres with 61 billion kg of CO2e. Caveats: the authors stress that scarce facility-level data limits the analysis, and indirect water and emissions use local grid averages and ignore power-purchase agreements.
magnitude: 176 TWh in 2023 (4.4% of US electricity), rising to roughly 325-580 TWh (6.7%-12.0%) by 2028 in the scenario range

design: Instrumental-variables continuous difference-in-differences on data-centre location attractiveness, plus a calibrated regional model
title: Is AI Trained on Public Money? Evidence from US Data Centers
venue: Swiss Finance Institute Research Paper No. 25-73 (SSRN 5475309)
data: US data-centre energy loads, utility electricity prices, and establishment-level revenues, employment and carbon emissions
findings: The authors instrument rising data-centre demand with location attractiveness in a continuous difference-in-differences design to test whether data-centre growth raises local retail energy prices or creates other local spillovers. They find no detectable local spillover effects from data-centre energy growth through 2023. A regional model calibrated to these null results suggests that shocks larger than those observed through 2023 could still raise household utility bills noticeably if not offset by regulation or outside supply. Caveat: the null applies to the 2010-2023 range of data-centre growth and the paper is a working paper; a separate IV study (Watten, Bistline and Blanford, 2026) finds modestly lower US retail rates, so results depend on design and sample.
magnitude: No detectable local spillover effects of data-centre energy growth on local retail energy prices, 2010-2023

design: Pre-registered randomised deactivation experiment (6 weeks vs 1 week) on 19,857 Facebook and 15,585 Instagram users
authors: Allcott, Gentzkow, Mason, Wilkins, Barberá, Brown et al.
title: The effects of Facebook and Instagram on the 2020 election: A deactivation experiment
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 121(21): e2321584121
data: 19,857 Facebook and 15,585 Instagram users (US adults using the platform more than 15 minutes per day) recruited via Meta; baseline, endline and post-endline surveys, validated turnout records, campaign-donation records and Meta platform data; 27% assigned to 6-week deactivation, the rest to a 1-week deactivation control
findings: A pre-registered experiment run with Meta, in which the treatment group was paid to deactivate for six weeks before election day and the control group for one week so that both experienced identical procedures. Deactivation reduced an index of political participation by 0.167 SD (Facebook) and 0.090 SD (Instagram), driven mainly by less online participation; Facebook deactivation cut news knowledge by 0.098 SD and trust in political information from Facebook by 0.040 SD, with no significant effect on the overall knowledge index (-0.033 SD, P=0.069). Effects on affective and issue polarization, perceived election legitimacy, candidate favourability and turnout were precisely estimated and close to zero (turnout effects larger than about 1.6 percentage points are ruled out); a possible reduction in net Trump votes after Facebook deactivation did not meet the pre-registered significance threshold. Caveats: US-only and short-run, partial equilibrium (others stayed on the platforms), self-reported outcomes and about 2 percentage points of differential attrition. A March 2026 PNAS correction only adds a reviewer funding disclosure.
magnitude: Political participation index -0.167 SD (Facebook) and -0.090 SD (Instagram); polarization and turnout effects close to zero

design: Randomised field experiment: algorithmic vs chronological X feed for 7 weeks (4,965 users)
title: The political effects of X's feed algorithm
data: 4,965 US X users recruited through YouGov who completed the post-treatment survey (6,043 completed the pre-treatment survey); survey outcomes, scraped followed-account data and feed content captured by a Chrome extension for 599 participants
findings: Users were randomised to an algorithmic or chronological feed for about 7 weeks, creating two experiments: switching the algorithm on for users who initially used the chronological feed, and switching it off for users on the algorithmic feed. Switching the algorithm on raised an engagement index by 0.14 SD and an index of policy and current-events attitudes by 0.12 SD towards more conservative positions, with no significant effect on affective polarization or self-reported partisanship. Switching the algorithm off produced no comparable effects, which the authors explain by persistent following of conservative political-activist accounts (+0.18 SD) acquired under the algorithm. The algorithm made conservative-annotated posts 2.9 percentage points (19.9%) more likely and news-organisation posts 15.5 percentage points (58.1%) less likely to appear. Caveats: US-only, opt-in YouGov panel, short-run self-reported attitudes, and a sample too small to test heterogeneity reliably (effects concentrated among Republicans and Independents).
magnitude: Switching the algorithm on shifted policy and news attitudes by +0.12 SD towards conservative positions; switching it off had no comparable effect

design: Two-stage randomised online experiment on Facebook Messenger (40-arm factorial, then adaptive assignment), n=15,292
title: Battling the coronavirus 'infodemic' among social media users in Kenya and Nigeria
data: Facebook Messenger users from Kenya (n = 7,498) and Nigeria (n = 7,794); outcome is stated intention to share COVID-19 misinformation versus factual posts
findings: The experiment tested interventions designed to reduce intentions to share COVID-19 misinformation without reducing intentions to share factual posts, using a factorial design followed by an adaptive design that shifted assignment towards treatments that worked better for similar earlier subjects. Warning flags and related-article suggestions, the tactics platforms already use, had precisely estimated null effects. Nudges to consider the accuracy of information reduced misinformation sharing by 4.9% relative to control (-2.3 percentage points, 95% CI -4.2 to -0.35). Caveat: the outcome is self-reported sharing intention rather than observed sharing, and the effect is modest.
magnitude: Accuracy nudges reduced misinformation-sharing intentions by 4.9% (-2.3 percentage points, 95% CI -4.2 to -0.35); warning flags and related-article suggestions had null effects

design: Two randomised experiments (training: 858 firms; conditional online purchase order: 283 firms) with follow-ups to 2025
title: Barriers to Market Access: Experimental Tests of Supply- and Demand-Side Strategies
venue: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11460
period: Training 2019; demand shock March-May 2022; follow-up surveys July 2021 and…
data: Small firms (about 5 employees on average) outside Tbilisi: 858 firms randomised to training (638 treated, 220 control); 283 firms randomised to control (131), low-offer (76, about US$130) and high-offer (76, US$780) purchase orders; surveys in 2021 (656 firms) and 2025 (616 firms) plus monitoring records
findings: Two randomised experiments test why small firms stay out of digital markets: a supply-side training in how to list on e-commerce platforms, and a demand-side offer to place an order if the firm sold online within two weeks. Training failed to raise digital participation: just over half of firms that signed up attended, and the long-run engagement index was negative and insignificant. The conditional order raised market access by 24 percentage points, but an offer six times larger produced only a modest additional increase and there was no complementarity with training (interaction point estimate 0.02, a tenth of the main effect). Effects largely dissipated as control firms caught up (35% of high-propensity control firms were online-ready by the 2025 follow-up, against none in 2021; treated firms stayed 14.7 percentage points higher but not significantly so), while baseline e-commerce readiness predicted long-run engagement. Caveats: small samples, imprecise interaction and heterogeneity estimates, and 2025 attrition.
magnitude: Conditional purchase order raised firms' online market access by 24 percentage points; e-commerce training had no effect on digital participation

design: Randomised controlled trial of freelance training and mentorship (2,000 participants; 70/30 split; mentorship sub-randomisation)
authors: Charles, Xia, Smith, Danon and Alhorr
title: Opportunities Without Borders? The Impact of Access to Remote Work for Refugees
venue: World Bank Social Policy and Labor Discussion Paper No. 2628
countries: Kenya (70% of sample), other East African countries including Rwanda and Uganda (19%), and other locations
period: Cohorts March-September 2024; endline surveys February-May 2025 (10-14 months…
data: 2,000 refugees and host-community members randomised (1,400 offered training, 600 control; 41% female, 42% forcibly displaced); endline survey with 1,344 responses (67.3% response rate) plus administrative and longitudinal qualitative data
findings: Participants were randomised to Na'amal's package of soft-skills training, three-week freelance training and, for a subset, five-month mentorship, versus a control group that received only self-guided soft-skills content. Take-up was partial: 51% of the treatment group attended any training and 24% at least half. Assignment raised the probability of having heard of Upwork by 5.4 percentage points (control mean 86%) and of ever creating an Upwork profile by 4.7 percentage points (control mean 63%, p<0.10), but produced no statistically significant effects on job applications, online work, hours worked or earnings. The authors attribute this 'conversion gap' to structural entry barriers (payment-system access, identity verification, application costs, no reputation signals) rather than skills. Caveats: low compliance, a less interactive platform for the control group, and a short follow-up.
magnitude: Training raised Upwork profile creation by 4.7 percentage points (control mean 63%) but had no significant effect on job applications, hours worked or earnings

design: Randomised controlled trial (lottery): app-based vs in-person business training vs control, 2,000 women entrepreneurs
title: Testing the Promise of Digital Scaling: In-Person versus App-Based Training for Women Entrepreneurs
venue: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 10992
data: 2,000 growth-oriented women entrepreneurs in Addis Ababa with at least secondary education, a smartphone and internet access; baseline and six-month follow-up surveys
findings: The trial randomised women entrepreneurs to an eleven-module smartphone training app (adapted from US mobile MBA-preparation courses, in Amharic and English), an in-person course with the same syllabus, or a control group. Initial take-up was high for both modalities (80% app, 76% in-person) but completion differed sharply: 22% for the app versus 71% in person, despite reminders, cash-prize draws and an offline mode. Both modalities produced statistically significant but modest improvements in business knowledge, and six months later negligible impacts on business practices and performance, so the in-person arm's higher completion bought no extra benefit. Caveats: the sample was deliberately selected (smartphone and internet access, interest in digital training) to favour the app, and the data cannot separate lack of capacity to implement the learning from other binding constraints.
magnitude: Completion rate 22% for app-based training versus 71% for in-person training; negligible impacts on business practices and performance from either

design: Cluster randomised trial across 270 schools: life-skills safe spaces alone or with digital literacy classes
authors: Chang, Ebrahim, Gulesci, Hailemicheal, Jagun and Rouanet
title: Safe Spaces to Digital Spaces: Short-Term Impacts of Life Skills and Digital Literacy Training for Adolescent Girls in Nigeria
venue: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11445
period: Midline survey 12 months after the end of the intervention (World Bank AGILE…
data: More than 8,000 adolescent girls (average age 16) in Grade 1 of senior secondary school across 270 schools; surveys of girls, caregivers and administrators
findings: Schools were randomised to a life-skills safe-space programme (10-month academic year, two to three sessions per week) or the same programme plus twice-weekly digital literacy classes in computer-equipped classrooms, versus control. Pooled across the three states, neither treatment significantly changed school enrolment, socio-emotional skills, digital literacy or marriage at midline; life skills modestly improved knowledge of topics such as sexual and reproductive health, climate change and gender-based violence. The digital component gave a modest 6% increase in a curriculum-aligned digital score pooled (not robust to multiple-testing adjustment) but a nearly 10% improvement in the multidimensional digital literacy index in Kaduna, where implementation was completed before midline (control mean 0.35). Caveats: practical digital training had not been rolled out in two of the three states by midline, so the pooled null mainly reflects implementation fidelity; these are short-term results.
magnitude: Where fully implemented (Kaduna), digital literacy training raised the digital literacy index by nearly 10% (control mean 0.35); no significant pooled effect on enrolment or digital literacy

design: Classroom-randomised field experiment (nearly 1,000 students): GPT-4 base vs GPT-4 tutor vs textbook control
authors: Bastani, Bastani, Sungu, Ge, Kabakci and Mariman
title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 122(26): e2422633122
data: Nearly 1,000 students in about fifty 9th-11th grade classes at one large Turkish high school; four 90-minute sessions, practice problems with AI access followed by a closed-book exam
findings: Classrooms were randomly assigned to control, GPT Base or GPT Tutor, with the AI available only in the practice phase and a closed-book exam on conceptually similar problems afterwards. Access raised practice performance by 0.137 (GPT Base, 48%) and 0.361 (GPT Tutor, 127%) on a 0-1 scale against a control mean of 0.28. On the unassisted exam, GPT Base students scored 0.054 lower (17% lower) than control, while GPT Tutor students were statistically indistinguishable from control (-0.004), so safeguards removed the harm but produced no learning gain. Students used the base tool as a crutch by copying solutions, and did not perceive any loss of learning. Caveats: a single school in an upper-middle-income country, short-run outcomes, and a tutor prompt that embedded teacher-provided solutions.
magnitude: Unassisted exam score 17% lower for students who had used unrestricted GPT-4 (GPT Base); practice scores +48% (GPT Base) and +127% (GPT Tutor)

design: Matched stacked event-study difference-in-differences on firm-quarter financials around 338 cyber incidents
title: How do cyber attacks impact corporate balance sheets and income statements? An empirical study
venue: 25th Workshop on the Economics of Information Security (WEIS), June 2026 (non-archival working paper)
data: 338 publicly known cyber incidents (178 data breaches, 139 ransomware, 21 other) at SEC-reporting firms matched to 338 same-industry controls on size and profitability; 63,846 firm-quarter observations
findings: Incident records are linked to quarterly SEC financial statements and compared with propensity-matched same-industry controls in a stacked event-study DiD. On average, incidents cause persistent increases in operating and capital expenditure financed through higher liabilities (peak about +6.9% in total liabilities and +7.1% in SG&A at two quarters after the incident) and sustained earnings declines. Effects differ by attack type: data breaches trigger balance-sheet expansion (total liabilities about +12.9% at Q3) to fund remediation while largely preserving profitability, whereas ransomware acts as an availability shock with falling gross profit, operating income and receivables and no capital restructuring. The authors note that these costs are only partially reflected in firms' qualitative disclosures. Caveats: only publicly known incidents at US listed firms, moderate size imbalance after matching, a non-archival working paper, and no evidence for developing-country firms.
magnitude: Data breaches: total liabilities about +12.9% three quarters after the incident; ransomware: earnings losses and falling operating income without balance-sheet expansion

design: Bed-weighted two-stage difference-in-differences event study of 8 ransomware attacks on California hospitals
title: Ransomware Attacks, ED Visits and Inpatient Admissions in Targeted and Nearby Hospitals
data: California ED and patient discharge data aggregated to facility-week; 8 care-disrupting ransomware attacks on 15 hospitals versus 355 unattacked hospitals; 17 nearby unattacked hospitals versus 20 others in the same hospital service area
findings: The design compares attacked hospitals with unattacked hospitals around each attack, and nearby unattacked hospitals with other hospitals in the same service area. Emergency department visits at attacked hospitals fell 8.10% in week 1 and 16.21% in week 2 relative to baseline (mean 740.90 weekly visits), and inpatient admissions fell up to 16.62% in week 2, returning to pre-attack levels by 8 weeks. At nearby unattacked hospitals ED visits rose by about 6.7%-7.1% for up to four weeks, with no significant change in inpatient admissions. Caveats: very small sample (8 attacks), California only, data end in 2020, utilisation rather than clinical outcomes are measured, and excluding one non-disruptive attack may modestly overstate harms.
magnitude: ED visits at attacked hospitals -16.21% in week 2 (95% CI -26.58 to -5.84); about +7.1% peak at nearby unattacked hospitals in week 3

design: Five-arm online randomised experiment (n=2,851) of a WhatsApp chatbot inoculation game
authors: Dugas, Pinzon, Lim, Vakis, Afif, Hasumi and Elfadel
title: Find the Fake: Boosting Resistance to Health Misinformation in Jordan with a WhatsApp Chatbot Game
venue: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 10933
data: 2,851 WhatsApp users aged 18+ recruited through Facebook advertisements; outcomes are discernment of headlines using misinformation techniques and discernment in sharing intentions
findings: Participants were randomly assigned to one of five arms delivered through a WhatsApp chatbot, with a pure control arm added four days after launch. Relative to placebo, the comprehensive game raised misinformation discernment by 0.29 SD and sharing discernment by 0.23 SD, lowering the likelihood of sharing misleading headlines by 0.30 SD without reducing sharing of accurate headlines. The brief game raised discernment by only 0.14 SD and cut sharing of misleading headlines by 0.33 SD, but also cut sharing of non-misleading headlines by 0.26 SD, consistent with more conservative responding. Infographics teaching the same techniques had no significant effect on discernment and marginal effects on sharing intentions. Caveats: recruited online via Facebook ads, outcomes are stated intentions measured immediately after the game, and effects are short-term in a single middle-income country.
magnitude: Comprehensive WhatsApp game raised misinformation discernment by 0.29 SD and cut sharing of misleading headlines by 0.30 SD; infographics had no significant effect on discernment

design: Official statistics series from smart-meter data (agency statistics; no causal design)
title: Data Centres Metered Electricity Consumption 2025
data: Electricity Supply Board (ESB) Networks meter data for all mains-connected meters; the CSO identified data-centre meter points among about 2.6 million meters; annual and quarterly GWh
findings: The CSO built a national series of data-centre electricity use from ESB Networks meter data by identifying data-centre meter points among roughly 2.6 million meters, noting that a small number of facilities account for most of the consumption. Data-centre metered consumption rose 10% in 2025, from 6,973 GWh to 7,663 GWh, against a 2% rise for all other users, lifting its share of total metered electricity to 23% from 5% in 2015. Quarterly consumption grew from 291 GWh in Q1 2015 to 1,991 GWh in Q4 2025 (+584%), and in 2025 the 23% data-centre share compared with 28% for all residential dwellings and 33% for Large Energy Users, a category that includes significant data centres. Caveats: the series relies on the CSO's classification of data-centre meters, and the release header says 2025 while the statistician's comment is dated 7 July 2026.
magnitude: Data centres used 23% of Ireland's metered electricity in 2025 (7,663 GWh), up from 5% in 2015; +10% in 2025 versus +2% for all other users

design: State audit combining economic-impact modelling, independent demand forecast, grid scenarios and tax-exemption review
authors: JLARC staff (Gribbin, Sarte, Miller, Berday-Sacks, Hopkins and Saunders)
title: Data Centers in Virginia
venue: Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission, JLARC Report 598 (Report to the Governor and the General Assembly of Virginia, 9 December 2024)
