data: Consultant economic-impact and grid models, an independent utility cost-recovery study, interviews with data-centre operators, utilities and localities, and state and local tax data
findings: The audit estimates that the data-centre industry contributes 74,000 jobs, $5.5 billion in labor income and $9.1 billion in GDP to Virginia annually, mostly from construction, and that data-centre revenue ranged from under 1% to 31% of total local revenue in five mature-market localities. An independent forecast finds that unconstrained electricity demand in Virginia would double within 10 years, driven mainly by data centres, and grid modelling concludes that building enough infrastructure for unconstrained demand would be very difficult and meeting half of it still difficult. Data centres currently pay their full cost of service, but a typical Dominion residential customer could see generation- and transmission-related costs rise by an estimated $14-$37 per month in real terms by 2040. The state sales-tax exemption saved the industry $928 million in FY23 and is used by about 90% of it; most data centres use about as much water as an average large office building or less, and backup diesel generators make up under 4% of Northern Virginia's nitrogen-oxide emissions. Caveats: Virginia-specific results that rest on consultant forecasts and operator interviews.
magnitude: 74,000 jobs and $9.1 billion annual GDP (mostly construction); unconstrained Virginia electricity demand would double within 10 years

design: Footprint accounting and scenario projection of data-centre electricity use (carbon, water, land)
authors: Aczel, Chamanara, Matin, Farsi, Marwala and Madani
title: Environmental Cost of AI's Energy Use: Carbon, Water and Land Footprints
venue: UNU-INWEH Research Report (doi 10.53328/INR26RMA002), United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health
countries: Global; site cases include Ireland, Mexico (Querétaro) and Uruguay
data: Global data-centre electricity demand (448 TWh in 2025; 945 TWh projected for 2030) converted with electricity-mix carbon, water and land intensities; headline figures as published in UNU's release of the report
findings: The report converts data-centre electricity use into carbon, water and land footprints instead of carbon alone, and compares footprints across the world's 20 largest data-centre hubs. As stated in UNU's press release, data centres used an estimated 448 TWh in 2025 and are projected to use 945 TWh by 2030, almost 3% of projected world electricity use, implying a carbon footprint of 399 million tonnes, 9.3 trillion litres of water (the basic annual domestic needs of 1.3 billion people in Sub-Saharan Africa) and 14,500 km² of land. The footprints do not move together: switching from coal to bioenergy cuts the carbon footprint of electricity by about 70% on average but raises its water footprint more than thirty-fold and its land footprint a hundred-fold. Inference is put at 80-90% of AI energy use, only 32 countries host AI-specialised data centres and about 90% of that capacity is in two countries, with local-pressure cases in Ireland, Querétaro (Mexico) and Uruguay.
magnitude: Data-centre electricity 448 TWh (2025) to 945 TWh (2030), with a 2030 water footprint of 9.3 trillion litres and land footprint of 14,500 km²

design: Descriptive analysis of Bank of Italy firm surveys (about 4,000 firms) with adoption and employment-growth regressions
title: Embracing the digital transition: the adoption of cloud computing and AI by Italian firms
venue: Banca d'Italia, Questioni di Economia e Finanza (Occasional Papers) No. 946, June 2025
data: Bank of Italy INVIND and Sondtel business surveys of about 4,000 industrial and non-financial service firms with at least 20 employees
findings: The paper uses two waves of the Bank of Italy's firm surveys to describe the uptake of cloud computing and AI and to correlate adoption with firm characteristics and employment growth. Cloud use rose from 28% of firms in 2020 to over 50% in early 2024 with minimal variation across sectors, while AI adoption rose from 4% to 13% and tends to be experimental or task-specific. Adoption is strongly associated with firm size, export activity, group affiliation and innovation capacity, and AI uptake is also linked to managerial quality and prior digital investment. Adoption of advanced technologies is positively correlated with realised and expected employment growth, and firms expect generative AI to transform rather than displace jobs. Caveats: correlational, self-reported survey evidence for one advanced economy, with no causal identification.
magnitude: Cloud adoption 28% (2020) to over 50% (early 2024) of Italian firms with 20+ employees; AI adoption 4% to 13%

design: Composite index of national cybersecurity commitments from verified country submissions (194 countries)
title: Global Cybersecurity Index 2024 (5th edition)
countries: 194 countries (193 ITU Member States and the State of Palestine)
data: Country questionnaires verified by ITU, with 172 national focal points, scored on legal, technical, organizational, capacity-development and cooperation pillars
findings: ITU's fifth Global Cybersecurity Index scores 194 countries on five pillars from verified government submissions collected in 2023-24 and, instead of rankings, assigns countries to five tiers. The global average score reached 65.7 out of 100, up 27% since 2020; 46 countries are in Tier 1 (30 would have been under the previous edition) and 105 are in Tiers 3 and 4, with the legal pillar strongest on average and capacity development and technical pillars weakest. Tier 1 includes developing economies such as Bangladesh, Brazil, Ghana, India, Indonesia and Tanzania, yet 89% of high-income countries have a national incident-response team (CIRT) compared with 46% of lower-income countries with an operational one. Caveat: the index measures stated commitments and institutions (inputs), not realised security outcomes, and rests on self-reported submissions.
magnitude: Global average score 65.7/100 (+27% since 2020); 46 countries in Tier 1; national CIRTs in 89% of high-income countries versus 46% of lower-income countries

design: Difference-in-differences (RA, IPW, AIPW) of 300 firms starting overseas data collection vs 1,500 controls
title: The Productivity Effects of Cross-border Data Flows: Evidence from Japanese firm-level data
data: Original surveys of Japanese manufacturing and service firms in 2019 (4,227 responses) and 2021 (6,722) merged with annual productivity measures for 2019-2022; 300 treated 'switcher' firms and 1,500 controls
findings: Survey questions identify firms that began collecting data abroad between 2019 and 2021, and the 300 'switchers' are compared with 1,500 firms that never collected data overseas in a DiD setting with three estimators that give similar results. Starting cross-border data flows is associated with 4-5% higher labour productivity (ATT 0.044-0.047) and 5-6% higher TFP (0.054-0.056) over 2021-22, with larger effects in 2022 (AIPW 0.061 for labour productivity and 0.076 for TFP) and pre-treatment coefficients close to zero. More productive firms are more likely to start transferring data abroad, so self-selection is strong. Caveats: Japanese firms only, treatment is a firm decision rather than a policy change, and the implications for data-localisation rules are inferred rather than tested.
magnitude: Starting cross-border data transfers: labour productivity +4-5% and TFP +5-6% over 2021-22 (ATT 0.044-0.047 and 0.054-0.056)

design: Longitudinal audit of robots.txt and Terms of Service restrictions on 14,000 web domains behind AI training corpora
authors: Longpre, Mahari, Lee, Lund, Oderinwale, Brannon et al.
title: Consent in Crisis: The Rapid Decline of the AI Data Commons
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37 (NeurIPS 2024); arXiv:2407.14933
data: 14,000 web domains underlying the C4, RefinedWeb and Dolma training corpora; robots.txt files and Terms of Service tracked over time
findings: The authors audit the data-use preferences that 14,000 web domains behind major AI training corpora express through robots.txt and Terms of Service, and track them over time. In a single year (2023-2024) the restrictions made roughly 5% or more of all tokens in C4, and 28% or more of its most actively maintained, critical sources, fully restricted from use, and including Terms of Service crawling restrictions, 45% of C4 is now restricted. They also document a proliferation of AI-specific clauses, acute differences in restrictions across AI developers, and inconsistencies between sites' stated Terms of Service and their robots.txt. Caveats: the audit measures stated permissions rather than actual crawling or enforcement.
magnitude: In one year (2023-24), about 5%+ of all C4 tokens and 28%+ of its most actively maintained critical sources became fully restricted; 45% of C4 restricted under Terms of Service

design: Cross-country legal database of digital-trade regulation (121 economies, nine regulatory areas)
authors: Molinuevo, Sadikova, Schwind and Daza Jaller
title: Digital Trade Regulatory Readiness: A Global Database (v2.0)
countries: 121 economies (118 countries and 3 US states), of which 95 developing
period: Regulations in force as of the 2025 database release
data: More than 13,000 datapoints, including over 5,200 regulatory measures in effect, on electronic documents, e-signature and digital ID, paperless trade, online consumer protection, data protection, AI, cybersecurity and cybercrime, cross-border data and intermediary liability
findings: World Bank experts coded laws and regulations on digital trade for 121 economies, of which 95 are developing, with each positive datapoint traceable to a specific legal provision. On cross-border data, broad economy-wide data localisation requirements are rare: no country in the database requires localisation of all personal and non-personal data, but 12 countries require localisation of all personal data (10 local storage, 2 domestic processing, with Kenya having both). The report treats restrictions on cross-border transfers as deviations to be analysed separately from the rest of the regulatory framework and presents the database as a basis for comparative analysis rather than estimating effects. Caveats: it records the law on the books rather than enforcement or economic outcomes, and covers a selected sample of economies.
magnitude: 12 of 121 economies require localisation of all personal data (10 local storage, 2 domestic processing); none requires it for all personal and non-personal data

design: Representative driver surveys plus administrative data on three platforms in India, Indonesia and Kenya
authors: Adhvaryu, Atela, Brailovskaya, Dua, John, Joshi and Royono
title: Platform Work: Evidence from Drivers in India, Indonesia, and Kenya
region: South Asia; East Asia and Pacific; Sub-Saharan Africa
data: Surveys and administrative data from representative samples of drivers on three leading platforms, combining platform earnings with operating-cost data
findings: The authors document the composition, earnings and labour-market trajectories of platform drivers using representative surveys and platform administrative data, and compute earnings net of operating costs in PPP terms. Platform flexibility lets drivers work substantially more than full-time equivalent, producing higher monthly net earnings than low-skill or casual jobs even though hourly net earnings are comparable or lower than those outside options. Drivers who exit in India and Indonesia do so to take better-paying full-time positions, whereas Kenyan drivers often exit involuntarily and return to offline driving with adverse financial consequences. One-third of drivers across countries use platform work to supplement earnings in emergencies or slow periods, which suggests it acts as a financial safety net. Caveat: descriptive evidence from drivers on three platforms, with no causal estimate of the effect of platform entry.
magnitude: One-third of drivers rely on platform work to supplement earnings in emergencies or slow periods; monthly net earnings exceed low-skill alternatives

design: School-level randomised trial of on-the-ground implementation support for Khan Academy in 83 schools
title: How In-School Supervised Ed-Tech Support Produces Massive Learning Gains: A Khan Academy Field Experiment in India
data: 83 residential government middle schools in Uttar Pradesh, all with access to Khan Academy; platform usage and mathematics achievement
findings: All 83 schools had Khan Academy, but randomly selected treatment schools received on-the-ground lab-in-charges whose sole job was to secure reliable connectivity, simplify rostering, protect weekly practice time, supervise in-class use, coordinate content with teachers and monitor progress. The intervention increased platform usage from 7.2 to 47.4 minutes per week. Mathematics achievement rose by almost half a standard deviation over 31 weeks, with gains broad-based across achievement levels and question difficulty. The authors conclude that the binding constraint on effective computer-assisted learning at scale is organisational structure that ensures sustained, productive use, not the technology or content. Caveat: the intervention bundles supervision and implementation support, so the effect of Khan Academy itself is not separately identified, and the setting is residential government schools.
magnitude: Usage rose from 7.2 to 47.4 minutes per week and mathematics achievement by almost 0.5 SD over 31 weeks

design: RCT (7,750 students) of a recommendation system on an edtech app, then regression discontinuity over five months
authors: Agrawal, Athey, Kanodia, Nath and Palikot
title: The Economics of Algorithmic Personalization: Evidence from an Educational Technology Platform
period: RCT followed by five months of deployment
data: Users of Freadom, an English-learning app for Indian children: RCT with 7,750 students, plus user cohorts around an eligibility threshold for the RDD
findings: The authors design, test and scale a collaborative-filtering recommendation system for Freadom, an English-learning app for Indian children. In an RCT with 7,750 students, personalization deployed in a single content section raised engagement by 60% in that section and by 14% app-wide. A regression discontinuity around an eligibility threshold tracks effects over five months of deployment and yields estimates 2.5 times the RCT benchmark, the opposite of the usual 'voltage drop' in scale-ups, so for algorithmic interventions RCT estimates may be lower bounds. Benefits are front-loaded, concentrating in users' first weeks, and the decline in predicted match quality as users exhaust their best content suggests content availability becomes the binding constraint. Caveat: the outcome is engagement with the app, not measured learning.
magnitude: Personalization raised engagement 60% in the treated section and 14% app-wide (RCT, 7,750 students); RDD estimates were 2.5 times the RCT benchmark

design: Country case study of a ransomware crisis and policy response, using government data and published loss estimates
authors: de Salins, Murillo Velazquez and Mora Flores
title: Costa Rica - Case Study: From Cyber Disaster to Digital Resilience
venue: World Bank, Digital and AI Series (report 215451, 30 September 2026), with the Government of Costa Rica
data: Government records and published estimates for the 2022 ransomware incidents (Conti and Hive) affecting nearly 30 public institutions; GDP-loss estimate from Vergara Cobos (2024)
findings: This case study documents the 2022 Conti and Hive ransomware attacks on Costa Rica's Ministry of Finance, Social Security Fund and other bodies, which led to a national emergency, and draws lessons for developing countries. Aggregate economic losses are put at up to 2.4% of GDP (citing Vergara Cobos 2024), direct government recovery costs were about US$31.5 million, and 49 government services were disrupted for between 24 and 204 days. The export sector lost an estimated US$125 million in the first 48 hours and about US$38 million per day thereafter, 2022 customs revenue was US$129 million (0.15% of GDP) below 2021, 158,255 medical appointments including 1,439 surgeries were rescheduled, and about 12,000 teachers' pay was delayed. The government refused ransom demands of US$10 million (later raised to US$20 million), channelled about US$10 million of emergency funding through disaster-management instruments, and grew its National Cybersecurity Directorate from 3 staff in 2022 to 22 in 2025. Caveat: the headline loss figure is a secondary estimate rather than a causal measurement, and the report is co-produced with the government studied.
magnitude: Aggregate losses up to 2.4% of GDP; direct government recovery costs US$31.5 million; 49 services disrupted for 24-204 days

design: Descriptive review of a cyber-event database (162 countries), official fraud statistics and industry surveys
title: The Rise of Cyber Events and Digital Fraud in the Financial Sector
countries: 162 countries in the cyber-event database; fraud trends for selected jurisdictions
data: Database of cyber events across 20 industry sectors in 162 countries, official cyber-enabled and payment-related fraud statistics, industry scam surveys and media reports
findings: The paper reviews public data on cyber events and digital fraud in finance, using a cyber-event database covering 20 sectors in 162 countries plus official fraud statistics and industry surveys. Financial-sector cyber events account for about 10% of cyber events over the past decade and have grown tenfold, concentrated in banking and securities, while cyber-enabled fraud has nearly tripled to around 2.5 million cases in 2022 and remains underestimated because of underreporting. Credit transfers and credit cards dominate scam payments, with rising crypto-related fraud; industry studies cited by the paper put global scam losses near US$1 trillion in 2024 and, for some developing countries, at 2.5%-4.2% of GDP, while advanced economies incur higher individual losses. Caveats: these are descriptive trends from heterogeneous, partly industry-sourced data, reporting is uneven across jurisdictions (notably Africa and the Middle East), and the loss estimates are not causal.
magnitude: Financial-sector cyber events up tenfold and cyber-enabled fraud nearly tripled in a decade; industry estimates of scam losses of 2.5%-4.2% of GDP in some developing countries

design: Randomised field experiment (700+ users): three weeks without automatic media downloads on WhatsApp
title: Misinformation Beyond Traditional Feeds: Evidence from a WhatsApp Deactivation Experiment in Brazil
period: Three weeks before Brazil's 2022 presidential election; survey a few days after…
data: More than 700 WhatsApp users; post-election survey measuring exposure to and belief in false rumours, polarization and subjective well-being
findings: Participants were randomly assigned to switch off WhatsApp's automatic download of images, video and audio during the weeks before Brazil's 2022 presidential election, a multimedia 'deactivation' that mirrors Facebook deactivation experiments for a messaging app where misinformation circulates as forwarded media. The intervention reduced recall of widely circulating false rumours by 0.38 SD, with a smaller reduction in recall of true headlines. It produced no significant change in belief accuracy, political polarization or well-being, consistent with minimal-effects theories of mass media. Effects on accuracy differ by exposure: heavy consumers of political content on WhatsApp improved at identifying false rumours, while those who rarely received political news became significantly worse. Caveats: a relatively small sample, short-run outcomes measured a few days after the election, and self-reported measures.
magnitude: Multimedia deactivation cut recall of false rumours by 0.38 SD; no significant effect on belief accuracy, polarization or well-being

design: Firm-level regressions with simultaneous-equation (exclusion-restriction) estimates, Kenya 2016 ICT survey
title: Cyberattack, cyber risk mitigation capabilities, and firm productivity in Kenya
data: Kenya 2016 Enterprise ICT Survey (stratified random sample; 3,530 of 4,000 targeted firms responded); estimation samples of about 1,600-2,300 firms
findings: The authors regress firm labour productivity (turnover per employee) on whether a firm suffered a virus attack or online crime, then add simultaneous-equation estimates that use sector- and region-level breach prevalence as exclusion restrictions. In the baseline estimates a virus attack is associated with about 35% lower labour productivity (33% for SMEs, 46% for large firms) and online crime with 27% lower productivity (26% for SMEs, not significant for large firms). The simultaneous-equation coefficients are much larger (about -2.9 log points for virus attacks), so magnitudes are sensitive to specification. Upskilling mitigates the damage, especially for SMEs, while IT policy and IT security capabilities raise productivity but do not offset the breach effect. Caveats: cross-sectional 2016 survey data from one country, self-reported incidents and strong exclusion restrictions.
magnitude: Virus attack associated with about 35% lower labour productivity (33% SMEs, 46% large firms); online crime with 27% lower (26% SMEs)

design: Difference-in-differences around the EU DMA browser choice-screen mandate (Firefox on iOS and Android)
authors: Akesson, Amlani, Cepeda Suarez, Chissell, Hunt, Luca and Petrie
title: Active Choice Interventions at Scale: Browser Defaults under the Digital Markets Act
period: First 15+ months after the choice-screen mandate
data: Firefox usage on iOS and Android and browser market-share data
findings: The study uses difference-in-differences around the DMA choice-screen mandate, which requires gatekeepers to prompt users to choose a default browser, to test whether active choice mitigates preset-default effects. From month 15 onward, Firefox usage was 91% higher on iOS and 13% higher on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual. The platform gap is consistent with rollout differences, since iOS reached existing users while Android mainly reached new devices. Market-share data corroborate movement away from defaults, but the gains on iOS were concentrated in Chrome rather than smaller browsers, with Safari declining on iOS and Chrome declining on Android.
magnitude: From month 15, Firefox usage was 91% higher on iOS and 13% higher on Android than the no-mandate counterfactual

design: Difference-in-differences of Android apps in EU5 vs US-only apps around the May 2018 GDPR rollout
title: The GDPR and SDK Usage In Android Mobile Apps
countries: European Union (five major European countries) and United States
data: Android app data on Software Development Kits (SDKs) used per app, with monthly-active-user weights to measure average user exposure
findings: The authors compare the number of non-Google SDKs per Android app in the EU5 with US-only apps before and after the GDPR took effect in May 2018. The count of non-Google SDKs fell by 3.6% in EU5-only apps and by 8.7% in apps multihoming the US and EU5, mostly among lower-ranked apps. Weighting by monthly active users, average user exposure to SDKs did not fall significantly in EU5-only or multihoming apps relative to US-only apps. The authors conclude that the GDPR had only limited effects on the SDK layer and did not materially reduce user exposure to the most prevalent SDK ecosystems.
magnitude: Non-Google SDKs per app fell 3.6% (EU5-only apps) and 8.7% (apps in both US and EU5) after the GDPR; no significant fall in user-weighted SDK exposure

design: Correlational comparisons and country fixed-effects panel regressions (14 countries, 2010-2022, 182 country-years), plus a model-based simulation of a sharing mandate; commissioned by a tower company
authors: Raúl Katz, Fernando Callorda and Ramiro Valencia (Telecom Advisory Services)
title: The Independent Tower Industry as a Key Enabler of the Development of African Telecommunications
venue: Telecom Advisory Services white paper commissioned by SBA Communications (March 2024)
countries: Angola, DR Congo, Egypt, Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Morocco, Mozambique, Nigeria, Rwanda, South Africa, Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia
data: GSMA Intelligence coverage, subscriber and market-structure data; TowerXchange tower counts and ownership; ITU ICT Regulatory Tracker (sharing mandates) and ICT price baskets; Ookla speeds; interviews with regulators
findings: Commissioned by SBA Communications, a tower company; the evidence is correlational and model-based rather than causally identified. Countries where independent tower companies own more than 40% of towers and tower density exceeds 150 per million people (Kenya, South Africa, Nigeria, Ghana, Zambia) have 8.09 percentage points higher 4G coverage (89.69% vs. 81.59%), 35% faster mobile broadband, 130% higher capital spending per capita (US$8.82 vs. US$3.83), mobile broadband prices of 1.99% rather than 4.62% of monthly GNI per capita, and 7.42 percentage points higher adoption. In country fixed-effects regressions, a 10% increase in independent towers is associated with 5.95% higher 4G coverage, 3.29% higher broadband adoption, 5.07% faster download speeds, a 1.38% lower HHI and a 7.82% improvement in affordability. Chaining a regression on the ITU sharing-mandate indicator with published elasticities, the authors simulate that mandating infrastructure sharing in an average African country would raise unique mobile broadband users by 14.63% and GDP per capita by 4.82% over eight years (0.59% a year). Recommended reforms: a legal framework recognizing passive infrastructure providers, specific tower regulation, no service concession for tower companies, harmonized central and municipal rules, and fast permits.
magnitude: Leaders in independent tower ownership have 8.09 percentage points higher 4G coverage (correlational); a simulated sharing mandate raises unique mobile broadband users by 14.63% and GDP per capita by 4.82% over eight years

design: Calibrated task-based growth-accounting projection (Acemoglu 2024 framework: GDP share of tasks affected x labor cost savings) with an adoption path extrapolated from the diffusion of PCs, the internet, smartphones and cloud computing
authors: Penn Wharton Budget Model (Alexander Arnon; directed by Kent Smetters)
title: The Projected Impact of Generative AI on Future Productivity Growth
venue: Penn Wharton Budget Model, University of Pennsylvania (policy brief, 8 September 2025)
data: Eloundou et al. (2024) task-automation categories applied to 784 detailed SOC occupations; BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics employment and annual wages (2021-2024); Real-Time Population Survey 2024 (26.4% of workers used generative AI at work, 33.7% of adults outside work); historical adoption series for PCs, the internet, smartphones and cloud computing (CPS supplements, Annual Business Survey, Pew,…
findings: A calibrated projection rather than an estimate of realized effects. Following Acemoglu's task-based framework, it combines the share of GDP in tasks affected by generative AI with labor cost savings, scaled by an adoption path built from the diffusion of PCs, the internet, smartphones and cloud computing. About 40% of current labor income is exposed, 23% of exposed tasks are eventually automated, and cost savings rise from about 25% to 40%. Productivity and GDP levels end 1.5% higher by 2035, nearly 3% higher by 2055 and 3.7% higher by 2075 than without AI. The boost to annual TFP growth peaks at about 0.2 percentage points in 2032 and fades to a permanent lift of just under 0.04 points, so AI raises the level of activity but not its long-run growth rate. Exposure is highest in office and administrative support (75.5% of tasks) and peaks around the 80th-90th earnings percentiles. The projection omits new products and tasks and rests on limited early adoption data.
magnitude: Productivity and GDP levels +1.5% by 2035, nearly +3% by 2055 and +3.7% by 2075 relative to a no-AI path; the annual TFP-growth boost peaks at about 0.2 pp in 2032 and fades to a permanent lift of under 0.04 pp

design: Calibrated task-based macroeconomic scenario model (AI automation and augmentation of cognitive tasks, capital supply schedule, search-and-matching unemployment, ideas channel) run for three illustrative scenarios and for scenarios implied…
authors: Anton Korinek, Charles I. Jones, Szymon Sacher, Tess Cotter and Peter McCrory
title: Economic Scenarios for Transformative AI
venue: The Anthropic Institute Working Paper 2026-02 (Econ Scenario Explorer: anthropic.com/institute/econ-scenarios)
period: 2026-2030 (scenario horizon, anchored in mid-2026 with 2024 as base period);…
data: US Current Population Survey (2025 annual averages; IPUMS-CPS 2010-19 labor flows), JOLTS, national-accounts R&D share and standard macro parameters; AI exposure and use anchors from observed Claude usage (Massenkoff and McCrory 2026: affected-task share 0.14 in mid-2026) and the Census Bureau Business Trends and Outlook Survey (18% of firms using AI in late 2025); Morning Consult online survey of 10,980 US adults…
findings: Scenarios, not predictions: a calibrated task-based model in which AI automates or augments a growing share of cognitive work (62.4% of US employment) and displaced workers search for new jobs under frictions. Relative to a no-AI path, US GDP in 2030 is 1.6% higher in a modest scenario, 8.3% in a substantial one and 32.4% in an extreme one. Wages in cognitive occupations change by +0.4%, -0.3% and -11.5% while other wages rise 1.1%, 5.9% and 33.6%; cognitive-worker unemployment reaches 2.9%, 4.5% and 17.9%, and the labor share falls from 60% to 59.4%, 56.1% and 45.2%. In the extreme scenario capital income is 81.4% above the no-AI path while total labor income is roughly unchanged, and holding cognitive workers' income at its no-AI level would take transfers of about 9% of GDP. Run through the model, a survey of US adults implies GDP 8.6% above the no-AI path. The model omits policy responses, business cycles, financial disruption and robotics, and results are sensitive to how readily capital supply and cognitive wages adjust.
magnitude: US GDP in 2030 relative to a no-AI path: +1.6% (modest), +8.3% (substantial), +32.4% (extreme scenario); in the extreme scenario the labor share falls from 60% to 45.2% and cognitive-worker unemployment reaches 17.9%

title: Generative AI: Catalyst for Growth or Harbinger of Premature De-Professionalization?
venue: The World Economy 49(8): 1626-1654 (2026); earlier version World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 10915
countries: None (theoretical model; stylized facts from the United States, China and cross-country sectoral data)
data: No new micro data: parameters from the literature (elasticity of substitution 0.5; sectoral income elasticities 0.5, 1.4, 1.6 and 1.8; labor-productivity growth 8%, 4%, 2% and 1% a year in agriculture, manufacturing, high-skill and low-skill services) and stylized facts from the GGDC 10-Sector Database, US and China industry earnings (2022), Trade in Value Added data on IT-input and export intensity (2020), US…
findings: A four-sector growth model with non-homothetic preferences (agriculture, manufacturing, high-skill tradable services, low-skill services), simulated over 100 years: model-based scenarios, not causal estimates. If AI raises productivity growth only in high-skill services (by 50%), real-income growth rises by just 0.046 percentage points at first and real income ends 2.4% above the no-AI path after 100 years; gains in all four sectors lift it 19%, and 28% when AI also creates new products that shift demand toward skill-intensive services. Concentrated gains make the employment share of high-skill services peak earlier and lower, shifting jobs toward low-skill services ('premature de-professionalization'). In a small open economy, delayed adoption while AI lowers world prices of high-skill services can erode comparative advantage and leave a commodity exporter's jobs concentrated in agriculture and low-skill services. High-skill services employ 13%-20% of the workforce in high-income countries but 0%-4% in lower-middle- and low-income countries.
magnitude: Working-paper simulations: real income after 100 years is 2.4% higher than without AI if AI lifts only high-skill-services productivity growth (initial growth boost 0.046 pp), 19% higher if all four sectors gain, 28% higher if AI also shifts demand toward new products

title: Navigating the Age of AI: Implications for Poland's Economy (What AI means for Growth, Firms and Jobs)
venue: World Bank Group report (Washington, DC), 2026; MANAGE-AI model documented in a separate 'Appendix Book'
period: 2025-2035 (CGE scenario projections versus baseline); readiness diagnostics…
data: MANAGE-AI CGE model with the baseline calibrated to Poland's macro-fiscal indicators, population growth and employment rate to 2025 (AI adoption frozen at 2025 levels), AI entering as an intermediate service and as intangible capital, occupation-level substitution elasticities calibrated to ILO generative-AI exposure scores (Gmyrek et al. 2025) and sector-specific logistic diffusion curves calibrated to Eurostat…
findings: Computable general equilibrium scenarios from a new World Bank model (MANAGE-AI), measured against a baseline in which AI adoption stays at 2025 levels. With the share of Polish firms using AI rising from 8.4% to close to 45% by 2035, real GDP ends 1.3% to 12.1% above baseline: 10.9% in a policy-consistent scenario with high labor mobility and front-loaded adoption, and 5.5% from technology alone, while delaying adoption to the early 2030s cuts the 2035 gain to about 5.2%-6.6%. Net employment stays close to baseline when labor is mobile (about 3,000 jobs lower) but is about 341,000 lower when mobility is low; employment falls 24.8% in finance and rises 18.7% in construction. The gains accrue almost entirely to capital: capital returns rise 15.1 percentage points above baseline while total labor income is flat. Only 8% of Polish firms use AI, against an EU average of 17%.
magnitude: Real GDP 1.3% to 12.1% above the no-further-adoption baseline by 2035 (+10.9% in the policy-consistent scenario with high labor mobility)

venue: SSRN working paper (2025); also World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11263
data: 285 million Lightcast online job postings (1 January 2018 to 30 June 2025; about 60% of JOLTS vacancies) aggregated to about 6.75 million state x industry (NAICS 2-digit) x occupation (ISCO-08 4-digit) x quarter cells including zeros; GenAI exposure from Gmyrek, Berg and Bescond (2023); AI-substitution score = inverse of the Pizzinelli et al. (2023) AI-complementarity index; outcome is the inverse hyperbolic sine of…
findings: Difference-in-differences and event study around ChatGPT's release (November 2022), comparing US job postings for occupations with above- versus below-median AI-substitution scores within the same generative-AI exposure decile; pre-trend tests and 400 placebo assignments support the design. Postings in more substitutable occupations fell 12% on average relative to less substitutable ones, widening from 6% in the first year to 14% in the second and 18% in the third. Declines are larger for entry-level and lower-credential postings (18% for postings requiring no advanced degree, 20% for those requiring no extensive experience) and in administrative support (40%) and professional services (30%), while finance, transportation and public administration show no significant decline. Postings measure labor demand, not employment or wages, and the estimate is a relative effect between occupation groups, not the aggregate effect of generative AI.
magnitude: Postings for above-median AI-substitution occupations fell 12% on average relative to below-median occupations after ChatGPT (6% in year 1, 14% in year 2, 18% in year 3), conditional on GenAI exposure (PRWP 11263 version)

title: Who Takes the Hit? The Uneven Impacts of Generative AI on Labor Demand Across Countries
venue: SSRN working paper (2026); background paper for the World Development Report 2026
countries: 84 countries: 42 high-income (e.g. United States, United Kingdom, France, Germany, Poland) and 42 middle- and low-income (e.g. Mexico, Colombia, India,…
data: 555 million Lightcast online job postings in 84 countries aggregated to about 5.1 million country x industry (20) x occupation (about 400 ISCO-08 4-digit) x quarter cells; employment-share weights from ILOSTAT labor force surveys with equal weight per country; country moderators: ChatGPT users per internet user, internet use, smartphone ownership, years of schooling, English proficiency, net exports of IT and…
findings: Difference-in-differences and event studies (PPML) around ChatGPT's release across 84 countries, comparing job postings for occupations above versus below the median in AI-substitution vulnerability, controlling for generative-AI exposure and monetary-policy sensitivity. Postings in more vulnerable occupations fell 5.5% overall, but effects differ sharply by income: 5.8% on average in high-income countries, widening from 3.6% in the first year to 8.9% in the third, versus 1.5% and statistically insignificant in middle- and low-income countries. Cross-country associations (not causally identified) show larger displacement where income and generative-AI uptake are higher. With a continuous measure, the most- versus least-substitutable occupations show a 14% decline in high-income countries and a significant 5.2% decline elsewhere, suggesting displacement has begun to reach the most exposed jobs in poorer countries too. Postings cover the formal, mostly white-collar segment of labor markets.
magnitude: High-income countries: postings for above-median AI-substitution-vulnerability occupations fell 5.8% on average relative to less substitutable occupations (3.6% in year 1 to 8.9% in year 3); middle- and low-income countries: 1.5%, statistically insignificant
